Work on gene therapy ground to a halt. “We were all very much aware of what happened,” Doudna recalled. “That made the whole field of gene therapy go away, mostly, for at least a decade. Even the term gene therapy became kind of a black label. You didn’t want that in your grants. You didn’t want to say, ‘I’m working on gene therapy.’ It sounded terrible

item.title: 2025 Yearly Review
item.description: “!!” I want to start with an exclamation. This year has been one of that year that I had been waiting for decades to happen to me. From the year 2023, it finally crossed the Tipping Point and started getting crazier. There were parts about my identity that I really got to explore, go deep into, and really uncover myself piece by piece. Like going petal by petal in a lotus flower. 🪷
item.content:
“!!” I want to start with an exclamation. This year has been one of that year that I had been waiting for decades to happen to me. From the year 2023, it finally crossed the Tipping Point and started getting crazier. There were parts about my identity that I really got to explore, go deep into, and really uncover myself piece by piece. Like going petal by petal in a lotus flower. 🪷

In the year 2024, I got the first clear glimpse. In the year 2025, I cleared my doubts, and learned about my path. In the year 2026, the path will be done, and I feel that a new journey is already waiting for me. I don’t know how/what it will be, but it is surely going to demand more energy and vigor from my part.

In my own words, I wrote in my yearly review for 2024: “2023 was speeding with insights. Its been a slow year compared to 2023 because everything was about calming down.” That’s why 2025 happened, going supersonic. The questions I said that will get answered in 2024’s review got answered as well.

I have started using emacs more with almost exact setup on my phone as well. Really tops Obsidian, Notion or any of that stuff because its the same workflow that I have on my mac as well. Its so much elegant now.

These are my notes in org roam. It looks really beautiful and getting more and more connected each year. I wait for the day when I can throw it all on a AR setup and traverse through nodes like planets and galaxies in games.

Finally, I found who I was in relation to this world. After some time, no place was distant. I was at home almost all the time wherever I was. It got to the point when I knew that I wasn’t the only witness to my life.

It all started with a firm conviction. A plan that I had for a long long time; one that my being had been waiting for, unaware without an idea of what would be coming. Its as if I projected one of my very first and favorite novel onto my life: “The Alchemist.” I even listened to that book in Nepali saying “Kimiyagar”. Just like him, I didn’t know why but an unknown force pulled me towards an unknown place. I felt stupid at times to be walking in the dark, but in the end, that journey was meant to be mine; just like Santiago’s journey was meant to be his and his only. Yes, he would have been deemed a fool if the story didn’t end in riches, but who is keeping the tabs anyway?

I left my home in search of answers that I’d been seeking. I knew I had to walk this path alone, and it became so. This was the very first moment of my life where I actually left “home”. The first 10 minutes of it, I can almost taste all of it even today. That journey was a lot. I started with my expectations of where I would go, but let myself be guided freely. I ended up in places I hadn’t even planned to go. A lot of unknowns, yet with a sense of familiarity in conviction. Every place started like a stranger that I wanted to run away from asap, but ended up knowing that they’ve been my besties all along. They made me cry as well as cried on my shoulder like family.

I was looking for specific something. In that process I came to know, the best of things are not meant to be looked for. The best of things find you. You don’t find them. This is a very contradictory thing to say, yet its one of the most truthful things I can tell you. Think of it like this: Clear your pond of all the dirt that you have accumulated over the years. Nature will come to adorn your pond: birds, fishes etc. But if you just justify your laziness and your pond gets dirty, inaction will kill all the vibes. So, non-action is the key, not inaction. And there is a night and day of a difference between these two.

I saw both good and worse parts of humanity in same place. I saw truthful and liars in same robes. I saw power and surrender in same place. I felt fear and courage in same place. I saw death and beauty in same place. I heard the hardest of cries and playful laughter in the same place. I was silent and beaming with answers in same place. The duality of it, almost as if everything was a stage, set for my eyes to understand reality in its full glory. And it was just the start of 2025.

I travelled far and wide. I cried my eyes out in pain. I laughed with all my heart. I cried my eyes out in peace. I saw it all, that too in a very short time span. Literally made me binge it all in one go.

This was what I wrote in my diary when I returned: “When I truly seek, I have always been found. Thanks to everyone for loving me like its favorite child and treating me this way. I will do everything I can to give as much as I can. I know my actions for my personal seeking has been done. Those will be minor part of a major life force. I will be the torch bearer of life itself. The essence. The fragrance. I will make sure that I smell like life itself every day.”

The convictions that found me led me to finding so much more. Overflowing with insights, I couldn’t even keep track of things. Answers coming at supersonic speed. There were years where I struggled to even get one. This was year where I got answers to those questions that I didn’t know I had deep longing for.

I’d chosen Purple 🟣 for 2025, and that was not a coincidence. That was a conviction that could have only come from within. And life truly showed me that color. Now, I know what I needed to know. There are things that I know that I don’t know, and its okay. There are things that I don’t know that I don’t know, and that’s okay too.

So much convoluted talk. Basically, the summary is I finally got answers that I’ve been searching for all my life. Exactly like a lost child finds home. For 2026, there is no color, no shape, no form, no name. Just presence speaking for itself. One intention speaking: “Be.” “Be.” Not A, not C. Just “Be.” 🫠

And I realized one major problem with my concepts that I had last year. The drawing that I had on my last year review about what creation/enlightenment failed to take into account the infinite nature of being. “The infinity”. There is no circle that binds either creation or enlightened beings. There is no Yin and Yang because its empty and boundless at the same time. Just like you cannot count the moments you lived even if you tried to break it down. You will end up going in an infinite regress on what counts as a moment. Just like Cantor showed us uncountable infinities with whole numbers.

The usual part of my yearly reviews I do is talking about what I read this year. I didn’t watch much of movies/series this year. Nothing of note there. :

Completed this year

  • The Beginning of Infinity ( Started with The Beginning of Infinity. Ended with it as well. Its truly the beginning of Infinity for me starting next year. A great read on optimism, and our ability as humans to create better future. )
  • Category Theory for Programmers by Bartosz ( Had to re-read and understand the details I had been studying for quite some time. )
  • The Little Prince ( Such a beautiful read. “It is only with the heart that one can see rightly; what is essential is invisible to the eye.” I think adults should read this every year so that you retain that innocence, and don’t turn into a boring adult. )
  • How to succeed at Mrbeast Production ( Short read, good enough to understand few ideas on how anything goes viral. )
  • At the eleventh hour ( Biography of Swami Rama, wanted to know this person a little more )
  • High Agency Blog ( Would definitely recommend this one as well. Longer than a usual blog but truly worth it.)
  • Category Theory Illustrated ( Available as a blog or book. Basic yet real good intro to get the ideas through. Helped me so much to clarify what I’d already studied. )
  • Laghu Parashari ( Started on Vedic Jyotish basics. Couldn’t find time to go deep into that one area. )

Skimmed through

  • A Million Thoughts: Learn all about meditation from a himalayan mystic after his 15000 hours of intense practice by Om Swami ( Found him through reels. He’s knowledgeable, and has done a lot of spiritual Sadhana. Just picked this book up to see if there was specific something that I was trying to understand. )
  • The Pathless Path: Imagining a New Story for Work and Life by Paul Millerd ( Really good book if you still haven’t understood work life balance and being in general. I’d discovered same principles personally, and this is how I would have most likely structured too. So, definitely would recommend this. )
  • Introspect by visakanv ( Wanted to learn his perspective but was raw-dogging my own reality. So, didn’t go much further. )
  • Do Nothing ( I wanted to see it from a different person’s perspective. Literally felt redundant to me personally, so skimmed fast. )

Still In Progress

  • Mahabharat by Ved Vyas ( Raw dogging both Sanskrit and Hindi directly from Gita Press. Still in Adi Parva. )
  • I am That by Nisargadatta Maharaj ( Restarted again towards the end of this year. Finally understood the title. I didn’t have the intention to just mark it as complete last year. Same now. Just a few chapters over the span of the year. Has made me laugh more than anything else this year. )
  • Lessons on Vedic Astrology
  • Brihat Parashara Hora Shastra ( Covered Jyotish basics. Haven’t found time to dig deeper. I like anything that has liberation as it’s prime goal. I was quite surprised when I found out that the intention of this field was Liberation too. I just had different views because of how people propagated its knowledge. )
  • Adult Piano Adventures ( Practicing it slow but its hard to do so when you are moving constantly between places. )
  • Godel Escher Bach ( Opened a few pages but didn’t go through much this year. )
  • The Brothers Karamazov ( Haven’t found time to really dig on fiction this year because I feel like I need to get engulfed by it, and haven’t had much time that way. Want to enjoy fiction like fine wine. )

Re-read this year

  • The Joy of Abstraction by Eugenia Cheng ( Summarized, re-read in detail to get the concepts clear this time )
  • The Zen and Art of Motorcycle Maintenance ( Felt much better when I revised my highlights as if philosophies were written first and covered with more for easy digestion. )

Notes

  • This year was not that as huge in terms of books because I was reading something else: people and their stories. I sat together with my grandfathers over fire listening and recording their stories. I learned about my ancestors, their history, their migration stories and so on. Learned that we can’t even escape our ancestry. As I travelled more, I got to listen to a lot more stories.
  • I sat together with spiritual people over fire listening to their stories. I listened, and they told me so much more than what I was asking for. They felt home with me like I felt home with them. For the first time, I felt seen in that world.
  • I finally understood how a truly lived life is full of contradictions. Just like Love. One who is living from experience, and not memories.
  • I got to live with my parents for almost 8 months without interruption, first time after turning into an adult. Literally had to treat them like children because they were automatic, yet innocent. I brought their scars to the surface, made them cry a gazillion times; and now they love me more than they used to. I am a warm menace, that’s all. LOL. I taught them just like I was teaching myself. I showed them my world, what matters to me and why. They still aren’t fully convinced, but they are already off to a great start.
  • Built app to help people fight their fear and recognize themselves. Wrote a manifesto. (https://maitreyatools.com) 🐦‍🔥
  • Participated in a national protest that too from the front. First time for everything I guess. Wrote another manifesto. No stone pelting or violence, but exactly opposite of that. Saw so much more than what I was expecting. That’s life. Felt all kind of emotions at the same time. Rightly so. I didn’t want to get involved so soon into Politics, but when time calls for it, I couldn’t let it pass. I did my part. Lets see what more I will do over time. I think there is a lot to come but lets stop at that for now.
  • I finally found the simplicity on the other side of complexity that I had been resolving for a decade personally.
  • This year is the oldest I’ll ever be. I’ll start getting younger and younger, starting this year. The Divine told me this. 🤭

Finally, I’ll recognize that what’s represented by that name I gave myself years ago subconsciously which is at the top of this blog too. “There are no accidents, Shifu”, said Oogway too.

item.content:
Quotes

Quotes on being good CEO

CEO

Basically, CEOs have five essential choices for deploying capital—investing in existing operations, acquiring other businesses, issuing dividends, paying down debt, or repurchasing stock—and three alternatives for raising it—tapping internal cash flow, issuing debt, or raising equity.

Role of a CEO that most people don’t think is role of a CEO. Everyone thinks its just about operations.

Singleton focused Teledyne’s capital on selective acquisitions and a series of large share repurchases. He was restrained in issuing shares, made frequent use of debt, and did not pay a dividend until the late 1980s. In contrast, the other conglomerates pursued a mirror-image allocation strategy—actively issuing shares to buy companies, paying dividends, avoiding share repurchases, and generally using less debt. In short, they deployed a different set.

Call it Singletonville, a very select group of men and women who understood, among other things, that:

  • Capital allocation is a CEO’s most important job.
  • What counts in the long run is the increase in per share value, not overall growth or size.
  • Cash flow, not reported earnings, is what determines longterm value.
  • Decentralized organizations release entrepreneurial energy and keep both costs and “rancor” down.
  • Independent thinking is essential to long-term success, and interactions with outside advisers (Wall Street, the press, etc.) can be distracting and time-consuming.
  • Sometimes the best investment opportunity is your own stock.
  • With acquisitions, patience is a virtue, as is occasional boldness.

Isaiah Berlin, in a famous essay about Leo Tolstoy, introduced the instructive contrast between the “fox,” who knows many things, and the “hedgehog,” who knows one thing but knows it very well. Most CEOs are hedgehogs—they grow up in an industry and by the time they are tapped for the top role, have come to know it thoroughly. There are many positive attributes associated with hedgehogness, including expertise, specialization, and focus. Foxes, however, also have many attractive qualities, including an ability to make connections across fields and to innovate, and the CEOs in this book were definite foxes. They had familiarity with other companies and industries and disciplines, and this ranginess translated into new perspectives, which in turn helped them to develop new approaches that eventually translated into exceptional results.

Warren Buffett looked back on his first twenty-five years as a CEO and concluded that the most important and surprising lesson from his career to date was the discovery of a mysterious force, the corporate equivalent of teenage peer pressure, that impelled CEOs to imitate the actions of their peers. He dubbed this powerful force the institutional imperative and noted that it was nearly ubiquitous, warning that effective CEOs needed to find some way to tune it out.

For Henry Singleton in the 1970s and 1980s, it was stock buybacks; for John Malone, it was the relentless pursuit of cable subscribers; for Bill Anders, it was divesting noncore businesses; for Warren Buffett, it was the generation and deployment of insurance float.

At the core of their shared worldview was the belief that the primary goal for any CEO was to optimize long-term value per share, not organizational growth.

Summary

CEOs need to be understanding their role about making returns to their shareholders. Understanding the key piece: capital allocation is the key responsibility of a CEO.

Kindle highlights (2020)

  • loc 97 - You really only need to know three things to evaluate a CEO’s greatness: the compound annual return to shareholders during his or her tenure and the return over the same period for peer companies and for the broader market (usually measured by the S&P 500).

  • loc 125 - He was known as “the Sphinx” for his reluctance to speak with either analysts or journalists, and he never once appeared on the cover of Fortune magazine.

  • loc 125 - He was known as “the Sphinx” for his reluctance to speak with either analysts or journalists, and he never once appeared

  • loc 136 - His success did not stem from Teledyne’s owning any unique, rapidly growing businesses. Rather, much of what distinguished Singleton from his peers lay in his mastery of the critical but somewhat mysterious field of capital allocation—the process of deciding how to deploy the firm’s resources to earn the best possible return for shareholders

  • loc 140 - CEOs need to do two things well to be successful: run their operations efficiently and deploy the cash generated by those operations.

  • loc 143 - Basically, CEOs have five essential choices for deploying capital—investing in existing operations, acquiring other businesses, issuing dividends, paying down debt, or repurchasing stock—and three alternatives for raising it—tapping internal cash flow, issuing debt, or raising equity. Think

  • loc 152 - The heads of many companies are not skilled in capital allocation. Their inadequacy is not surprising. Most bosses rise to the top because they have excelled in an area such as marketing, production, engineering, administration, or sometimes, institutional politics. Once they become CEOs, they now must make capital allocation decisions, a critical job that they may have never tackled and that is not easily mastered. To stretch the point, it’s as if the final step for a highly talented musician was not to perform at Carnegie Hall, but instead, to be named Chairman of the Federal Reserve.1

  • loc 167 - Specifically, he believed in an extreme form of organizational decentralization with a wafer-thin corporate staff at headquarters and operational responsibility and authority concentrated in the general managers of the business units.

  • loc 183 - I think you will find that a disproportionate number of successful coin-flippers in the investment world came from a very small intellectual village that could be called Graham-and-Doddsville.

  • loc 192 - Like Singleton, they developed unique, markedly different approaches to their businesses, typically drawing much comment and questioning from peers and the business press. Even more interestingly, although they developed these principles independently, it turned out they were iconoclastic in virtually identical ways

  • loc 260 - The residents of Singletonville, however, represent a refreshing rejoinder to this stereotype. All were first-time CEOs, most with very little prior management experience. Not one came to the job from a high-profile position, and all but one were new to their industries and companies. Only two had MBAs.

  • loc 312 - At bottom, these CEOs thought more like investors than managers.

  • loc 314 - When their stock was cheap, they bought it (often in large quantities), and when it was expensive, they used it to buy other companies or to raise inexpensive capital to fund future growth.

  • loc 341 - This fox-like outsider’s perspective helped these executives develop differentiated approaches, and it informed their entire management philosophy. As a group, they were deeply independent, generally avoiding communication with Wall Street, disdaining the use of advisers, and preferring decentralized organizational structures that self-selected for other independent thinkers.

  • loc 371 - And yet virtually all of these CEOs shrank their share bases significantly through repurchases. Most also shrank their operations through asset sales or spin-offs, and they were not shy about selling (or closing) underperforming divisions.

  • loc 385 - Tom Murphy and Dan Burke were probably the greatest two-person combination in management that the world has ever seen or maybe ever will see. —Warren Buffett

  • loc 396 - CBS spent much of the 1960s and 1970s taking the enormous cash flow generated by its network and broadcast operations and funding an aggressive acquisition program that led it into entirely new fields, including the purchase of a toy business and the New York Yankees baseball team.

  • loc 404 - In contrast, Murphy’s goal was to make his company more valuable. As he said to me, “The goal is not to have the longest train, but to arrive at the station first using the least fuel.”

  • loc 408 - Murphy acquired more radio and TV stations, operated them superbly well, regularly repurchased his shares, and eventually acquired CBS’s rival broadcast network ABC. The relative results speak for themselves.

  • loc 410 - Paley’s QE2 was deceptively simple: focus on industries with attractive economic characteristics, selectively use leverage to buy occasional large properties, improve operations, pay down debt, and repeat.

  • loc 417 - In a typical roll-up, a company acquires a series of businesses, attempts to improve operations, and then keeps acquiring, benefiting over time from scale advantages and best management practices.

item.title: Salt Fat Acid Heat
item.description:
One sentence summary

  • Salt enhances flavor
  • Fat amplifies flavor and makes appealing textures possible
  • Acid brightens and balances
  • Heat determines the texture of food.

Human Body

  • Our taste buds can perceive five tastes : saltiness, sourness, bitterness, sweetness, and umami, or savoriness.
  • Flavor lies at the intersection of taste, aroma, and sensory elements including texture, sound, appearance, and temperature. Since aroma is a crucial element of flavor, the more aromas you perceive, the more vibrant your eating experience will be. This is why you take less pleasure in eating while you’re congested or have a cold.

Salt

  • A smaller amount of salt applied while cooking will often do more to improve flavor than a larger amount added at the table.
  • Use more salt while boiling vegetables because most of it will go down the drain.
  • Used properly, salt minimizes bitterness, balances out sweetness, and enhances aromas, heightening our experience of eating.
  • Example: Imagine taking a bite of a rich espresso brownie sprinkled with flaky sea salt. Besides providing the delightful experience of its delicate flakes crunching on the tongue, the salt minimizes the espresso’s bitterness, intensifies the flavor of the chocolate, and offers a welcome savory contrast to the sugar’s sweetness.
  • This is one of the few times I’ll insist on anything in this book: if you’ve only got table salt at home, go get yourself some kosher or sea salt right away.
  • Because solar salts are harvested using low-yield, labor-intensive methods, they tend to be more expensive than refined sea salts. Most of what you’re paying for when you buy these salts is their delightful texture, so use them in ways that allow them to stand out. It’s a waste to season pasta water with fleur de sel or make tomato sauce with Maldon salt. Instead, sprinkle these salts atop delicate garden lettuces, rich caramel sauces, and chocolate chip cookies as they go into the oven so you can enjoy the way they crunch in your mouth.
  • Keep two kinds of salt on hand: an inexpensive one such as bulk-bin sea salt or kosher salt for everyday cooking, and a special salt with a pleasant texture, such as Maldon salt or fleur de sel , for garnishing food at the last moment.
  • Salt also unlocks many aromatic compounds in foods, making them more readily available as we eat. The simplest way to experience this is to taste an unsalted soup or broth. Try it next time you make Chicken Stock . The unseasoned broth will taste flat, but as you add salt, you’ll detect new aromas that were previously unavailable. Keep salting, and tasting, and you’ll start to sense the salt as well as more complex and delightful flavors: the savoriness of the chicken, the richness of the chicken fat, the earthiness of the celery and the thyme.
  • This flavor “unlocking” is also one reason why professional cooks like to season sliced tomatoes a few minutes before serving them—so that, as salt helps the flavor molecules that are bound up within the tomato proteins, each bite will taste more intensely of tomato.
  • Though we typically turn to sugar to balance out bitter flavors in a sauce or soup, it turns out that salt masks bitterness much more effectively than sugar.
  • See for yourself with a little tonic water, Campari, or grapefruit juice, all of which are both bitter and sweet. Taste a spoonful, then add a pinch of salt and taste again. You’ll be surprised by how much bitterness subsides.
  • Tasting and adjusting—over and over again as you add ingredients and they transform throughout the cooking process—will yield the most flavorful food.
  • Tuscans don’t add salt to their bread but more than make up for it with the copious handfuls they add to everything else.
  • In Japan, steamed rice is left unseasoned to act as the foil for the flavorful fishes, meats, curries, and pickles served alongside it. In India, biryani , a flavorful rice dish layered with vegetables, meat, spices, and eggs, is never left unsalted.
  • If you’re not sure salt will fix the problem, take a spoonful or small bite and sprinkle it with a little salt, then taste again. If something shifts and you sense the zing! , then go ahead and add salt to the entire batch.
  • Some ingredients and cooking methods require giving salt enough time to penetrate food and distribute itself within it. In other cases, the key is to create a cooking environment salty enough to allow food to absorb the right amount of salt as it cooks.

Physics of salt

  • The distribution of salt throughout food can be explained by osmosis and diffusion , two chemical processes powered by nature’s tendency to seek equilibrium, or the balanced concentration of solutes such as minerals and sugars on either side of a semipermeable membrane (or holey cell wall).
    • Diffusion , on the other hand, is the often slower process of salt moving from a saltier environment to a less salty one until it’s evenly distributed throughout. Sprinkle salt on the surface of a piece of chicken and come back twenty minutes later. The distinct grains will no longer be visible: they will have started to dissolve, and the salt will have begun to move inward in an effort to create a chemical balance throughout the piece of meat.
    • Water will also be visible on the surface of the chicken, the result of osmosis. While the salt moves in , the water will move out with the same goal: achieving chemical balance throughout the entire piece of meat.
    • Given the chance, salt will always distribute itself evenly to season food from within, but it affects the textures of different foods in different ways.
    • Since diffusion is a slow process, seasoning in advance gives salt plenty of time to diffuse evenly throughout meat. This is how to season meat from within. A small amount of salt applied in advance will make a much bigger difference than a larger amount applied just before serving. In other words, time, not amount, is the crucial variable.
    • Because salt also initiates osmosis, and visibly draws water out of nearly any ingredient it touches, many people believe that salt dries and toughens food. But with time, salt will dissolve protein strands into a gel, allowing them to absorb and retain water better as they cook. Water is moisture: its presence makes meat tender and juicy.
    • Think of a protein strand as a loose coil with water molecules bound to its outside surface. When an unseasoned protein is heated, it denatures : the coil tightens, squeezing water molecules out of the protein matrix, leaving the meat dry and tough if overcooked. By disrupting protein structure, salt prevents the coil from densely coagulating , or clumping, when heated, so more of the water molecules remain bound. The piece of meat remains moister, and you have a greater margin of error for overcooking.
  • This same chemical process is the secret to brining, the method in which a piece of meat is submerged in a bath of water spiked with salt, sugar, and spices. The salt in this mixture, or brine , dissolves some of the proteins, while the sugar and spices offer plenty of aromatic molecules for the meat to absorb.
  • The larger, denser, or more sinewy the piece of meat, the earlier you should salt it. Oxtails, shanks, and short ribs can be seasoned a day or two in advance to allow salt time to do its work. A chicken for roasting can be salted the day before cooking, while Thanksgiving turkey should be seasoned two, or even three, days in advance.
  • The colder the meat and surrounding environment are, the longer it will take the salt to do its work, so when time is limited, leave meat on the counter once you season it (but for no longer than two hours), rather than returning it to the fridge.
  • But wait much longer than that, and they will dry out and develop a leathery texture and a cured, rather than fresh, flavor.
  • If you’ve salted some meat but realize you won’t be able to get to it for several days, freeze it until you’re ready to cook it. Tightly wrapped, it’ll keep for up to two months. Simply defrost and pick up cooking where you left off.
  • Unlike meat, the delicate proteins of most fish and shellfish will degrade when salted too early, yielding a tough, dry, or chewy result. A brief salting—about fifteen minutes—is plenty to enhance flavor and maintain moisture in flaky fish.
  • Season all other seafood at the time of cooking to preserve textural integrity.
  • Salt requires water to dissolve, so it won’t dissolve in pure fat. Luckily, most of the fats we use in the kitchen contain at least a little water—the small amounts of water in butter, lemon juice in a mayonnaise, or vinegar in a vinaigrette allow salt to slowly dissolve.
  • Or, dissolve salt in water, vinegar, or lemon juice before adding it to fat for even, immediate distribution.
  • Don’t let this absorption imbalance affect how you season a fatty cut.
  • Add a pinch of salt to eggs destined for scrambling, omelettes, custards, or frittatas before cooking. Lightly season water for poaching eggs. Season eggs cooked in the shell or fried in a pan just before serving.
  • The three most valuable tools to encourage salt diffusion are time, temperature, and water.
  • If you are cooking something big or dense and want to get salt into it, season the ingredient as early as possible to give salt the time to travel to the center.
  • Heat stimulates salt diffusion. Salt will always diffuse more quickly at room temperature than in the fridge.
  • Water promotes salt diffusion. Use watery cooking methods to help salt penetrate dense, dry, and tough ingredients, especially if you don’t have time to season them in advance.

Vegetables and fruits

  • Most vegetables and fruit cells contain an undigestible carbohydrate called pectin . Soften the pectin through ripening or applying heat, and you will soften the fruit or vegetable, making it more tender, and often more delicious, to eat. Salt assists in weakening pectin.
  • Season vegetables with large, watery cells—tomatoes, zucchini, and eggplant, for example—in advance of grilling or roasting to allow salt the time to do its work.
  • When in doubt, salt vegetables before you cook them. Toss vegetables with salt and olive oil for roasting. Salt blanching water generously before adding vegetables. Add salt into the pan along with the vegetables for sautéing.
  • Because salt will continue to draw water out of vegetables and fruits and eventually make them rubbery, be wary of salting them too early—usually 15 minutes before cooking is sufficient.
  • While mushrooms don’t contain pectin, they are about 80 percent water, which they will begin to release when salted. In order to preserve the texture of mushrooms, wait to add salt until they’ve just begun to brown in the pan.
  • In order to flavor dried beans from within, add salt when you soak them or when you begin to cook them, whichever comes first.
  • Legumes and grains are dried seeds—the parts of a plant that ensure survival from one season to the next. They’ve evolved tough exterior shells for protection, and require long, gentle cooking in water to absorb enough water to become tender.
  • Taste potatoes that were simmered in salted water for a little while before being roasted, and you’ll be shocked by the difference—salt will have made it all the way into the center, doing its powerful work of seasoning from within along the way.

Protecting color and minerals of beans

  • Properly seasoned cooking water encourages food to retain its nutrients. Imagine that you’re cooking green beans in a pot of water. If the water is unseasoned or only lightly seasoned, then its concentration of salt—a mineral—will be lower than the innate mineral concentration in the green beans. In an attempt to establish equilibrium between the internal environment of the green beans and the external environment of the cooking water, the beans will relinquish some of their minerals and natural sugars during the cooking process. This leads to bland, gray, less-nutritious green beans.
  • On the other hand, if the water is more highly seasoned—and more mineral rich—than the green beans, then the opposite will happen. In an attempt to reach equilibrium, the green beans will absorb some salt from the water as they cook, seasoning themselves from the inside out.
  • They’ll also remain more vibrantly colored because the salt balance will keep magnesium in the beans’ chlorophyll molecules from leaching out. The salt will also weaken the pectin and soften the beans’ cell walls, allowing them to cook more quickly. As an added bonus, there will be less of an opportunity for the green beans to lose nutrients because they’ll spend less total time in the pot.
  • Salads made with boiled vegetables—be it potatoes, asparagus, cauliflower, green beans, or anything else—are most delicious when the vegetables are seasoned properly while they’re cooking.
  • Salt sprinkled on top of one of these salads at the time of serving won’t make as much of a difference in flavor as it will in texture, by adding a pleasant crunch.

Bread

  • It turns out that the dough tightened immediately because salt aids in strengthening gluten , the protein that makes dough chewy and elastic. As soon as I allowed the dough to rest, the gluten relaxed, and the pizzas that night emerged from the oven as delicious as always

When salting meat for cooking, any time is better than none, and more is better than some. Aim to season meat the day before cooking when possible. This is illustrated beautifully in a slice of prosciutto: the lean muscle (rosy pink part) has a higher water content, and thus can absorb salt readily as it cures.
