  • When mathematicians tried to make the idea of numbers very precise, they found they had to deal with sets first, and then build numbers out of particular sets. When mathematicians became really serious about developing mathematics completely rigorously, they started with sets. Set theory was developed as a foundation of mathematics.
  • Set theory starts with the concept of membership as a basic concept, and builds up from the idea of elements being members of sets. By contrast, category theory builds up from the notion of relationships which is why our basic concepts in category theory are elements (objects) and relationships (arrows) between them, rather than membership. Comparing set theory with category theory for same definition of sets.
  • Category theory takes sets and functions as the basic starting point, rather than sets and membership. But these ideas are converse of each other. From memberships, functions can be built and vice versa. Its like choosing what you consider as more fundamental and start there.

Function

  • In categorical approach, function is a relationship between sets. Goes from one set to another.
  • There are restrictions on what is a function. Classical definition of a function with domain and co-domain.
    • Every element needs to map to at least some output.
    • One input can’t produce two different outputs. However, we can have multiple inputs producing one output.
  • Let A and B be any sets. A function A -f-> B assigns to every element a ∈ A an element f(a) ∈ B.
  • In very formal set theory the definition happens by means of “ordered pairs”: we construct a new set from A and B consisting of pairs of elements, one from A and one from B, representing the input–output pairs that define f
  • f: A -> B means from set A to set B
  • f: a |-> b means from element a to element b
  • Let f, g be functions A B. We say f = g as functions whenever ∀a ∈ A f(a) = g(a)

Structure : Identities and Composition

Identity
Given any set A there is an identity function A A which just sends every element of A to itself. We can call it 1A and define it by ∀a ∈ A 1A(a) = a.
Composition
We define the composite function g ◦ f by: (g ◦ f)(a) = g(f(a))

This is pretty plain definition of function identity and composition. Nothing too fancy here.

Making a category of sets and functions

  • Need to check that identity really behaves like identity, both on the left and right, and composition is associative.

Identity

Even when we zoom in to individual elements of set, we see the identity structure.

Associativity

For A -f-> B -g-> C -h-> D, we need to show that : (h ◦ g) ◦ f = h ◦ (g ◦ f ) that is, ∀a ∈ A: ((h ◦ g) ◦ f)(a) = (h ◦ (g ◦ f ))(a)

If we apply functions to both, we finally come at h(g(f(a))) which proves that it follows associativity.

Category of sets and functions [ Formalised ]

This category is typically written as Set and is given by:

  • objects: all sets
  • morphisms: a morphism A B is a function A B
  • identities: given a set A, the identity is the identity function 1A
  • composition: composition of morphisms is composition of functions.

Now, this Set becomes a prototype to be able to use in larger mathematical structures. That way we can move from elements in traditional sets to treating structures as categorical Set.

Large world of mathematical structures

From the miniature world where we were looking at each element, we will zoom out and see larger category. The restrictions are the structures.

Sets
No structure
Monoids
Binary Operation, Identity
Groups
Binary Operation, Identity, Inverses

Homomorphism

  • Any function between two algebraic structures – like monoids, groups, posets etc. – that preserves their operations and properties.
  • The small object is a monoid and the relationship between monoids is also a monoid. Then that relation is called monoid homomorphism.

Monoids

  • We need to define “function between monoids” as part of large category.

Understanding previous definitions of monoids as Set

A monoid has:

  • data: a set of objects
  • structure: an identity and a binary operation
  • properties: unitality and associativity.

So it can be broadly summed up as a “set equipped with extra structure (satisfying some properties)”. Whenever we have “sets-with-structure” we can look for “sensible” functions between them, that is, functions that respect that structure.

  • Looking at previous example

    • Monoid of natural numbers N under addition (N, +, 0) and monoid of integers Z under addition (Z, +, 0).
    • Now, we are trying to map function between the monoids. f: N -> Z with f(n) = n, so every natual number is mapped to itself as an integer.
      • Now, the binary operation must hold in this new function that we created. i.e. f(n+m) = n + m and f(n) + f(m) = n + m. Since we got, f(n+m) = f(n) + f(m) this holds the binary operation a.k.a preserves addition.
      • Functions like f(n) = n + 1 however isn’t a sensible function because it leads to f(n+m) = n+ m+ 1 and f(n) + f(m) = n + 1 + m + 1 = n + m + 2. So, it doesn’t preserve addition.
      • Also our structure needs to respect identity of monoid structure as well. In this case, f(0) = 0, which is identity in Z as well, so good. Preserves identity.

Monoid Morphism / Monoid Homomorphism

  • A structure preserving morphism that leaves things the same.
  • Let A and B be monoids, and write the identity as 1 and the binary operation as ◦ in each case. Then a monoid homomorphism from A to B is a function f : A -> B on the underlying sets, such that
    • f respects ◦ ( Binary operation ) : for all x, y ∈ A we have f(x ◦ y) = f(x) ◦ f(y), and
    • f respects the identity: f(1) = 1.

In general not every function on the underlying sets will respect the monoid structure, so this is a restriction to some special functions.

Then, we finally get our category Mnd whose objects are all the monoids and whose morphisms are all the monoid morphisms between them.

Groups

A group is a monoid with some extra structure, so a group homomorphism should at least be a monoid homomorphism, but it should also preserve the extra structure. So we might think that a group homomorphism f : A -> B should be a function on the underlying sets such that:

  • the binary operation ◦ is respected: ∀x, y ∈ a, f(x ◦ y) = f(x) ◦ f(y),
  • the identity 1 is respected: f(1) = 1, and
  • inverses are respected: ∀x ∈ A, f(x−1) = (f(x))-1

The interesting thing in groups is that preserving the operation often forces identity and inverse preservation, due to the existence of inverses.

Posets

Relation ≤ is a poset. An order preserving function f: A -> B between posets satisfies : if x ≤ y in A, then f(x) ≤ f(y) in B.

Order Preserving poset

Poset N with ≤. Define f(n) = n+1 If m ≤ n, then f(m) = m+1 ≤ n+1 = f(n) which is preserving order.

Not order preserving poset

Poset N with ≤. Define f(n) = -n, e.g. m ≤ n ; then f(1) = -1 ≥ -2 = f(2) Which reversed the order It doesn’t always preserve order. So, not order preserving poset.

Category of posets

  • Objects are posets
  • Morphisms need to be order preserving functions preserving ≤ .

Example

Here, there are three different orderings:

  1. The way which the arrows are drawn in: where a -> b whenever a is a factor of b. Written as operation |.
  2. THe usual ordering according to size a ≤ b
  3. The physical levels on the drawing ( How many prime factors for each element depends on what level it is in ) Written as operation <>

So, we can define binary relationships here. Given a number a, N(a) be the number of terms in prime factorization. Then for each level of cube, we can write N(a) ≤ N(b).

a N(a)
42 3
6, 14, 21 2
2, 3, 7 1
1 0

So, we have three orderings: (A, |), (A, ≤), (A, <>).

The factor operation is order preserving because (A, |) -> (A, ≤) But the hierarchy operation is not order preserving because 6 lies above 7 in hierarchy level. So, the hierarchy operation 7 <> 6 will imply 7 ≥ 6. So, the order isn’t preserved.

Top

Category of topological spaces Top where:

  • objects: all the topological spaces
  • morphisms: a morphism A B is a continuous function A B.

Homotopy is the notion of continuous deformation which is in some sense really the point of topology, but it requires more dimensions of thought than are available in the category of spaces and continuous maps. One way to deal with those higher dimensions is to go into higher-dimensional category theory, which we will briefly discuss at the end of the book. Another way is to try and work out how to detect traces of the higher dimensions in lower-dimensional algebra so that we can avoid creating new types of algebra to deal with it.

Normal Categories

  • Sometimes we get a little bored of all these parentheses so we might omit them and just write Fx, Fy and Ff trusting that using uppercase and lowercase letters makes the point that F is applied to the lowercase letters.
  • These morphisms between categories are so important that they have an actual name rather than just “morphisms of categories”: they are called functors.
  • The property of preserving identities and composition is called functoriality.

Matrices

  • One of my favorite examples is the category of matrices. In this category again it’s not the objects that are really interesting but the morphisms: the morphisms are matrices. That is, we regard matrices as a sort of map.
  • In a bit of a leap of imagination we can regard an a × b matrix as a morphism a b, in which case a b × c matrix is a morphism b c and the condition of composability matches the condition of when we can multiply matrices. We get a category Mat with
    • objects: the natural numbers
    • arrows: an arrow a b is an a × b matrix
    • composition: matrix multiplication.
  • This might seem like a weird category until we consider that one of the points of matrices is actually to encode linear maps between vector spaces. In that way, matrices really do come from some kind of map, it’s just that the encoding has taken them quite far away from looking like a map. That typically makes it very handy for computation (especially if you’re telling a computer how to do it) but can be quite baffling for students if they’re just told about matrices for no particular reason — like so much of math.

Isomorphisms

  • The harder conditions we put for sameness, it becomes more about the objects than the relationship and the patterns in it. So, we want to find some sense in which the object can be compared. And for that we need some notion of “sameness”.
    • e.g. Equality sign is a sign of sameness for algebraic equations.
    • Multiply sign is same as adding that number that many times.

Invertibility

  • A invertible arrow between them.
  • We can use that as one condition to say that they are same.
  • e.g. On real numbers, we can say addition is invertible. But multiplication by 0 or square root, they are not invertible. Either they don’t know where to go back to, or go to a different place than where they came from.

Isomorphism

  • Treated as same in category theory because they have same relationship with other objects in the category. i.e. Other object that has relation with two objects that are isomorphic, lets say a and b, can’t differentiate between a and b since it knows a and b only by the relationship it has with them. We don’t really look into the intrinsic property of the object.
  • By assuming object “x” and drawing relationship like this, it becomes clear.

So, the relationship of x with both a and b is essentially the same i.e. isomorphic. We can do this by drawing arrows towards x as well and pre-compose to see the same results. Very easy to go step by step using just plain categorical principles.

Definition

Definition of an inverse
Let a -f-> b be an arrow in a category C. An inverse for f is an arrow b -g-> a such that g ◦ f = 1a and f ◦ g = 1b.
  • From the properties of inverses, they are unique.
Definition of isomorphism
Let a -f-> b be an arrow in a category C. If f has an inverse we say that f is invertible and call it an isomorphism, and we say that a and b are isomorphic. We use the notation as in a ≅ b, or we write a -∼-> b.

Pre and post composition

  • Post composing by g means g after f. So, we apply f first, then g but is written as g . f
  • Pre composing by g means g before f. So, we apply g first and then to that result, apply f. So, its f . g

Isomorphism of sets

  • For isomporphism, we need the functions to be invertible. For functions to be invertible, we need to have one-to-one mapping between two sets.
  • This is however for finite sets. For infinite sets, we can turn things around because there is no size. As long as they are countably infinite, we can always create one-to-one mapping.
  • Also, not every functions inside isomorphic sets are isomorphic. If a function maps elements from set A into one element of set B, then it’s a valid function but not invertible. Thus, not isomorphic. So, functions that are isomorphisms between sets are called bijections.

Non categorical definition of bijection

  • A function A -f-> B is a bijection if for every element b ∈ B there is a unique element a ∈ A such that f(a) = b.
  • This is definition from our sets which is regarding each element.

Isomorphisms of large structures

  • Similar definition. Existence of an inverse that is structure preserving means the objects are isomorphic.

Monoids

  • Assuming monoid morphism A -f-> B and its inverse B -g-> A, we need to ensure that it preserves monoid structure. a.k.a. binary operation and identity.
  • Identity
    • Need to show g(1) = 1. Applying f to the left gives 1 i.e. f . g = 1 because f and g are inverses. Also applying f to the right gives 1 for the same reason. So, there is just one identity.
  • Binary Operation
    • g(b1 . b2) = g(b1) . g(b2)
    • By applying f to the left, we get b1 . b2 because f.g = 1.
    • By applying f to the right, we get f(g(b1) . g(b2)) and since f should respect binary operation by being a monoid mapping, it also resolves to b1 . b2
  • So, if f is a bijective homomorphism, then its an isomorphism of monoids and vice versa.
  • Example of monoid isomorphism:
    • Representation of number system as 1, 2, 3 .. and One, Two, Three … They have same structure, so shouldn’t be really counted as different.
  • If monoids have same elements but different structures, then they aren’t isomorphic as monoids, but as sets. Sets have loose structure compared to monoids.

Groups

  • Homomorphism of groups is just a homomorphism of underlying monoids. So, group isomorphism must be bijective homomorphism.
  • By definition of groups, they need to have inverses for each elements.
  • Rotation by 90 degrees or mod 4 clock both are groups since they have inverses for each elements, follow binary operation, and have identity.
  • By looking at the fact that we can map these two to one another clockwise, counter clockwise etc., they are isomorphic. They both are “cyclic group of order 4”.

Posets

  • Order preserving and bijection.
  • Inverse is automatically order preserving in a poset.

Topological spaces

  • In case of topological spaces, function that is continuous can have inverse function that is not continuous. So, bijection is not enough to ensure continuous map is an isomorphism in the category of spaces and continuous maps.
  • So, its a wrong notion of sameness in this case.
  • For topological spaces, there is “homeomorphism”. The reason why we call this is that our previous definition of isomorphism wasn’t sensitive enough to give us sameness for topological spaces.

Groupoids

  • More expressive than equivalence relations as things can be related in more than one way.
  • Each arrow needs to have its inverse in a groupoid.
  • Groupoids and topological spaces are related in the sense that inverse in topological path is like going backwards along the same exact path.

Thinking categorically

  • Become curious about a structure, in sets and functions.
  • Express it categorically, forget about the elements.
  • Take definition of other categories to see what it means.

Monics and Epics

Asymmetry of functions

  • Since functions can’t be isomorphic when they don’t have one-one mapping between elements, we can say isomorphism is generalization of symmetry of relations.

Injective Functions

  • Every output is hit at most once.
  • One-one, same output means same inputs.
  • A function f : A -> B is called injective if ∀x, y ∈ A, f(x) = f(y) => x = y.
  • e.g. f : N -> N where f(x) = x + 1 has mapping for all elements on the left to unique elements on the right but doesn’t say anything about element on the right to have input on the left. In this case, 0 won’t have an input. So, its only about one to one relationship. Injective still since the mapping is one to one.
  • To prove that a function is not injective we have to prove the negation of the definition of injective, that is: ∃ x, y ∈ A such that f(x) = f(y) but x ≠ y.

Surjective Functions

  • If co-domain equals range
  • Meaning that every output element has a mapping from one input element.
  • A function f : A -> B is called surjective if ∀b ∈ B ∃ a ∈ A such that f (a) = b.
  • e.g. f : N -> N where f(x) = x + 1 has mapping for all elements on the left to unique elements on the right but doesn’t say anything about element on the right to have input on the left. In this case, 0 won’t have a corresponding input. So, its not surjective.

Bijective Functions

  • If its both injective and surjective.
  • A function f : A B is called bijective if it is injective and surjective, that is: ∀b ∈ B ∃!a ∈ A such that f(a) = b. Here exclamation means “unqiue”.

Examples

  • A = φ, B = Z
    • For injective, the definition starts “for all x, y ∈ A”. We can now stop because A is empty, so whatever happens this condition is vacuously satisfied. Thus the function is injective.
    • For surjective there is a part of the definition that says “∃ a ∈ A such that. . . ” and then we’re in trouble because there is no element in A. The only way we could survive this is if the condition is vacuously satisfied, that is: the condition starts with “∀b ∈ B” so if B is empty then the condition is vacuously satisfied.
    • So, if it were A = φ, B = φ then that would have been bijective.

Monics: Categorical Injectivity

  • All the definitions before have elements tied to them. So, that’s not categorical. Now, we need to express them as sets and functions only, not sets and elements.
  • A morphism a -f-> b in a category C is called a monomorphism or monic if, given any fork diagram in C, f ◦ s = f ◦ t => s = t.

Now, this is since a categorical version of injectivity, it needs to be part of isomorphism as well.

Proposition: A function is injective iff it is monic in Set category.

Assume injective function f: a -> b . We assume to show its monic. Draw the fork diagram as above. Then, We want to show such that fs = ft, we need to prove s = t. By definition of injectivity above. fs = ft means: for all x belongs to a, f . s(x) = f . t(x) if f is injective , that impiles: for all x belongs to a, s(x) = t(x) thus s = t.

Proposition: A function f that is isomorphic is automatically a monic.

Let f: a -> b be an isomorphism with inverse g. Draw the fork diagram.

Then we need to show if fs = ft, then s = t Start with fs = ft => gfs = gft => s = t since gf = 1a. Thus, f is monic as required.

Split monic

Let f : a -> b be a morphism in a category. If there is a morphism g as shown here with gf = 1a then f is certainly monic and is called a split monic. Then g is called a splitting, left inverse or a retraction for f.

Epics: Categorical Surjectivity

  • In sets, injectivity and surjectivity didn’t look like other way round. But they do look like duals here.
  • Start by reversing the arrow diagram.
  • A morphism f : a b in a category is called an epimorphism or epic if, given any diagram as above: sf = tf => s = t.

Proposition: A function f is surjective iff its epic in Set category

Putting it with definition of image f, it can be put as Image(f) = { y ∈ b | ∃ x ∈ a such that f(x) = y }

We know that : b = Image(f) union Nonimage(f)

So, a function is surjective iff Image(f) = b.

Using the second arrow diagram, given sf = tf, we need to show s = t. Consider y ∈ b. Now, f is surjective, so ∃ x ∈ a such that f(x) = y.

Thus, s(y) = sf(x) by substitution from line above = tf(x) by hypothesis = t(y) by substitution from definition again Thus s = t as required.

By using a contrapositive example, we can prove the reverse.

Proposition: If f is an isomorphism, then f is epic

Same proof like monic with these new arrow diagram

Split epic

  • Let g: b a be a morphism in a category. If there is a morphism f as shown here with f g = 1b then g is certainly epic. Then g is called a split epic and f is called a splitting, a left inverse or a section for g.

Relationship with isomorphisms

  • If f is a split monic and a split epic, then it has an inverse on both sides, thus isomorphic.
  • A morphism can be monic and epic without necessarily being an isomorphism, if it doesn’t split. This can be understood when we get out of Sets. The examples and proofs we have done are comparison to Sets upto this moment.
  • Monic/Epic is a property of morphism, whereas splitting is a piece of structure.

Monoids

For example, consider the monoid of natural numbers N under addition. We will try to define a monoid homomorphism f to some other monoid M.

  • We know that 0 is the identity in N so it must go to the identity in M; we have no choice about that.
  • We can send 1 anywhere we want.
  • We know that 2 = 1+1 in N, and by the definition of monoid homomorphism we must have f(1 + 1) = f(1) + f(1) so we have no choice about where 2 goes: it has to go to f(1) + f(1).
  • Something similar is now true for every other natural number. Every n is a sum of 1’s and so we have no choice over where it goes: it has to go to the n-fold sum of f(1)’s.

What we’ve done here is based on the fact that N is the free monoid built up from a single element.

Proposition Let f: N -> Z be monoid homomorphism given by inclusion f(n) = n. Then f is epic in Mnd (Monoid category).

If we have sf = tf, then that means s and t agree on the image of f. However, 1 ∈ Z is the image of f because f(1) = 1 and so we must have s(1) = t(1) which in turn forces s = t. Because monoid is built on top of a single thing. So, this shows that f is epic even when it isn’t surjective.

f is also injective since it maps element by element on this case and that’s enough to ensure that its monic in Mnd. Now, in fact f is monic and epic, yet its not an isomorphism.

Density

  • Examples similar to monoids where morphisms are epic without being surjective.
  • A set is called dense inside B if closure of A is B; closure of A is essentially the most economical way to enlarge A just enough to make it a closed set.
  • This is related to how we can construct the real numbers from the rationals, by taking the closure under limits, which amounts to throwing in the irrational numbers.
  • This sort of thing happens any time something has been constructed “freely” from some generators. If the morphisms in that category preserve the structure, then all you have to know is where the generators go, and then there’s no choice of where the rest of the structure can go. You might also have seen this with vector spaces and basis elements. There’s a concept of “limit” and “density” in category theory that mimics the situation of limits and density in analysis.
  • One special case of injective functions is subset inclusions. For example we have seen the function N -> Z which just takes each natural number and sends it to the same number as an integer.
  • There’s no categorical reason that a subset inclusion is any better than any other kind of monic, and so in more general situations monics are used to indicate subobjects.

Higher Dimensions

  • Monic and epic are categorical versions of injective and surjective functions, and when we go into higher dimensions we want to generalize injective and surjective functions to the level of functors, that is, the morphisms in the category Cat. We can try looking for monics and epics in that category, but it won’t really give us “the right thing” because that is working at the wrong dimension.
  • Cat is really trying to be a 2-category (as we mentioned before) with a more subtle type of relationship between morphisms.

Universal Properties

  • The reason for trying to characterize things by universal properties is so that we find things that play analogous roles in different contexts.
  • How uniquely we can pin things down is important consideration with universal properties.
  • We may find several objects that all satisfy the property, but they will all be uniquely isomorphic so the category “can’t tell them apart”. Thinking categorically, we need to embrace that we can’t tell them apart, even though there are many.

Role vs Character

  • In category theory, we care about the role they play. Not the character that it has. e.g. 0 is representing nothing. But we can also describe it by role it plays: a number that when you add to something does nothing. That’s a role that it plays. And that’s a number that can only play that role.
  • Same goes for number 1 in multiplication.
  • They are thus called additive identity and multiplicative identity respectively.

Extremities

  • One sure shot way of understanding a problem by knowing its bounds.
  • Also by taking something into a different context where its extreme also tells us about a context. So many interesting ways to learn new things, find new patterns.
    • e.g. If I am 5'6’’ and I am the tallest in the room, it says that the room is full of short people.
  • In category theory, we are looking for extremities based on arrows. Where the arrows start and where the arrows end are usually the extremes. Not physical location on the drawing etc.

Initial Object

  • An object I in a category C is initial if for every object X ∈ C there is a unique morphism I -> X.
  • Its like having an end that you can attach to one end of your tape measure, a reference point.
  • Category of integers has no initial object, however category of natural numbers has 0 as initial object.
  • In a category with more than one object and no non-trivial morphisms, there is no initial object since there just aren’t enough morphisms. We need at least an object with a morphism going everywhere else. Though we might not draw it out loud, through composition that needs to be the case.
  • In this diagram, if composite g . f is not identity, then a can’t be initial because we have at least two different morphisms a -> a: composite g . f and identity 1a. And we can have infinite number of morphisms from a -> a since f and g don’t have to satisfy any other equation and every time we go around the loop we can have a different morphism.
  • In the case that they are in fact inverses, then this category exactly has four morphisms: f, g, 1a, 1b. All composites will be equal to one of these because f and g have to composite both ways around into identity. In this case, we see that a -1a-> a and a -f-> b, a is initial with unique morphisms. Same goes for b.
  • There we have two initial objects but categorically they’re not really different.

Uniqueness

Terminal Object

  • Now the end of category where all arrows lead upto.
  • If we reverse the arrows, where all all arrows start from.
  • An object T in a category C is terminal if for every object X ∈ C there is a unique morphism X -> T.

Proposition

Let T be a terminal object in a category C and T’ any object. The following are equivalent:

  1. T’ is a terminal object in C.
  2. T’ is uniquely isomorphic to T.
  3. T’ is isomorphic to T.

Using similar logic as initial object, these can be verified too.

Failure Cases for terminal and initial objects

  • When category has too few morphisms or too many morphisms.

Going on forever

  • The last case we talked about for natural numbers, we know that there is no terminal object but we can add an object called ω which every number points to assuming its the largest, then we have a terminal object. 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> ω. We can omit the arrows since we have been doing that for natural numbers all the time as they can be composed.

Branching

  • There might be a beginning or an end but not a place where everything begins or ends.

Going round in circles

  • No initial object, provided that the arrows were not inverses.

Parallel arrows

  • Too many morphisms to be unique

Disconnectedness

  • Too few arrows to be terminal or initial
  • “Locally initial” if there are disconnected regions with but those disconnected region has an initial or terminal object.

Case where object is both terminal and initial

  • If it has only one object and one identity morphism.
  • If more than one object but they are all uniquely isomorphic. THen every object is terminal and initial.

Examples in different contexts

Sets and posets

  • Empty one is initial and 1-element one is terminal in sets with structure: posets and topological spaces.

Monoids and Groups

  • They can’t be empty by definition.
  • Trivial monoid/group is one with a single example.
  • Unique function to that one element to itself is definitely a homomorphism. So, trivial group is terminal in category Grp. And also initial in Grp.
  • A null object in a category is one that is both terminal and initial.

Context

  • We can compare universal objects in different categories, or we might observe something being universal in one category, but not another.
  • For posets and topological spaces, we can follow dotted arrows and get to the empty set. For monoids and groups, the arrow takes us to 1-element set because they are bound by definition.

Duality

  • By turning arrows around, we get a dual version of every construction, every theorem.
  • Dual category For any category C the dual (or opposite) category Cop is given as follows.
    • objects: ob Cop = ob C
    • morphisms: given objects a, b, we have Cop (a, b) = C(b, a)
    • identities are the same
    • composition is reversed
  • The dual version is often indicated by the preﬁx “co-”. So for example:
    • we define products and then the dual concept is coproducts
    • we define limits and then the dual concept is colimits
    • we define equalizers and then the dual concept is coequalizers
    • we define projections and then the dual concept is coprojections.
  • The dual of dual category takes us back to original category.
  • A morphism f is epic in C if and only if it is monic in Cop .
  • If f is an isomorphism in Cop, then it is also an isomorphism in C. If something is exactly the same in both C and Cop, then its called self-dual.
  • Let C be a category. A terminal object in C is precisely an initial object in Cop .

Products and Coproducts

Idea

  • If we think about our 2 by 4 grid of objects above, what is the relationship between this grid and the numbers 2 and 4? We might say there are 2 rows and 4 columns, but that sort of presupposes an understanding of what rows and columns are. We might say its height is 2 and its width is 4, but that also presupposes concepts of height and width. Here is something we could say that’s (perhaps) more fundamental.
  • Imagine projecting shadows of our objects onto a wall. If we project in one direction (and perfectly line everything up) then we will see only 2 things, and if we project in the other direction we’ll see 4.

Definition

Given objects a and b in a category, a product for them is: an object a × b equipped with morphisms p and q as shown below such that given any diagram of this form there is a unique morphism x -k-> a × b making the following diagram commute.

  • For product, we need to draw the shape and make sure that we have a unique morphism.
  • This third diagram is a universal shape that we use to prove so many other stuff as well.
  • The morphism k in the third diagram is a type of comparison between the universal situation (the first diagram) and the non-universal one (the second diagram). Note that asking for the diagram to commute means that the triangle on each side commutes. Written out in algebra this means pk = f and qk = g
  • Uniqueness: it might not be the only morphism x -> a x b, but it has to be the only morphism that makes both of those side triangles commute.

Terminology

  • The morphisms p and q are called projections.
  • The morphism k is called a factorization. We are factorizing f and g.
  • There is a general type of diagram called a cone which consists of a vertex and the morphisms from that vertex to everything else. In this case the vertex is a × b and “everything else” is just the objects a and b.
  • The product is the universal cone, universal among all cones of this shape.
  • We say the universal property induces the factorization k.

Step by step

So, we start by understanding that there are two objects in a category. Then we define a product a x b. Then that product assumes two projections p and q to relate with objects a and b. By drawing these projections, we need to understand that we have created arrows. By definition of universal property, we are saying a x b is the best option that can project onto a and b. This is the understanding. Now, how do we prove its the best? We start by drawing another projection onto a and b: f and g. But why did we do that? To factorize these f and g using a factorization unique morphism k. Its like saying a x b is the least possible path to a and b and then any other path is basically a composition of some factor with that least possible path. That makes product the best path out there.

Products as terminal objects

  • Products are in fact a special type of terminal object. It’s just that a product in C isn’t a terminal object in C, it’s a terminal object in some more complicated category based on C, which I like to call a “souped-up” category.
  • We know that terminal objects are unique up to unique isomorphism, and products are a terminal object somewhere, so products must also be unique up to unique isomorphism.
  • There can be many relationships on the cone but only one that makes the diagram commute.
  • By definition of products, all morphisms can be factored with product being a component of it, that means all relationships from any object to terminal object will have a unique morphism to that product. So, that product becomes a terminal object since there will be unique morphism from every other object to product. We called it in a “souped up” category because if we define a and b as objects, they don’t have arrow upto product. That’s why product is not a terminal object in that category but in a “souped up” category.

Look at what we consider objects in this “souped-up” category to say that its a terminal object.

Products in set

  • Cartesian product is the categorical product in a set.
  • Need to remember that second lines are elemental mappings.
  • Let A and B be sets. Then the cartesian product A × B is the set defined by A × B = { (a, b) | a ∈ A, b ∈ B }
    • The elements (a, b) are called ordered pairs, and there are functions p and q as shown on the right called projections, sending an element (a, b) to a and b respectively.

Products in posets

If we now work through the definition of product in this context, we see that for the product of a and b we need:

  1. A diagram of the form shown here, which in this category just means that v is a multiple of both a and b.
  2. Given any such diagram with vertex x, we need a morphism x -> v. Here is a “translation” of what that means in this particular category. “Given x that is a multiple of both a and b, x is a multiple of v”

Then by these two ideas, we come to the definition of LCM. In a general poset we might generically call the ordering ≥ and in that case the definition of categorical product gives us this:

  1. an object v such that v ≥ a and v ≥ b, and
  2. for any object x such that x ≥ a and x ≥ b, we must have x ≥ v.

This is exactly the definition of least upper bound or supremum. The first point says that v is an upper bound for a and b, and the second point says that if x is any upper bound, it is greater than or equal to v.

Category of posets

Let (A, ≤) and (B, ≤) be posets. Then we can define an ordering ≤ on A × B by (a1, b1) ≤ (a2, b2) <=> a1 ≤ a2 and b1 ≤ b2 and this makes (A × B, ≤) into a categorical product (A, ≤) × (B, ≤) in Pst.

Monoids and groups

  • We have to start with groups (A, .) and (B, . ) and instead of making an ordering on A x B, we need to make a binary operation based on binary operations in A and B. Here dot means binary operation.
  • If we take group/monoid to be R under addition , categorical product R x R is to come up with definition of addition for these ordered pairs. e.g. (x1,y1) + (x2,y2)
  • Now, when we add this component wise we get (x1+x2, y1+y2)
  • On generalizing this, we get
  • Let (A, ◦, 1) and (B, ◦, 1) be monoids. We define a binary operation on A × B by (a1, b1) ◦ (a2, b2) = (a1 ◦ a2 , b1 ◦ b2 ). This makes A×B into a monoid with unit (1, 1), and it is the categorical product of the original two monoids.

Coproducts

  • A coproduct in a category C is a product in Cop.
  • Now, the arrows are reversed in the universal cone diagram.
  • A coproduct for a and b is an initial object in a category whose objects are cocones over a and b, that is, diagrams of the form shown on the right.
  • Coproducts are unique up to unique isomorphism (making cocones commute), there is symmetry in the variables, and there are n-fold versions.
  • Coproducts in set is just union.
  • Note that technically we shouldn’t say “A U B is a coproduct” without saying what the coprojections are, but we often do when the coprojections can be understood to be the “obvious” inclusions.
  • This is an important way of thinking about universal properties. In general it says there is a bijective correspondence between (co)cones and factorizations, so that we can equivalently encapsulate the information of any (co)cone as a single morphism to (or from) a universal one. It’s very handy because a cone generally involves many morphisms, and we can now encapsulate it as one morphism together with a “reference” cone.

Terminology

  • p and q are called coprojections or insertions.
  • Instead of a cone, this is now a cocone. In a cone we have projections pointing away from the vertex, and in a cocone we have coprojections pointing to the vertex. The coproduct is then the universal cocone.
  • The coproduct is written a union b, a u b, or a + b.

Coprdoucts in other categories

  • Inside a poset : In the poset of factors of n we saw that products are lowest common multiples. Coproducts are then highest common factors.
  • In the category of posets, we can take a disjoint union of two posets A and B and it will still be a poset: everything in the A part will simply be incomparable to everything in the B part.
  • For tosets, if we take the coproduct of two tosets A and B, the result is in general not a toset: the elements of A will be incomparable to the elements of B, and this is not allowed in a toset.
  • For monoids, if we take the disjoint union of A and B as sets then the result is not in general a monoid — we have a binary operation on the A part and a binary operation on the B part but we do not have a way of doing a ◦ b with an element from each side. So, if we restrict to the category of commutative monoids, everything in a co product can be expressed as “element of A . element of B” where dot is binary operation.
    • Very similar to writing it as ordered pairs (element of A, element of B) just that we have binary operation in between.
    • In category of commutative monoids, coproduct and product are the same.
    • Commutative groups are also called Abelian Groups.
    • Coproducts of groups are called “Free products” in group theory
    • Products of groups are called “Direct products” in group theory

Products examples in topological spaces

  • The product of a square and a line is a cube, because if you move a square in a line you sweep out a cube in the air.
  • The product of a circle with a circle is a torus (like the surface of a bagel), which I like to demonstrate by taking a slinky (essentially a circle) and wrapping it round on itself in a circle. You can even make a vertical cut in a bagel and then insert the bagel into the slinky-torus.

Analogies with numbers

  • Based on our understanding with commutativity, associativity, products, we can keep asking questions while playing with numbers like these ones:
    • Is there an identity?
    • Are their inverses?
    • Do we have something like unique factorization into primes? If so, what are the primes? This one is studied for groups and is particularly straightforward for Abelian groups, where there is a “fundamental theorem of Abelian groups” rather like the fundamental theorem of arithmetic (which says that every natural number can be uniquely expressed as a product of primes).

Pullbacks and pushouts

  • Our starting data so far has not been very general: it has not included any morphisms. For terminal/initial objects the starting data was trivial, that is, it was empty. For products/coproducts it was a pair of objects. In this chapter we are going to do a first example where the starting data is a diagram including some morphisms.
  • Pullbacks and pushouts are dual to each other.

Universal cone

  • A cone is an object v (the “vertex”) together with morphisms to every object in the starting diagram, such that everything commutes.
  • We can start with any diagram and build a cone from it.
  • For it to be universal, it needs to be universal among all cones of that shape. That is what we are doing on the third diagram. Asserting uniqueness through unique factorization from x to v, x -> v. And being a factorization, everything must commute of course. We can see that gray arrows on third diagram are commutative arrows. These are relations that can be derived by commutative laws.

Pullbacks

  • A product of two sets takes all the possible ways of making pairs, with one element from each set. But perhaps we want to make pairs that are coherent in some way, perhaps pairing up people who are the same height to be dancing partners, or pairing pants/trousers with shirts that are the same color: we do that using a pullback.
  • Ordering with some restriction basically but how is this a universal one?
  • Developing from the idea of universal cone, a limit over a diagram is a universal cone over it. A pullback in a category is a limit over a diagram of the given shape.

So, depending on how we draw the base objects and find a universal cone there, it gets named different things. Then cone here is vertex v together with morphisms a, b, and c making everything commute. We can draw it like a square after omitting the composition from v to c:

  • Then the universal property states: Given any square with vertex x, there must be a unique factorization as shown on the right. The factorization must of course commute here as well.
  • To indicate a pullback we often put a little corner sign at the top left, as shown here. It goes where the vertex of the universal cone is.
  • We can say a category has pullbacks when it has pullbacks over all diagrams of relevant shape. The shape involving three objects with two objects pointing to the third object as shown at the start of this section.

Pullbacks in sets

  • Its like a product but it also has to commute to third object C. So, its written as A XC B.
  • A XC B = {(a, b) ∈ A × B | s(a) = t(b)}
  • The square is a pullback, where p and q are the projections inherited from A × B.
  • Note that when we write the vertex of the pullback as A ×C B it only tells us what the corner object C is, without reference to the morphisms s and t. In some situations those are very natural, but I think it’s good to be aware that the notation is missing something.
  • Sometimes we talk about pulling back morphisms along each other. So we might say that p is the pullback of t along s, and that q is the pullback of s along t. Although the definition is symmetrical in s and t sometimes the situation isn’t. Sometimes one of the starting morphisms is more interesting and the other is in more of a supporting role.
  • In this diagram, every arrow is a subset inclusion function and forms this shape.

Definition of category using pullbacks

  • Set C1 of morphisms and C0 of objects, equipped with functions giving the source and target of each morphism.

A composable pair of morphisms looks like an ordered pair (f, g) but its not any old ordered pair. the two morphisms have to meet in the middle in order to be composable.

We are trying to define what a category is using pullbacks.

  • We take the pullback shown on the right; it’s a pullback in Set so can be defined as follows:
    • C1 XC0 C1 = { (f, g) ∈ C1 × C1 | t(f) = s(g) }
    • Then composition is defined as C1 XC0 C1 -> C1
  • The fact that composition is defined as pullback rather than the product is what makes it a partial binary operation rather than a binary operation since a binary operation on set is A X A -> A. j

Representing by elements of set.

Pushouts

  • A pushout is a universal cocone for a diagram of the shape shown in the first diagram below. That is, it is a vertex v and morphisms as shown in the second diagram, such that given any diagram as in the third diagram, there is a unique factorization as shown in the fourth diagram.
  • Represented by small corner marking the vertex of universal cocone.
  • Dually to pullbacks, these pushouts are :
    • Initial objects somewhere
    • Unique upto unique isomorphism
    • Canonically related to coproducts

Pushouts in sets

  • As for when we did the pullback property, it may help to think about what it means for the outside to commute. If we start with an element y ∈ A ∩ B and chase it around, we see that commutativity means f(y) = g(y), that is the functions f and g have to agree on the intersection A ∩ B.
  • This square is both a pullback and a pushout.
  • The diagram on the right has a pushout given by A U B / ∼ where the relation ∼ is generated by: s(c) ∼ t(c) ∀c ∈ C
  • The quotient map is a function A U B -> A U B / ~ which is unique factorization induced by universal property of coproduct.
  • So, defining a function out of a quotient like this V / ~ -> X. The item on the left will consists of elements of V at root but some will be identified under relation ~.

Pushouts in topology

  • Key way of glueing spaces together to make more complex spaces.

On one hand is a mobius strip. This shape famously has “only one side” as the front and back of the paper have been joined up. It also only has one edge, because the “right and left” edges of the strip of paper have been joined up. As it only has one edge, this means its edge (or boundary) is topologically a circle. Thus we can abstractly (though not physically) glue a disk onto that boundary.

Pushouts in other places

Groups

  • We already saw that coproducts are much more complicated for monoids and groups than for sets and posets. This is because of the binary operation: it means that after making the disjoint union of the underlying sets, we must then generate new elements produced by the binary operation.
  • To find pushouts of groups we have to start with the coproduct of groups, which we saw in the previous chapter is the “free product”, and then we have to do something analogous to quotienting out by an equivalence relation. In group theory this is provided by the theory of quotient groups. The idea is that one can “divide” a group by a special kind of subgroup, called a normal subgroup. We have actually seen an example of this although we didn’t put it that way: the integers modulo n can be constructed as a quotient group where you start with the integers and then quotient by the subgroup consisting of all the multiples of n.

Algebraic topology

  • Algebraic topology is about making relationships between spaces and groups.
  • A big problem is then actually calculating what the fundamental group is as a group, rather than just as an abstract definition. Pushouts help us do this because of a wonderful theorem called Van Kampen’s theorem.
  • The pushout method works much better if instead of using groups we use groupoids.

More general universal properties

  • Terminal and initial objects are cocones over empty diagrams: no objects and no morphisms.
  • Products and coproducts are cocones over discrete diagrams: no morphisms.
  • Pullbacks and pushouts are cocones over diagrams with just two morphisms pointing in opposite directions.
  • There are other properties like equalizers and coequalizers. They are cocones over parallel pair of arrows.
  • We also defined limits which are universal cones over a diagram and colimits which are universal cocones. They are superset of all these.
  • Equalizers and pullbacks are interchangeable in the presence of products, that is, we can make equalizers out of pullbacks and products, and we can also make pullbacks out of equalizers and products. It is perhaps more intuitive to state the result about limits in terms of products and equalizers, as products deal with multiple objects and equalizers deal with multiple morphisms between the same objects, and that is really the two features that a diagram can have.

Functors

  • Functor is a function on underlying data, preserving structure.
  • Functor is function between two categories.
  • In this case the definition of functor consists of a function on sets of objects, and a function on every homset. This is for small category.
  • Let C and D be (small) categories. A functor F : C -> D is given by
    • a function F : obC -> obD, and
    • for all objects x, y ∈ C, a function F : C(x, y) -> D(Fx, Fy) satisfying the following conditions called functoriality:
      • on identities: for all objects x ∈ C, F(1x) = 1Fx and
      • on composites: for all morphisms x -f-> y -g->z ∈ C, F(g ◦ f) = Fg ◦ Ff.
  • More generally, Let C and D be categories. A functor F : C -> D associates:
    • to every object x ∈ C an object Fx ∈ D,
    • to every morphism x -f-> y ∈ C a morphism Fy -Ff-> Fy ∈ D satisfying functoriality as above.
  • Like we talked about, after functors are applied, it need to satisfy identity and composition again.
  • In terms of definition of category with C1 and C0 where one is morphism and another set of objects, in that context, we can see functor as pair of functions that make the diagram commute.

Functors between small examples

  • Considering posets as categories, functor is aautomatically a order preserving function as well. For a -> a’, we get a morphism Fa -> Fa’ and since a ≤ a’, Fa ≤ Fa'.
  • In monoids and groups, the monoid homomorphism are the functors between those categories. The functorality maps out to preserving identity and binary operation in case of monoids which is same as conditions for monoid homomorphism.

Functors from small drawable categories

  • There is nothing left to specify or check as we know that identities must go to identities, and there are no non-trivial composable morphisms anyway. Note that Fa and Fb could be the same set, and Ff could itself be the identity: identities must be mapped to identities, but non-identities are allowed to be mapped to identities.
  • A functor A -> Mon just picks out a monoid homomorphism (and by implication, a pair of monoids for the source and target as well). In general a functor A -> C just picks out a morphism in C.
  • In this drawing, the top-and-right composite is Ft ◦ Ff which equals F(t ◦ f) by functoriality of F; similarly the left-and-bottom composite equals F(g ◦ s). The commutativity of the original square tells us t ◦ f = g ◦ s, so we must also have F(t ◦ f) = F(g ◦ s). So the second square commutes.
  • Let J be a finite category and C be any category. Then a diagram of shape J in C is a functor.
  • Let F : C -> D be a functor, and f an isomorphism in C with inverse g. Then Ff is an isomorphism in D with inverse Fg.
  • The fact that isomorphism is still an isomorphism after applying a functor is called preservation.

Free and Forgetful functors

  • When we were looking at products of posets we took products of their underlying sets and then constructed a “natural” ordering on that set. Without saying so, we were invoking a functor Poset Set , which takes each poset and “forgets” that it’s a poset. Without saying so, we were invoking a functor Poset -> Set which takes each poset and forgets that its a poset.
  • Functors that forget structure are called forgetful functors. They are often denoted U ( for underlying), so for poset A, we call its underlying UA.
  • Other forgetful functors are Grp -> Mnd, Abelian -> Grp, Toset -> Poset, Anything with structure -> Set.
  • The relationship they often have with a functor going the other way which does the “opposite” of forgetting structure: it creates structure freely and is called a free functor. By contrast, sometimes forgetful functors do not have a relationship with such a functor, and that is in itself interesting.
  • Order preserving functions between posets then become functors between special categories. Then we get a functor Pst -> Cat
  • We can express monoids as one object categories. If we decide in advance what the single object is going to be, then we get a functor Mnd -> Cat.
  • Free functors are harder than forgetful functors.
  • Without imposing any unnecessary constratints or using any extra information, we have to make Set -> Mnd or something like this.
    • e.g. Start with any set A and produce monoid of words in the elements of A. This is called a free monoid on A.
    • e.g. A -> {*} will turn every word to series of asterisks. So, this is like a free monoid functor.

Preserving and reflecting structure

  • In the forwards direction we have the question of preservation: given a type of structure in C, if we apply F does it still have that structure in D?
  • In the backwards direction we have the question of reflection: if we apply F to something in C and the result has a particular structure in D, can we conclude that it already had that structure in C?
  • Last time we talked about the split epics vs epics. Now, functors don’t preserve epics as structure but always preserve split epics.
  • Structures preserved by all functor are generally called absolute.
  • e.g. Those with rules where “for all” exists, they are easier to preserve even when compressed. Those with rules where “there exists”, they are harder to preserve when it compresses the structure.

Example 1

  • As the target category has only one object and only one morphism, we have no choice about where F can send everything: every object has to go to the single object and every morphism goes to the identity. Functoriality has to hold because the only morphism in the target category is the identity, so every equation of morphisms just reduces to an identity equalling itself.
  • Now we just check that this functor sends a non-isomorphism to an isomorphism. The single non-trivial morphism in C is not an isomorphism as it has no inverse, but it is mapped to the identity in D which is an isomorphism. So we see that F does not reflect isomorphisms.

Example 2

  • If we have two parallel arrows that are not equal instead of the diagram on the left in first example, then the diagram does not commute, as there are two paths with same endpoints whose composites are not the same.
  • Now if we again take the functor to the category , the parallel arrows will both be mapped to the identity, so the non-commutative diagram is mapped to a commutative diagram. This is thus a functor that does not reflect commutative diagrams.

General ideas

In Set any one-element set is terminal, and the empty set is initial. We can compare this with various categories of sets-with-structure.

  • In the category Pst of posets and order-preserving maps, any one-element poset is terminal and the empty poset is initial. So the forgetful functor Pst -> Set preserves terminal and initial objects.
  • In the category Grp of groups and homomorphisms, the trivial group has one element (the identity) and is both terminal and initial. So the forgetful functor Grp -> Set preserves terminal objects but not initial objects, because if we apply it to the initial object in Grp we do not get the initial object in Set.
  • In the category Top of topological spaces and continuous maps any one-point space is terminal and the empty space is initial. So the forgetful functor Top -> Set preserves terminal and initial objects.

Contravariant functors

  • It reverses the direction of morphisms and switches the order of composition.
  • F(g ◦ f) = Ff ◦ Fg.
  • A contravariant functor is a functor Cop -> D.

Algebraic Topology

  • The elements of the fundamental group are the homotopy classes of loops. This means, essentially, that we count loops as the same if they’re not really different, but you can continuously deform one into the other without breaking it or going over a hole in the space. We talked about this before in small categories as well.

Categories of categories Cat

  • Now, we want to show that there is an identity functor, composition of functors, and that axioms hold. So, its a bigger category.

  • By restricting the size of category we’re talking about, we avoid creating self-referential categorical loop.

  • First level is small categories which can be represented as sets (homsets). Then we make category Cat of small categories and all functors between them. We don’t include any of examples of “large categories of mathematical structures” like Set, Pst, Top etc,. for now. And it can’t of course contain Cat itself to avoid self-reference.

  • Then next level up is locally small categories. If morphisms between any two objects form a set, however the objects might form a large collection. So, in category Set, the objects are all possible sets. Set is locally small.

  • Then we make category CAT of locally small categories and all functors between them.

  • A poset is a category in which there is at most one morphism between any pair of objects. This means we have an “inclusion” functor Pst Cat which simply sends each poset to itself as a category.

  • If we define monoids as sets with a binary operation, then to construct an “inclusion” functor Mnd Cat we have to fabricate a single object from somewhere. We could decide that every monoid is going to become a one-object category with the same single object, say ∗. However, sending every monoid to itself expressed as a category is not quite as straightforward as for posets.

  • There are various forgetful functors from Cat to Set including functors that:

    1. send a small category to its set of objects,
    2. send a small category to its set of morphisms, or
    3. send a small category to its set of connected components.

  • The forgetful functors to Set are in a sense excessively forgetful. They don’t just forget structure, they also forget data. A more “sensible” forgetful functor would only forget the structure of a category, not the data, and that means that we wouldn’t land in Set but in the category of graphs.

  • Given a graph A, the free category on it has

    • objects: the same objects as A, and
    • morphisms: finite composable strings of morphisms in A.
    • Note that finite composable strings include strings of length 0 (empty strings), which will be the identities. Composition is then given by concatenation, just like for words in the free monoid, but with the extra composability condition.

  • At the top we have a category of “data equipped with a particular kind of structure”, together with structure-preserving maps. In good situations the free and forgetful functors are in a special relationship called an adjunction, which can be expressed via universal properties in various ways that are beyond our scope here. The composite UF is then a functor from the category of underlying data to itself, and has many excellent properties. It is a prototype example of what is called a monad. Monads are then an abstract way to study “sets with structure”, and more generally the category of data at the bottom could be something other than Set, in which case monads give us a very general way to study algebraic structure. In fact, at an abstract level this is a definition of algebra: something that can be studied via monads.

Terminal and Initial Categories

  • Given any category C there is a unique functor C -> 1 which is one object one morphism category,
    • all objects of C must go to single object of 1
    • all morphisms of C must go to identity morphism of 1
    • Functorality holds because everything is identity.
    • This is our terminal category.
  • For intial category, we can try taking empty category 0, which has no objects and no morphisms. There is then a unique functor to any category C, just like a mapping was defined from empty set to each element. And functorality is vacuously satisfied. So, its the initial category.

Products and Coproducts of categories

  • Composition is componentwise. We take the composite in C and composite in D individually, and then put them together in an ordered pair.
  • So, is identity.
  • (f2, g2) ◦ (f1, g1) = (f2 ◦ f1, g2 ◦ g1).
  • 1(c,d) = (1c, 1d).

Observations

  • Products of posets in the category Pst correspond to products of posets expressed as categories, in Cat.
  • Products of monoids in the category Mnd correspond to products of monoids expressed as categories, in Cat.
  • This can be said by saying that Pst -> Cat and Mnd -> Cat preserves products.

Isomorphism of categories

  • By definition, an isomorphism in Cat must be a functor with an inverse functor, but the question is what that means: how we might characterize that directly, and what relationship it gives us between isomorphic categories.

Given pair of functors with F and G being inverses. In terms of their representation as sets and functions, they look like this. We know that the identity functor acts as the identity function on both objects and morphisms, and that composition of functors happens by composition of the functions at the level of objects and morphisms. So F1 and G1 must compose to the identity function both ways round, and similarly F0 and G0. This says we must have a bijection at the level of objects and a bijection at the level of morphisms, as well as the usual functoriality. This means that C and D have same structure, just different names on objects and morphisms. And interesting thing is it doesn’t have to be one isomorphism. There can be other isomorphisms as well. So, saying two categories are isomorphic is different from actually specifying an isomorphism between them. So, we need to know what’s the “right” notion of sameness for categories.

  • In order to say that a functor F : C -> D is invertible it needs to have an inverse G, which means GF = 1C and FG = 1D. Now we unravel what this means: for two functors to be equal they have to have the same action on objects and on morphisms.
  • So for the first equation, on objects we’re saying ∀c ∈ C, GFc = c. We get something similar for the second equation.
  • BUt notions for sameness “wants” to be little weaker so that we don’t have tighter condition to say that they follow the same structure. Equality is too hard.
  • So, better notion of sameness is like this:
    • On morphisms: strictly invertible, so ∀ f ∈ C, GFf = f and similarly for the composite FG.
    • On objects: only invertible up to isomorphism, so ∀c ∈ C, GFc ≅ c and similarly for the composite FG.

Full and Faithful functors

  • We should not look at the set of morphisms overall, but we should look at individual homsets. This comes down to the difference between the two definitions of category we’ve seen:
    • By homsets: for every pair of objects a, b a set of morphisms C(a, b).
    • By total set of morphisms: a set C1 of morphisms equipped with source and target functions to the set C0 of objects.
  • Let F : C -> D be a functor.
    • F is called faithful if for all x, y ∈ C the function C(a, b) -> D(Fa, Fb) is injective. We also sometimes call this locally injective.
    • F is called full if for all x, y ∈ C the function C(a, b) -> D(Fa, Fb) is surjective. We also sometimes call this locally surjective.
    • If for all x, y the function C(a, b) -> D(Fa, Fb) is a bijection then we say F is full and faithful.
  • Locally means that we are watching those up real close.
  • In practice we often unravel the definitions as follows.
    • Full: ∀ Fx -h-> Fy ∈ D, ∃ x -f-> y ∈ C such that Ff = h.
    • Faithful: ∀ f,g: x -> y ∈ C, Ff = Fg ==> f = g.
    • Full and faithful: ∀ Fx -h-> Fy ∈ D, ∃! x -f-> y ∈ C such that Ff = h
  • Let F : C -> D be a full and faithful functor and a -f-> b be a morphism in C. Then f is an isomorphism iff Ff is an isomorphism.
  • Earlier on we said that if we express posets as categories then the functors between them are precisely the order-preserving functions. Likewise if we express monoids as one-object categories then the functors between them are precisely the monoid homomorphisms. What is this saying about the “inclusion” functors Pst -K-> Cat and Mnd -Σ-> Cat? ==> Its saying that the functors K and Σ both are full and faithful.
  • Full and faithful means “isomorphism at the level of morphisms” and “bijection up to isomorphism” for level of objects.
  • A functor F : C -> D is essentially surjective (on objects) if ∀ d ∈ D, ∃ c ∈ C such that f(c) ≅ d.
  • A functor F : C -> D is a pointwise equivalence if it is full and faithful, and essentially surjective on objects.
  • Suppose F : C -> D is full and faithful. Then F is “essentially injective on objects” as in the above definition.

Natural Transformations

  • Relationship between functors
  • Start by assuming that only possible notion of relationship between functions is equality, while knowing that for functors its too strict.
  • Given functors F, G: A -> B, a natural transformation α from F to G is depicted, or as α: F => G, and is given by:
    • for all objects x ∈ A, a morphism Fx -αx-> Gx ∈ B, such that
    • for all morphisms x -f-> y ∈ A the following square called the naturality square commutes.
  • The morphism αx is called component of α at x.
  • We think of natural transformation as 2-dimensional, like surface connecting paths made by functors.

Shape

  • The way we have drawn shape of natural transformation, we say that F and G have to be parallel, which means they have same endpoints. The shape of α is then called “globular”.
  • These square shapes are called “cubical”. In many situations, we define the cubical natural transformations using the definition of globular ones. e.g. In this cubical one below, we can say natural transformation α QF => GP. So, that way we study the cubical transformation as globular as well.
  • The reason why we even have cubical is it’s more naturally arising in higher dimensional spaces, so sometimes more productive.

Functor Categories

  • Assembling category can be done in so many different ways. We thus have had different definitions of category.
  • Now, we can assemble category using natural transformations as morphisms between functors and functors themselves. This is similar to when we did define category using functors as morphisms.
  • Given categories C, D, the functor category [C, D] has
    • objects: functors C -> D
    • morphisms: a morphism F -> G is a natural transformation.
  • Identities and composition for natural transformation are componentwise.
  • Given a functor F : C -> D the identity natural transformation 1F : F => F has all identity components.
  • Consider functors and natural transformations as shown below. The composite natural transformation β ◦ α : F => H is defined by the following components: for each x ∈ C, (β ◦ α)x = βx ◦ αx
  • That is Fx -(β . α)x -> Hx = Fx -αx-> Gx -βx-> Hx . This is also known as vertical composition.
  • A general principle is that functor categories inherit more of their properties from the target category than from the source category.
    • If D is discrete (only has identity morphisms) then the functor category [C, D] is discrete.
    • This principle can be useful to study a category C via functors into a category that we know has a lot of excellent structure, such as Set.
    • Given a category C, a functor Cop -> Set is called a presheaf on (or over) C. The category of presheaves over C is the functor category [Cop , Set].

Diagrams and cones over diagrams

  • Functor categories give us a way to define cones over general diagrams, in order to define limits over general diagrams.
  • A diagram of shape I in a category C is a functtor D: I -> C. We can imagine I to be a quintissential commuting square category, or a parallel pair of arrows, if we want to visualize. The functor then picks out a specific diagram of that shape in the category C.
  • To pick out a vertex, we use little technical trick: constant functor. A functor that sends every object to the same place. Since its a functor, it not just sends every object to same object, say v, but every morphism as well to identity on v.

Constant functor

Let I and C be any categories, and v an object of C. We write Δv: I -> C for the constant functor at v, defined as follows:

  • Given diagram D : I -> C, a cone over it with vertex v is a natural transformation Δv => D.
    • Taking I to be 0 -f-> 1 as category
    • Functor D: I -> C gives us this diagram in C : D(0) -D(f)-> D(1)
    • A natural transformation α : Δv => D has a component Δv(i) - αi -> D(i) for each object i ∈ I.
    • But αv(i) = v for all objects because of that assumption about I, we then have this:
      • αv(i) = v -α0-> D(0)
      • αv(i) = v -α1-> D(1)
    • For naturality, we only have one non-trivial morphism f ∈ I to consider.
  • Finally naturality corresponds to commutavitiy of every triangle necessary in a cone over diagram D, with each naturality square collapsing into a one triangle. This way of expressing general cones is the basis of general definition of “limit over a diagram of shape I”.

Natural Isomorphisms

  • An isomorphism in a functor category is a natural transformation with an inverse.
  • Natural transformation is an isomorphism iff all its components are isomorphisms.
  • A natural transformation is an isomorphism in the category [C, D] if and only if for all x ∈ C the component α x : Fx -> Gx is an isomorphism in D.
  • The inverse is components wise and vice versa.
  • An invertible natural transformation is called a natural isomorphism. If there is a natural isomorphism F => G we often write F =∼=> G or F ≅ G and say F and G are naturally isomorphic.
  • So, now we have two equivalent characterizations of natural isomorphisms:
    • abstract/categorical: isomorphisms in a functor category
    • concrete/pointwise: each component is an isomorphism
  • One is a concrete set of conditions to check to ensure that some abstract principle holds, and the abstract principle is then the thing that enables us to do things. The key is to know how the two are related. This is often generally referred to as coherence conditions.

Equivalence of categories

  • Using this “morphisms of functors” to make our nuanced version of sameness, called equivalence.
  • With isomorphism, we invoked some equalities between objects because isomorphism involves a pair of functors such that FG = 1 and GF = 1.
  • A functor F : C -> D is an equivalence if there is a functor G: D -> C and natural isomorphisms GF ≅ 1C and FG ≅ 1D . Then we say the categories C and D are equivalent, and that F and G are pseudo-inverses.
  • F and G are like “inverses up to isomorphism”
  • A functor is an equivalence if and only if it is a pointwise equivalence, that is, full and faithful and essentially surjective on objects.
  • The general idea is that equivalent categories are “the same” in an appropriate sense. Categories are isomorphic if they have exactly the same object and arrow structure, so the only difference is that everything is renamed. Categories are equivalent if they have the same arrow structure but the objects can be “fattened up” a bit by having many isomorphic copies, or “thinned down” by identifying isomorphic objects (making them the same). In the process of fattening or thinning we just have to be careful to adjust the morphisms appropriately so that they effectively stay the same,
  • A category is called indiscrete (or chaotic) if it is equivalent to the terminal category.
  • Indiscrete is basically way to make the objects the same without actually identifying them. This is the right level of nuance in a category.
  • Discrete and indiscrete categories have opposite universal properties. They are analogous (ideologically and formally) to discrete and indiscrete spaces in topology: in a discrete space all points are considered to be far apart, and in an indiscrete space all points are considered to be close together. The analogy is made formal by expressing the universal properties, by something called adjunctions.

Examples of equivalence in large categories

  • We have always said monoid is one-object category. In one sense, its not the same because monoid has underlying data a set of elements whereas a one object category has an object and morphisms. So, this sense of “is” is via equivalence in structure.
  • Deﬁning G is “easy” as we just send a one-object category to the monoid of its morphisms. But deﬁning F is “hard” because we have to decide which one-object version of the monoid to choose. However, it’s not excessively hard: we could just decide that the single object is always going to be ∗, say. In that case GF really is the identity on Mnd, but FG is only isomorphic to the iden- tity on ooCat. This is because if we start with a one-object category whose single object is not ∗, when we come back again via FG we will land on a category with the same monoid of morphisms, just a diﬀerently named single object. This is not really diﬀerent, just isomorphic.
  • Also, the pointwise way of looking at it is that G is surjective but F is only essentially surjective.
  • Both are full and faithful because a functor between one-object categories is precisely a monoid homomorphism.

When we first defined categories, we had a prototype category given by sets and functions. Now we get a prototype 2-dimensional category given by categories, functors and natural transformations. We say “2-category” instead of “2-dimensional category” so that it’s less of a mouthful.
