  • Physical Readiness: Good vision and hearing.
  • Intellectual Readiness: Remember letters and how they combine to a word.
  • Language Readiness: Ability to use sentences, speak clearly.
  • Personal Readiness: Ability to work with other children, follow guidelines etc.
Second stage
Starting to read very simple materials. Master of some hundred words. Can read simple materials independently. Start finding meaning from symbols on a page.
Third stage
Building a vocabulary fast. Unlock meaning through context. Starts reading for fun too.
Fourth stage
Refine the skills previously acquired.

Questions for active reading

We will need to have answer to first three questions to answer the fourth one. Inspectional Reading tends to answer the first two. Analytical the third and syntopical the fourth.

  1. What is the book about as a whole?
  2. What is being said in detail, and how?
  3. Is the book true, in whole, or part?
  4. What of it?

Classifying a reading material

First way

Expository Books
Conveys knowledge. Opinions, Theories, Hypotheses, or Speculations for which claim is made.
  • History Books : Narration of events. Chronotopic. ( Chronos being time , and topos being place )
  • Philosophy Books: Seeks truths rather than account of particular events, but employs common knowledge for it.
  • Science and Mathematics: Special experience to explain any point.
Poetry
Conveys artistic view.

Social Sciences :

Second way

Practical Books
Ends in action. Emphasis on application. Need to convert knowledge into rules of operation eventually.
  • Guidebooks, Manuals, Moral Treatises ( Like something on how economic, ethical, or political morals teaching how to act).
  • Books starting with “The Art of”, “How to”.
  • Questions about end of anything or the purpose it serves.
  • “Should/Ought/Good/Bad/Means” etc. used frequently.
Theoretical Books
Ends in knowledge.
  • Reportorial, Mathematical, or Statistical Studies that present, but don’t tell us what we should do or not do.
  • Questions about validity of something.
  • Uses “Is” instead of “should/ought” etc.

  • Example

    The Critique of Pure Reason and The Critique of Practical Reason classifies this distinction clearly. The first is about what is and how we know it, not how to know it. So, it’s theoretical. The second is about how we should conduct ourselves in a virtuous way. So, it’s practical.

Book Titles

  1. Knowing how “Principles of Psychology” is alike “Elements of Geometry” where principles and elements almost mean the same thing.
  2. Knowing how two books are alike and different based on some practical terms, we know what we can understand from the title.

How to make a book your own

  1. Underlining
  2. Vertical lines at the margin
  3. Stark, asterisk, or markers at the margin.
  4. Number in the margin :: To indicate sequence of points made by author in developing an argument.
  5. Numbers of other pages in the margin :: To follow a sequence to a consistent or contradictory opinions
  6. Circling key words or phrases
  7. Writing in the margin, top, or the bottom of the page.

Stating with brevity

  1. Don’t take sample summaries as if they are the only formulation of book’s unity. They can be different, and one better than the other.
  2. Though readers are different, the book is the same. So, there will always be a possibility of check of how accurate this summary is.

Aristotle’s summary of Odyssey

A certain man is absent from home for many years; he is jealously watched by Poseidon, and left desolate. Meanwhile his home is in a wretched plight; suitors are wasting his substance and plotting against his son. At length, tempest-tossed, he himself arrives; he makes certain persons acquainted with him; he attacks the suitors with his own hand, and is himself preserved while he destroys them.

Of Aristotle’s Ethics

This is an inquiry into the nature of human happiness and an analysis of the conditions under which happiness may be gained or lost, with an indication of what men must do in their conduct and thinking in order to become happy or to avoid unhappiness, the principal emphasis being placed on the cultivation of the virtues, both moral and intellectual, although other goods are also recognized as necessary for happiness, such as wealth, health, friends, and a just society in which to live.

Of Adam Smith’s Wealth of Nations

This is an inquiry into the source of national wealth in any economy that is built on a division of labor, considering the relation of the wages paid labor, the profits returned to capital, and the rent owed the landowner, as the prime factors in the price of commodities. It discusses the various ways in which capital can be more or less gainfully employed, and relates the origin and use of money to the accumulation and employment of capital. Examining the development of opulence in different nations and under different conditions, it compares the several systems of political economy, and argues for the beneficence of free trade.

Darwin’s Origin Of Species

This is an account of the variation of living things during the course of countless generations and the way in which this results in new groupings of plants and animals; it treats both of the variability of domesticated animals and of variability under natural conditions, showing how such factors as the struggle for existence and natural selection operate to bring about and sustain such groupings; it argues that species are not fixed and immutable groups, but that they are merely varieties in transition from a less to a more marked and permanent status, supporting this argument by evidences from extinct animals found in the earth’s crust, and from comparative embryology and anatomy.

Using Locke’s Essay Concerning Human Understanding

You may recall our observing that Locke himself summarized his work by saying that it was “an inquiry into the origin, certainty and extent of human knowledge, together with the grounds and degrees of belief, opinion and assent.” We would not quarrel with so excellent a statement of plan by the author, except to add two subordinate qualifications to do justice to the first and third parts of the essay: it will be shown, we would add, that there are no innate ideas, but that all human knowledge is acquired from experience; and language will be discussed as a medium for the expression of thought, its proper use and most familiar abuses to be indicated.

Outlining a book

  • Just like Stating with brevity means seeing the parts as a whole, we would like to see what parts make up the whole. We are trying to find the organization of parts that account for the whole.
  • One is simplifying the book, another is trying to bring complexity into our understanding.
  • For large books, it can span several pages.
  • We don’t have to follow the apparent structure of the book as indicated by it’s chapters.
  • Purpose of outlining is to necessarily verify our brief summary on the basis of our outline. It should be supportive to our main theme.

Sample Outline

The whole book is about so and so and such and such. That done, we might obey the third rule by proceeding as follows: (1) The author accomplished this plan in five major parts, of which the first part is about so and so, the second part is about such and such, the third part is about this, the fourth part about that, and the fifth part about still another thing. (2) The first of these major parts is divided into three sections, of which the first considers X, the second considers Y, and the third considers Z. (3) In the first section of the first part, the author makes four points, of which the first is A, the second B, the third C, and the fourth D. And so on and so forth.

Example 1 :: The United States Constitution

FIRST: The Preamble, setting forth the purpose(s) of the Constitution;
SECOND: The first Article, dealing with the legislative department of the government;
THIRD: The second Article, dealing with the executive department of the government;
FOURTH: The third Article, dealing with the judicial department of the government;
FIFTH: The fourth Article, dealing with the relationship between the state governments and the federal government;
SIXTH: The fifth, sixth, and seventh Articles, dealing with the amendment of the Constitution, its status as the supreme law of the land, and provisions for its ratifications;
SEVENTH: The first ten amendments, constituting the Bill of Rights;
EIGHTH: The remaining amendments up to the present day.

Example 2 :: Division of the First Article of U.S. Constitution

II, 1: Section I, establishing legislative powers in a Congress of the United States, divided into two bodies, a Senate and a House of Representatives;
II, 2: Sections 2 and 3, respectively describing the composition of the House and Senate and stating the qualifications of members. In addition, it is stated that the House has the sole power of impeachment, while the Senate has the sole power of trying impeachments;
II, 3: Sections 4 and 5, having to do with the election of members of both branches of Congress and with the internal organization and affairs of each;
II, 4: Section 6, stating the perquisites and emoluments of members of both branches, and stating one limitation on civil employment of members;
II, 5: Section 7, defining the relationship between the legislative and executive departments of the government and describing the President’s veto power;
II, 6: Section 8, stating the powers of Congress; II, 7: Section 9, stating some limitations on the powers outlined in Section 8;
II, 8: Section 10, stating limitations on the powers of the states and the extent to which they must give over certain powers to the Congress.

Discovering the author’s intentions

  • We are trying to start by finding what questions the author starts with.
  • Fallacy of thinking you can discover what was in an author’s mind from the book he has written.

Theoretical Questions

  • Does something exist?
  • What kind of thing is it?
  • What caused it to exist, or under what conditions can it exist, or why does it exist?
  • What purpose does it serve?
  • What are the consequences of its existence?
  • What are its characteristic properties?
  • What are its relations to other things of a similar sort, or of a different sort?
  • How does it behave?

Practical Questions

  • What ends should be sought?
  • What means should be chosen to a given end?
  • What things must one do to gain a certain objective, and in what order?
  • Under these conditions, what is the right thing to do, or the better rather than the worse?
  • Under what conditions would it be better to do this rather than that?

Terms

  • Terms are words/sentences/phrases that are used with similar meaning through the text.
  • Can be synonyms.
  • Same word might not refer to the same term.
  • Coming to Terms with the author means we agree on the meaning of words as used by the author.
  • Philosophers can often coin their own terms.
  • Different philosophers can use same common word as different terms.
  • Find meaning of term using context, and by finding other places it’s used in.
  • Single word is rarely repeated all over the place since it makes the text boring. So, synonyms are likely to be expected.
  • Single word may be related to multiple terms or single term related to multiple words.
  • “Illustration”, “Reading for Enlightenment”, “the process of passing from understanding less to understanding more by the operation of your mind upon a book” all mean the same term.
  • words used to arouse emotions, move us to action, change our minds etc.
  • Readers must usually come to terms with an author first before starting to understand the author’s discussions.

Finding key terms

  1. Frequent repetition
  2. Words that give you trouble. Maybe to author as well.
  3. Technical
  4. Explicit stress
  5. Typographical Marks ( Quotation / Italics )
  6. Discussion about the word before mentioning it

Example

  1. Adam Smith
    • labor
    • capital
    • land
    • wages
    • profits
    • rent
    • commodity
    • price
    • exchange
    • productive
    • unproductive
    • money
  2. Darwin
    • variety
    • genus
    • election
    • survival
    • adaptation
    • hybrid
    • fittest
    • creation

Key Sentences

  • Know the type of sentences:
    • Propositions
    • Problem Statements
    • Answers
    • Wishes/Intentions
  • Need to be able to slow down at key sentences while reading a book. Not everything is to be read at the same pace.
  • Author’s ideas not ours.
  • Terms make up propositions. By understanding proposition conveyed, we come to terms with the author.
  • Pausing over sentences that interest us rather than over ones that puzzle us is the single most obstacle to reading well.
  • Best guide to check whether we have understood propositions or not. Not knowing this means we got words from the author, not thought or knowledge. Think of it as translation in the same language.
    • Can you point to some experience you have had that the proposition describes or to which the proposition is in any way relevant?
    • Can you exemplify the general truth that has been enunciated by referring to a particular instance of it?
    • Imagining a possible case is as good as an actual one. Not being able to do this means we imparted words, not wisdom.
  • Be aware of propagandist/orator who try to leave certain things unsaid, just to ensure that they could be challenged if they were made explicit.
  • Always make sure of common notions used by the author. They may not be as common as the author’s thinking.

Finding propositions

Propositions are statements about what the author is proposing. Smallest logical element that we can work with.

  • Finding sentences that together form a sequence.
  • Finding something that’s stated by the author.

Finding arguments

  1. If you find conclusion first, look for reasons. If you find reasons first, see where they lead.
  2. Discriminate between the kind of argument that points to one or more particular facts as evidence for some generalization and the kind that offers a series of general statements to prove some further generalizations.
  3. Observe the things the author says he must assume, what he says can be proved, and what need not be proved because it’s self-evident.

Finding solutions

  1. Which of the problems that the author tried to solve did he succeed in solving?
  2. In the course of solving these, did he raise any new ones?
  3. Of the problems that he failed to solve, old or new, which did the author himself know he had failed on?

Criticizing a book

  • Even when saying that we agree, reader must be able to give grounds for agreeing, disagreeing, or even for suspending judgement.
  • Being passive and pliable is not same as teachable. For being teachable, you need to be able to exercise the power of independent judgement.
  • Understand the location and purpose of rhetoric correctly.
  • Suspend judgement until we’re satisfied with first two stages of reading. Then comes the right as well as the duty to turn critic.
  • Identifying criticism doesn’t mean disagreement. Criticism needs to be repeated in their own words, just to verify that they have understood the argument. Else, ignore it.
    • One who puts up a criticism with serious understanding, it’s a delight.
  • If the arguments need other book to be properly discussed, those works must be read before making a fair criticism.
  • Disagreements need to be resolved. Often times, emotion can color thoughts.
  • Inequality of knowledge is always curable by instruction.
  • Disagreement is related to either teaching or being taught.
  • The reader who doesn’t distinguish between the reasoned statement of knowledge and expression of opinion, isn’t reading to learn.
  • There is nothing that we know that is sure of not getting invalidated in the future. New evidence can surely invalidate.
  • A reader must say that he understands before he starts saying more about it. If he doesn’t understand, keep working on it. In case, the book itself is faulty, the reader must be able to locate reasons why it’s such a case. This requires great rigor on reader’s part before a judgement.
  • To resolve any dispute:
    • We need to acknowledge the emotions we bring to the table. We may even think we have reasons, when all we have are strong feelings.
    • We must make our assumptions explicit. What can then happen is that author and reader might have started with different assumptions. Good disagreement should not be in regards to assumptions.
    • An attempt for impartiality is a good antidote for blindness that’s almost inevitable.

Aids to Reading

  • No book should be, because no book can be, read entirely and completely in isolation.

Relevant Experiences

  • Common experience doesn’t have to be shared by everyone to be common. Common is not the same as universal. e.g. Experience of being a child of parents isn’t shared by orphans, but is considered to be common.
  • Mostly relevant to fiction and philosophy.
  • Special experiences required for understanding scientific literature.

Other Books

  • Not only are many of the great books related, but also written in a certain order that shouldn’t be ignored. 
    They may try to read The Federalist Papers without having first read the Articles of Confederation and the Constitution. Or they may try all these without having read Montesquieu’s The Spirit of Laws, Rousseau’s The Social Contract, and Locke’s second treatise Of Civil Government.
  • Great authors, by being great readers themselves, are constantly engaged in conversation with each other.
  • The chronology is often the easiest way to see the relationship, but there can be other ways too.
  • Very important in philosophy because philosophers are great readers of each other.

Commentaries and Abstracts

  • Should be used sparingly, thus being wise with their usage. The reason being commentators aren’t always right about comments into a book. They purport to tell everything that one has to know about the topic. e.g. Handbooks and manuals are often particularly misleading.
  • Another reason is that they may not be exhaustive, even if they are correct.
  • So, a maxim about commentary is to never use a commentary until after you have read the book.
  • An abstract cannot replace the reading of a book, but can tell us whether we want to read that book or not.

Reference Books

  • Dictionaries and Encyclopedias are two primary kinds of reference books frequently used.
  • Try to use context to find meaning of words as much as you can.
  • To use reference book, we need to vaguely understand it first. Else, you have 100 meanings in dictionary. Now, you can take it all wrong.
  • We need to be able to ask intelligent question to reference book to get an intelligent answer.
  • We need to know how information is organized in a reference book in order to use it effectively. Better read the author’s advice on how to use it.
  • There shouldn’t be opinions on reference books.
Santayana’s remark about the Greeks—that they were the only uneducated people in European history—has a double significance. The masses were, of course, uneducated, but even the learned few—the leisure class—were not educated in the sense that they had to sit at the feet of foreign masters. Education, in that sense, begins with the Romans, who went to school to Greek pedagogues, and became cultivated through contact with the Greek culture they had conquered.
  • Trying to use dictionary to settle argument about communism, or justice, or freedome is utter foolishness, since some of those theories came before a dictionary came.
    • So, dictionaries should be used without any judgement.
  • Don’t forget dictionary is a book about words, not about things. 
    1. WORDS ARE PHYSICAL THINGS—writable words and speak-able sounds. There must, therefore, be uniform ways of spelling and pronouncing them, though the uniformity is often spoiled by variations, and in any event is not as eternally important as some of your teachers may have indicated.
2. WORDS ARE PARTS OF SPEECH. Each single word plays a grammatical role in the more complicated structure of a phrase or sentence. The same word can vary in different usages, shifting from one part of speech to another, especially in a non-inflected language like English.
3. WORDS ARE SIGNS. They have meanings, not one but many. These meanings are related in various ways.
4. WORDS ARE CONVENTIONAL. They are man-made signs. That is why every word has a history, a cultural career in the course of which it goes through certain transformations.
  • Though the word “encyclopedia” is Greek, they didn’t have one. The reason why dictionaries came in the first place is when Romans tried studying Greek.
  • The first alphabetically ordered encyclopedia didn’t appear until about 1700.
  • Previously, knowledge war arranged based on seven liberal arts – grammar, rhetoric, and logic ( the trivium ); arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and music ( the quadrivium ).
  • Best encyclopedia is one arranged by both alphabets as well as by topic. For that reason alone, we need to understand how important the index is in a encyclopedia.
  • Facts should never be argued about in the first place. Encyclopedias should only be about facts, and nothing else.
  • Encyclopedias can properly describe a theory which is no longer held to be correct, when it is associated with a topic; but that doesn’t mean it’s putting false facts in there.
  • They shouldn’t be used to pursue understanding, which requires both imagination and reason.

Syntopicon

  • 3000 subjects or topics with references to pages where the subject is discussed.
  • Helps starting out any syntopical reading project.
  • Can help in three ways:
    • Initiatively: Help you start on particular ones on the subjects in which they are interested.
    • Suggestively: You can read relatively short passages from a large number of authors. So, suggests where to look deeply.
    • Instructively: Give direction to the reader, help compare based on different works and different authors, helps show multiple meaning of same passage because it’s repeated in different sections.

Pyramid of Books

  1. Books that teach both how to read and how to live :: < 1 out of 100 or 1000 or even 10000. No more than a few thousand books.
    • Worth reading analytically once. Skillful may get it in one run.
    • You might return to them but they will most likely always remain in the shelf.
    • You have milked it dry. The book unlikely has anything more to give to you.
  2. Out of few thousand such books, probably < 100 can’t be exhausted even by the best reading we can manage.
    • We know that when we have completed the book analytically, but have a suspicion as to there is more than that you got. If you knew immediately, you would have read it. Analytical reading demands us to. But at the time, we don’t know what is that we missed.
    • You cannot stop thinking about the book. Finally, you return to it when a remarkable thing happens.
  3. Of those books you return to, most will feel that there was less than you remembered. This is because you grew with time as well.
  4. Of those books you return to, there are very few books which you feel like have grown with you on returning to the book. < 100. Number decreases based on what appeals an individual reader.
    • You see things that you had never seen before.
    • Your previous understanding was true, and is true now, but in a different way.
    • You accessed the book on different surface level than you did the last time.

Levels of Reading

The levels of reading mean that they follow one after the another. You cannot skip the first and go to the second level.

Elementary Reading

It is about learning the basic rules so that we are able to understand what each sentence is saying.

  • Goal

    1. What is the sentence trying to say?
    2. Are you able to not look at dictionary all the time, not stumble over grammar and syntax?

  • Tools to employ

    • Vocabulary
    • Elemental Reading Skills
    • Grammar Rules and Mechanics

Inspectional Reading

Reading done the best given limited amount of time. Answers to questions in goal section can be written down in on the contents page, outline or anywhere possible so that we can come to it later for analytical reading even after months.

  • Goal

    1. To know whether this book deserves an analytical reading by answering the following questions:
      1. What is the book about?
      2. What is the structure of the book?
      3. What are it’s parts?
    2. Find answer to whether this book deserves more reading in limited amount of time.

  • Types

    Not necessarily distinct for experienced readers. Should be performed as separate at the starting phase though.

    1. Systematic Skimming/Pre-reading
    2. Superficial Reading

  • Tools to employ

    • Preface
    • Table of Contents
    • Random skimming

  • Rules

    • Skimming

      1. Look at the title page, and preface if available.
      2. Study the TOC.
      3. Check the index to estimate the range of topics covered and kinds of books and authors that are referred to. Look at some passages cited to some interesting terms.
      4. Look at the chapters that seem to be pivotal to its argument based on our current bias.
      5. Randomly turn the pages, read some paragraphs or pages in sequence, not more than that.

  • Suggestions

    • While tackling a difficult book for the first time, try to go one shot to the end, rather than stop where you get stuck.
    • Consulting footnotes, scholarly commentaries, and other sources for help without first reading it ourselves hinder our reading for understanding than boost it.
    • Don’t lose sight of the whole by nitpicking while going through for the first time. You will miss the forest for the trees.
    • Reading speed should vary based on complexity and nature of what material we read.
    • Racing through even the hardest way is the best way to read it inspectionally. Don’t be afraid to seem superficial.

  • What not to do

    • Not read inspectional when reading analytically or merging these two steps into one.

Analytical Reading

  • Reading done the best given unlimited amount of time.
  • Chewing and digesting what you can read.
  • Outlining a book and Interpretation of book meet at the level of propositions and arguments. By dividing the book into parts, we understand what points are being made. Out of those points, some will be questions and some answers. Some taken together make an answer. Now, we understand what the content of the book is.

  • Tools to employ

    1. Stating with brevity
    2. Outlining a book
    3. Discovering the author’s intentions

  • Rules

    • First Stage :: Finding what a book is about

      1. Classify the book according to kind and subject matter. Classifying a reading material
      2. State what the whole book is about with the utmost brevity. ( One or at most a few sentences ) Stating with brevity
      3. Enumerate its major parts in their order and relation, and outline these parts as you have outlined the whole. Outlining a book
      4. Define the problem or problems the author is trying to solve.

    • Second Stage :: Coming to Terms (Interpreting its contents)

      1. Find the important words and come to Terms.
      2. Mark the most important sentences and find propositions.
      3. Locate or construct the basic arguments in the book by finding them in connection of sentences. Key Sentences
      4. Find out what author’s solutions are.

    • Third Stage Part 1 :: Maxims of Intellectual Etiquette while criticizing a book

      1. You must be able to say, with reasonable certainty, “I UNDERSTAND”, before you can say any one of the following things: “I AGREE,” or “I DISAGREE,” or “I SUSPEND JUDGEMENT”.
      2. When you disagree, do so reasonably, and not disputatiously or contentiously.
      3. Respect the difference between knowledge and mere personal opinion, by giving reasons for any critical judgement you make.

    • Third Stage Part 2 :: Points of criticism

      • If the reader has done his due part, then the final conversation of reader with the author during disagreement “I understand but I disagree” can be made with following remarks:
        1. You are uniformed :: Saying that he lacks some piece of knowledge that is relevant to the problem at hand. e.g. Darwin lacked knowledge of genetics. In science, later researches often point this out.
        2. You are misinformed :: Saying that author asserts what is not the case. It’s a claim to have knowledge he doesn’t possess.
        3. You are illogical :: That he has committed a fallacy in reasoning. Inconsistency or incompatibility between assumptions and answers.
        4. Your analysis is incomplete :: If we fail to raise first three points before we come to this, that means we agree with author as far as he has gone. This is saying that author hasn’t solved all the problems he started with, or hasn’t made good use of his materials as possible, or hasn’t seen potential ramifications, or has failed to make distinctions that are relevant to the argument. e.g. Aristotle’s Politics because of erroneous acceptance of slavery. Euclid’s postulates about relation of parallel lines etc.

Syntopical Reading

  • Comparative Reading
  • Knowing that to answer the question, we need to read more than one book.
  • Curious paradox is involved in syntopical reading.
  • Identification of subject matter must follow the reading, not precede it.
  • Reading inspectionally becomes very necessary at this point. So, both inspectional and analytical reading come as a part of syntopical reading.
  • Inspectional reading helps us to give idea of our subject so that our subsequent analytical reading is productive, and helps cut down our bibliography to a reasonable size.
    • You need to know how to read some books faster than others.
  • We aren’t concerned about author’s questions when reading syntopically. It’s about us and our concerns.
  • Everything we read must try to lighten up our ignorance about the question we have asked ourselves.
  • But we must also agree that an adequate understanding of the problem isn’t always available until we have inspected many of the books from our original list.
  • Unless you know what books to read, you cannot read syntopically, but unless you can read syntopically, you do not know what to read.
    • Asking for help with someone familiar with it might also turn out to be a hindrance than of help.
    • For this reason, syntopicon is a great tool.

  • Goal

    • To properly formulate answer to a question on a broad topic

  • Difficulty

    If you are just trying to read about love, it’s hard to skip any material at all.

    Stones are said to love the center of the earth. The upward motion of fire is called a function of its love. The attraction of iron filings to a magnet is described as an effect of love. Tracts have been written on the love life of amoebae, paramecia, snails, and ants, to say nothing of most of the so-called higher animals, who are said to love their masters as well as one another. When we come to human beings, we discover that authors speak and write of their love for men, women, a woman, a man, children, themselves, mankind, money, art, domesticity, principles, a cause, an occupation or profession, adventure, security, ideas, a country life, loving itself, a beefsteak, or wine. In certain learned treatises, the motions of the heavenly bodies are said to be inspired by love; in others, angels and devils are differentiated by the quality of their love. And of course God is said to be Love.

    What kind of love are you trying to understand becomes a pressing question now. Then, as you narrow down, love can sometimes be attributed as just desire by some writers, mystical by others, and logical by another group. They can completely disagree about what love is. Even if you dissect deep enough, there are still plenty of questions as to how it changes, differences between motherly love and child’s love, etc.

  • Tools to employ

    • Read more than one book
    • Use a syntopicon
    • Take help from one already familiar on the subject
    • Library
    • Reference section of books

  • Rules

    1. Finding the relevant passages. Identifying the relevant books as well as relevant passages at the same time might be difficult. As we start our reading list, it’s easier to make these two steps coalesce.
    2. Bringing the authors to terms. Identifying the different wording but same terminology used by different authors into one that you choose. It means you are forcing author to use your language. If it coincides, we should tend that as merely accidental. So, it’s in one way like translation.
    3. Getting the questions clear. We need to frame a set of neutral questions to shed light on our problem, to which each of our authors will try to answer. Also, we have to accept that an author might not give answer to any of our questions. Sometimes, we may have to implicitly tell the answers if not stated explicitly.
      • Questions should be put in an order that’s helpful for our investigation. The first questions usually have to do with existence or character of the phenomenon or idea we are investigating. Final set of questions might have to do with consequences of answers to previous questions.
    4. Defining the issues
      • Not all authors agree or disagree on all or some points that they have made in their book. There could well be more than two alternative answers given by different authors.
      • Differences in answers can be ascribed to differences in conception of question or different views on the subject.
      • Sorting and arranging of controversies, as well as constituent issues, is essential.
    5. Analyzing the discussion
      • Is it true? What of it?
      • Truth is to be found in the conflict of opposing answers, many of which will have persuasive evidence and convincing reasons to support them.
      • Thus, we must ask questions in a certain order, and be able to defend that order.
      • More general issues should precede less general ones, and relations among them should be clearly indicated.
      • We must be able to point to the texts in the books examined that support our classification of answers.
      • Now, it may result in a detailed question that may lay groundwork for a complete work in itself. That’s how an original thinker is born.
      • We need to be very objective else it’s just a mere voice in the discussion. It should be “Dialectial Objectivity”.

Special Notes on Reading Specific Books

Practical Books

  • Practical books can never solve the practical problems with which they are concerned. It can be solved by action alone.
  • Practical books can state rules, but can state principles that underlie the rules to make them digestable.
    • Principles generally are theoretical in sense, even for a practical book.
  • Presentation of rules OR Principles that generate rules. eg. Driver’s manual vs Books in Economics and Politics.
  • There will always be mixture of oratory and propaganda in practical books. It will try to persuade you. We just need to make sure that we identify its oratory. We don’t need to be emotionally restraint, but just enough to not take bad deals.
  • “Personality” of author is more important in these cases than theoretical books. e.g. Knowing about Greek society at the time of Aristotle can put us in light of his comments on slavery.
  • Are the two most important questions in case of practical books.
  • This question changes to Is it the best way to seek it?

Rule Book

  • Look for imperative rather than declarative sentence, which is a rule.
  • If rules follow principles, significance of principles found in rules is in the actions they recommend.
  • We not only need to figure out whether rules can be derived from principles, but also figure how they should be applied in practice.

Imaginative Literature

  • Though it’s hard to define rules to read imaginative literature, skill to read such books is more widely possessed.
  • Many of us know that we liked a novel, but can’t give a clear account on why we liked it.
    • Those who cannot say what they liked about a book haven’t dived beyond the obvious surface of the book.
  • Beauty is harder to analyze than truth, and such books are more for pleasure, than for teaching.
  • Know that author tries to maximize the latent ambiguities of words for richness.
  • Metaphors and multiplicity of meanings can lead to an entire different outcome which is perfectly fine.
  • Rules on how to not read it:
    • Don’t try to resist the effect that the work has on you. We must allow it to move us, let it do whatever it wants to do on us.
    • Don’t look for terms, propositions, or arguments in imaginative literature.
    • Don’t criticize fiction by standards of truth or with standards of communication of knowledge.
  • The truth of a imaginative literature is it’s verisimilitude.
  • Rules are not to spoil enjoyment of a novel or a play, but to enrich pleasure by knowledge of sources of delight.
  • For the final question, “What of it” is irrelevant to reading of stories and poems. But some stories like “Animal Farm” etc. are powerful attacks on totalitarianism. So, they can lead to action, but isn’t necessary that they do so.
  • Fiction is important because it has the power to move the unconscious.

Rules

  • Structural Rules

    • Classify a work of imaginative literature according to its kind. e.g. Play, Novel, Poem
    • Must grasp the unity of the whole work. e.g. For story it’s the plot.
    • Need to know where it begins, and where it comes out at.

  • Outlining

    • Elements of fiction are its episodes and incidents, its characters, and their thoughts, speeches, feelings, and actions.
    • Terms are connected in propositions. Elements of fiction are connected by the background against which they stand out in.
    • Just like we move from evidence to conclusion in expository book, we after being acquainted with characters join them in the imaginary world, and live it in imaginative literature. The unraveling of the plot is the dynamic connection.

  • Critical Rules

    • Don’t criticize until you fully appreciate what the author has tried to make you experience. Criticism is only applied to what he makes of it, not what we make of it. We cannot change the world he create as we like, and criticize it.

Suggestions for stories

  • Read it quickly and with total immersion. Read in one sitting if possible so that the unity of plot doesn’t escape you.
  • Try as hard as you can to live in his world, not yours. Don’t judge unless you have lived it completely to your ability.
  • Terms of story are its characters and incidents. This doesn’t mean remembering every character and every relation. We need to understand the action of main characters.
  • A story is like life itself; in life, we do not expect to understand every events as they occur, at least with total clarity, but looking back on them, we understand.
  • As a story’s finished, all speculations are meaningless. Preludes are ridiculous. Life goes on, but the story does not. We have to accept it and move on.
  • Fictions do make us empathize with some character, and that’s most likely the reason we like any story. We suspect life as we know is unjust. Our stories, by doing a just ending, makes it extremely satisfying to us. Even with high tragedy, we are convinced that our hero comes to understand his fate even though he may not deserve it. This is the kind of satisfying remark to good stories.
  • “As long as man is man, they will go on satisfying him, giving him something that he needs to have—a belief in justice and understanding and the allaying of anxiety.”

On Epics

  • A long epic poem is apparently the most difficult thing a man can write.
  • Epics are hard to read because they are written in verse. They demand a lot of attention, involvement, and imagination on the parts of the reader.
  • e.g. Iliad and Odyssey of Homer, Dante’s Divine Comedy, Milton’s Paradise Lost, and Virgil’s Aeneid.

Suggestions for plays

  • Play too is story, added with the fact that we have to be more active to create the background, which is not available in play like in novels.
  • Play can’t be completely apprehended without acting on stage. So, we as readers need to supply that dimension.
  • The final question about understanding a play is to try directing the play. Try to make characters say the line, put emphasis on words, see the climax in action.
  • Shaw’s plays were written not just to be acted, but to be read as well. Aristophanes plays had leading actor step out of character every now and then to deliver something for the audience like political speech.
  • Read puzzling pieces out aloud with expression.

On Tragedy

  • The tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles, and Euripedes, the plays of Shakespeare, Molière’s comedies, the works of a very few moderns—are very great indeed, for they contain within them some of the deepest and richest insights men have ever expressed in words.
  • The first advice while reading a tragedy is to remember that the essence of tragedy is time, or rather lack of it. None of the Greek tragedies wouldn’t have resolved simply if there was enough time.
  • The second advice is that we should imagine words being spoken by people of enormous stature.

On Lyric Poetry

  • Poetry is kind of spontaneous overflowing of the personality.
  • A good poem can be worked at, re-read, and thought about over and over for the rest of your life. You will never stop finding new delights in there.
  • Great poems can grow alongside us, thus unlocking something that we had never seen before during our last read.
  • The first rule is to read it without stopping, whether you think you understand it or not.
  • The second rule is to read it again but out loud.
  • Know whether the words pop out because of the rhythm, repetition, or a sequence. This helps us discover our understanding of the poem.
  • Good lyrics describe conflict. Sometimes, it is just implied not stated. Conflict can be between people, images, or ideas. e.g. Love and Time, Life and Death, Transience and Eternity of Beauty etc.

On Reading History

  • History as written restricts us to essentially narrative accounts, thus a story.
  • History is implicit in time, whether they’re ordered or not.
  • Like law assumes that recent accounts of eyewitnesses can’t be true, it’s a foolish excuse to expect that out of historical narratives.
  • Historian doesn’t make up the facts, still history is more close to fiction than to science.
  • It’s essential to recognize which way the historian we are reading is operating. Thus, we must read multiple account if we really want to understand an event or period.
  • Example of how impactful a piece of history is:
Let us take the example of Thucydides. You may be aware that he wrote the only major contemporary history of the Peloponnesian War at the end of the fifth century B.C. In a sense, there is nothing to check his work against. What, then, can we expect to learn from it?
Greece is now a tiny country; a war that occurred there twenty-five centuries ago can have little real effect on our life today. Everyone who fought in it is long dead, and the specific things for which they fought are long dead, too. The victories are now meaningless, and the defeats without pain. The cities that were taken and lost have crumbled into dust. Indeed, if we stop to think of it, almost all that remains of the Peloponnesian War is Thucydides’ account of it.
Yet that account is still important. For Thucydides’ story —we might as well use that word—has had an influence on the subsequent history of man. Leaders in later eras read Thucydides. When they found themselves in situations that even faintly approximated that of the tragically divided Greek city-states, they compared their own position to that of Athens or Sparta. They used Thucydides as an excuse and a justification, and even as a pattern of conduct. The result was that by ever so little, perhaps, but perceptibly, the history of the world was changed by the view held of a small portion of it by Thucydides in the fifth century B.C
Thus we read Thucydides not because he described perfectly what happened before he wrote his book, but because he to a certain extent determined what happened after.
  • Read history to learn the way men act in all times and places, especially now.
  • While reading history book, we need to precisely know what it is about and what it is not about.
  • How an author outlines history book e.g. based on decade, based on wars, based on other rubrics of his own choosing is an important question to be answered while reading history.
  • We expect a historian to be informed by reading other sources on it. We can then identify misuse of sources etc.
  • History not only is account, but changes other pieces of history that follow it, by result of their effects in later time.
  • History is for giving us direction of practical, political action.

Reading biographies and autobiographies

  • Definitive biographies cannot be written about living persons.
  • Since the ability to gather materials is different from the talent for shaping those into a good book, definitive biographies aren’t always easy to read.
  • “Boswell’s Life of Johnson” is interesting in that regards.
  • An authorized biography tries to show everything in the best light possible, thus not that great either.
  • We want biographies to be as accurate as the ycan be.
  • Some good biographies : Izaak Walton’s Lives of his friends, the poets John Donne and George Herbert, John Tyndall’s account of his friend Michael Faraday in Faraday the Discoverer. Plutarch’s Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans are didactic with a moral purpose.
Incidentally, Plutarch’s is another historical work that has exercised a profound influence on subsequent history. For example, just as Plutarch shows Alexander the Great modeling his own life on that of Achilles (whose life he learned about from Homer), so many later conquerors have tried to model their lives on that of Plutarch’s Alexander.
  • Everyone has secrets they cannot divulge or some illusions about themselves. Every book is tainted by the character of the author in some respect.
  • Read as many biographies as you can if you really want to know about the person, including his own autobiography if there is one.

Reading about current events

  • As much as we cannot know about veracity of history, we cannot know facts even for the current events.
  • Reporters tell stories, and mostly they are parts of fact, not fact itself.
  • Ask these questions because it always matters what reporter’s mind is at when reading about current events:
    1. What does the author want to prove?
    2. Whom does he want to convince?
    3. What special knowledge does he assume?
    4. What special language does he use?
    5. Does he really know what he is talking about
  • Try to know whom the author is trying to convince. Do you fall in that category? If you don’t belong to the audience for which it is intended, you may not want to read it.
  • Know what “opinions” and “prejudices” the author has.
  • Keep note of special trigger words that author is using to trigger a certain reaction from us.
  • Be very aware while reading books and articles about current events. We don’t have to be this aware while reading Aristotle or Shakespeare.

A note on digests

  • Reading for information about understanding – how others have understood it.
  • A summary only functions well if it impelled us to read the original since it was merely informational.
  • The more succinct a digest is, the question of what’s left out becomes more critical. So, it can be very demanding and difficult to know what was left out.

On Reading Science and Literature

  • Today, science tends to be written by experts for experts.
  • Read the great scientific classics of our tradidion like Newton’s Principia Mathematica. These are read to understand the history and philosophy of science, not get contemporary knowledge in Science.
  • Scientific objectivity isn’t about not having a bias. It’s about honest confessions of bias beforehand.
  • Suggestions for reading classical scientific books:
    • Understand the presuppositions.
    • Look for inductive arguments primarily, but know that we may not follow the evidence for these because of the lack of expertise in the field.
  • Science needs new words to improve the language and the language needs new words to improve science as well.

Mathematics

  • Some psychologists think we have “symbol blindness” which might be the reason for being afraid of maths.
  • We learned our language twice: once by speaking and once by reading. For maths, it’s almost only writing.
  • So, the deal might be that we are puzzled at the elementary level in Maths. We need to learn its vocabulary, grammar, and syntax properly to understand treatises written with it.
  • The beauty of mathematics is that unlike we cannot truly comprehend each other’s emotions and relations, we can perfectly communicate what we can express in mathematical language.
  • Start with “Elements of Geometry” by Euclid to see how beautiful and satisfying maths can be.
  • Quod erat facendium ( What is required to do )
  • Quod erat demostradum ( What is required to prove )
  • The truth of the connection between postulates is what’s being proved.

  • Handling maths in scientific books

    1. Read elementary mathematics better than you think. Can start by reading classical Greek Mathematicians.
    2. Read from beginning to end – with pencil in hand – with a scratch pad. What seems difficult skip. It’s not necessary to read all proposition, construction problems, theorems, complicated stuff in detail, especially the first time.
    3. You can avoid diagrams if they trouble you.
    4. Think how difficult it would have been to communicate if there was no mathematics here. e.g. Galileo’s Two New Sciences.

On Reading Philosophy

  • Children ask amazing questions all the time. “Why are people”, “What makes the cat tick?”, “What’s the world’s first name?”, “Did God have a reason for creating the earth?”. The search for wisdom comes from a child’s mouth. Philosophy, according to Aristotle, begins in wonder. It begins in childhood, even if for most of us it stops there as well.
  • As we grow, our curiosity degrades in quality.
  • We must understand that the mind not agitated by good questions cannot appreciate the significance of even the best answers.
  • By telling a child there is no answer, even when there’s one, or demanding them to ask no more, we slowly poison their curiosity to ask only those questions what adults think are important.
    • Child will then start to think its impolite to be too inquisitive. Then and there, the questions start to switch from seeking understanding to seeking information.
  • Some good philosophical questions on being/existence:
    • What is the difference between existing and not existing?
    • What is common to all the things that do exist, and what are the properties of everything that does exist?
    • Are there different ways in which things can exist—different modes of being or existence?
    • Do some things exist only in the mind or for the mind, whereas others exist outside the mind, and whether or not they are known to us, or even knowable by us?
    • Does everything that exists exist physically, or are there some things that exist apart from material embodiment?
    • Do all things change, or is there anything that is immutable?
    • Does anything exist necessarily, or must we say that everything that does exist might not have existed?
    • Is the realm of possible existence larger than the realm of what actually does exist?
  • These questions start on the idea of becoming/non-becoming, but start a whole lot of other questions. About necessity and contingency; about the material and the immaterial; about the physical and the non-physical; about freedom and indeterminacy; about the nature and extent of human knowledge; about the freedom of the will etc.
  • There are two groups of questions:
    • Practical or Normative: Questions concerning good and evil, right and wrong, what’s to be done etc.
    • Theoretical or Speculative: Questions about being and becoming, have to do with what is or happens in the world
      • Metaphysical: Questions about being or existence. Work in the philosophy of nature.
      • Epistemology: Questions about our knowing anything, with the causes, extent, and limits of human knowledge, certainties and uncertainties with it etc.
  • Normative philosophy tend to seek goals like leading a good life, instituting a good society etc.
  • What is and what happens in the world OR What men ought to do or seek.
  • Questions about first order knowledge, about the content of our thinking when we try to answer first order questions.
  • These days most philosophers devote exclusively to second order questions because they feel like first order questions cannot be answered reasonably well. And they seek experts only opinions rather than populace these days.
  • Up to about 1930, philosophy books were written for general public. Hoped to be read by peers, but by intelligent folks as well.
  • In answering philosophical questions, there is only one method to employ. To think.
If your question were scientific, you would know that to answer it you would have to perform some kind of special research, either by way of developing an experiment to test your answer, or by way of observing a wide range of phenomena. If your question were historical, you would know that you would also have to perform research, although of a different kind. But there is no experiment that will tell you what all existing things have in common, precisely in respect to having existence. There are no special kinds of phenomena that you can observe, no documents that you can seek out and read, in order to find out what change is or why things change. All you can do is reflect upon the question. There is, in short, nothing to do but think.
  • So philosophers do think more profoundly about the common experience than rest of us have.
  • We need to understand what questions can a philosopher deal with, if that could instead be solved scientifically. Often times, philosophers don’t know that answer at the time of writing.
    • Example is how ancient philosophers asked about the difference between the matter of terrestrial and celestial bodies. Without telescope, they thought celestial bodies only changed in place. Until the discovery of a telescope, they didn’t know.

Common Exposition Methods Employed in Philosophy

  • Philosophical Dialogue

    • Adopted by Plato, in his Dialogues.
    • When the style is enriched by the high drama—some would say the high comedy—of the story of Socrates, it becomes enormously powerful.
    • But attempt at this by anyone except Plato had little success. Their dialogues are flat and dull, almost unreadable.
    • This is the way of simply keep asking questions.

  • Philosophical Treatise or Essay

    • Aristotle was Plato’s best pupil. He’s said to have written dialogues, but none has survived.
    • What survived are curiously difficult essays on different subjects. So, these can be notes taken by the students when they heard the master speak.
    • Immanuel Kant, though being influenced by Plato in philosophical sense, adopted Aristotle’s way of exposition.
    • There is a philosophical beginning, middle, and end.

  • Meeting of Objections

    • Developed in the Middle Ages and perfected by St. Thomas Aquinas in “Summa Theologica”.
    • Question raising and objection meeting.
    • Divided into parts, treatises, questions, and articles.
      • Question is posed. (Wrong) answer to it is given. Arguments are put forth in support of that wrong answer. Then they are countered by an authoritative text. The final answer is then given. Then reples to each of the arguments against each of the wrong answer.
    • This detailed recognition of conflicts, and reporting of different views is amazing.
    • At that time, philosophers should be prepared to defend their views in open public dispute.

  • Systemization of Philosophy

    • In 17th century, Descartes and Spinoza developed this style fascinated by the promised success of maths in organizing human knowledge about nature.
    • Tried giving same formal structure like Euclid did to geometry.
    • propositions, proofs, corollaries, lemmas etc.
    • Because of this, we can skip a great deal here like we can in Newton’s. But, we cannot do this with Aristotle’s or Kant’s.

  • Aphoristic Style

    • Adopted by Nietzsche in works like “Thus Spoke Zarathustra” and certain modern French philosophers.
    • The advantage of such style is that it is heuristic; the reader has more impression that more is being said than is actually said. So, it employs you to think as much as the philosophers. Hard to criticize.

Suggestions to read Philosophy

  • Discover the questions it is trying to answer.
  • Look for the controlling principle. It might sometime take years and many readings to discover this. The discovery that we come ono our own will be much more valuable than someone else’s ideas. Look if they agree throughout in their controlling principle.
    • For Plato it is that conversation about philosophical subjects is perhaps the most important of all human activities. He may not state it directly but there are traces of that in the writing.
    • In Ethics, Aristotle talks about a wide variety of things: happiness, habit, virtue, pleasure etc. but the controlling principle is that happiness is the whole of good, not the highest good.
    • In Kant’s, limitation of mind is a controlling principle.
  • In philosophy, we need to pay closest attention to philosopher’s principles. What he marks as self-evident. Some are drawn directly from experience.
  • “A philosopher, faced with a problem, can do nothing but think about it. A reader, faced with a philosophical book, can do nothing but read it—which means, as we know, thinking about it. There are no other aids except the mind itself.”
  • There’s utility in reading the works of other great philosophers who have dealt with same problems as your author. The philosophers carry a long conversation with each other in history of thought.
  • When philosophers disagree, it shouldn’t trouble us. If it is persistent disagreement, it may point to perhaps a great unsolved , or insoluble problem. Secondly, disagreements of others are relatively unimportant because we have to make up our own mind. We must answer for ourselves.

On Theology

  • Natural Theology and Dogmatic Theology
  • e.g. To find causation, you need to stop somewhere. Aristotle called this uncaused cause an unmoved mover.
  • Dogmatic Theology differs from Philosophy because the first principles are articles of faith adhered beforehand.
  • We should read dogmatic theology by accepting the first principles of author as true while reading the book.
A note on dogmatic theology:
The first mistake many readers make is to refuse to accept, even temporarily, the articles of faith that are the first principles of the author. As a result, the reader continues to struggle with these first principles, never really paying attention to the book itself. The second mistake is to assume that, because the first principles are dogmatic, the arguments based on them, the reasoning that they support, and the conclusions to which they lead are all dogmatic in the same way.
  • Reading canonical books like “Holy Bible” is similar to how a fledgling lawyer, in order to pass his bar exam, must read certain texts in a certain way to attain a perfect score.
  • So, we take their ways first to read it in their sense.
A note on dogmatic reader who's reading the canonical book:
He reads essentially without freedom; but in return for this he gains a kind of satisfaction that is possibly never obtained when reading other books.

On Reading Social Science

  • Aim is to create artificial models of society that allow us to explore social consequences of technological innovation.
  • The ease of reading social science is that we can add any term with society from “aberrant” to “zymotic”, and that sounds well. And we do likely have strong opinions already without much reading on these topics. The same fact makes the topic difficult to read. The very familiarity of terms and propositions in social science is an obstacle to understanding.
    • e.g. GNP ( Gross National Product ) can be used misleadingly without an understanding of what it means.
  • It is one thing to define a circle or an isosceles triangle; it is quite another to define an economic depression or mental health.
  • Much social science is a mixture of science, philosophy, history, and some fiction as well. The mixture changes which is the major issue.
  • To even answer what kind of book is this, it’s difficult. Though it is the most difficult, its essence cannot be negated.
  • And to answer the last question “What of it” is difficult because it is one thing to agree on the conclusions, and another to change your already owned opinions on it.
  • In social science, you have to read not one book but many to keep up with it. They update it with revised versions, new works come up rapidly rendering old ones obsolete.
  • It needs to be read syntopically.

Dialectical Objectivity

  • Looking at all sides and take no sides. A reader will fail to do that, but must try.
Perfect dialectical objectivity is not guaranteed by avoiding explicit judgments on the truth of conflicting opinions. Partiality can intrude in a variety of subtle ways—by the manner in which arguments are summarized, by shades of emphasis and neglect, by the tone of a question or the color of a passing remark, and by the order in which the various different answers to key questions are presented.
  • So, a reader must constantly refer back to the actual text, read relevant passages over and over, quote that while presenting that to a wider audience.
  • The language though when presenting the idea must not be author’s. It should accompany the quoted text, so that reader can judge for himself whether the interpretation of the author is correct.

Exercise in Syntopical Reading

The author of this book did do a full exercise to show how it’s done. It’s in “The Idea of Progress”

  1. Produce a list of works, a massive bibliography, to be examined for relevant passages. (450)
    • Done by inspectional reading of several times for many books. Educated guesses.
    • Progress in Titles.
    • Mostly focused on expository works. Not fictional or poetical works.
    • Including novels, plays, and poems in syntopical reading is difficult because:
      • Characters rarely take clear positions.
      • Backbone or Essence of the story is plot.
      • Hard to seperate irony and humor from logical undertaking.
    • Understanding what authors mean by progress and making a clear statement from our side.
      • Majority is “Likeable movement forward in time”. So, rather than a neutral movement in time, we decide to choose a favorable movement. And those who just care about movement become minority now.
  2. Now, we define the questions to which we expect authors to give answers on:
    • Does progress occur in history?
    • Is it a fact that general course of movement is in the direction of improvement?
  3. We also need to define possible answers to this, but must recognize different ways of saying one answer.
    • Yes
    • No
    • We cannot know
  4. Find out sub-ordinate issues even between authors who have a same answer. In this case, further questions can be:
    • Is progress necessary, or is it contingent on other occurences?
    • Will progress continue indefinitely, or will it eventually come to an end or “plateau out”?
    • Is there progress in human nature as well as in human institutions —in the human animal itself, or merely in the external conditions of human life?
  5. Even among progress authors, we can dive deep into the respects in which progress occurs. Identification of key respects in which they believe that progress occurs:
    • Knowledge
    • Technological
    • Economic
    • Political
    • Moral
    • Fine Arts

Highlights

Hence when we contrast active with passive reading, our purpose is, first, to call attention to the fact that reading can be more or less active, and second, to point out that the more active the reading the better.

The mistake here is to suppose that receiving communication is like receiving a blow or a legacy or a judgment from the court. On the contrary, the reader or listener is much more like the catcher in a game of baseball. Catching the ball is just as much an activity as pitching or hitting it. The pitcher or batter is the sender in the sense that his activity initiates the motion of the ball. The catcher or fielder is the receiver in the sense that his activity terminates it. Both are active, though the activities are different.

The analogy with writing and reading is almost perfect. The thing that is written and read, like the ball, is the passive object common to the two activities that begin and terminate the process.

If the book is completely intelligible to you from start to finish, then the author and you are as two minds in the same mold. The symbols on the page merely express the common understanding you had before you met.

Without external help of any sort, you go to work on the book. With nothing but the power of your own mind, you operate on the symbols before you in such a way that you gradually lift yourself from a state of understanding less to one of understanding more. Such elevation, accomplished by the mind working on a book, is highly skilled reading, the kind of reading that a book which challenges your understanding deserves.

Thus we can roughly define what we mean by the art of reading as follows: the process whereby a mind, with nothing to operate on but the symbols of the readable matter, and with no help from outside,* elevates itself by the power of its own operations. The mind passes from understanding less to understanding more.

The distinction between reading for information and reading for understanding is deeper than this. Let us try to say more about it. We will have to consider both goals of reading because the line between what is readable in one way and what must be read in the other is often hazy.

The first sense is the one in which we speak of ourselves as reading newspapers, magazines, or anything else that, according to our skill and talents, is at once thoroughly intelligible to us. Such things may increase our store of information, but they cannot improve our understanding, for our understanding was equal to them before we started.

The second sense is the one in which a person tries to read something that at first he does not completely understand. Here the thing to be read is initially better or higher than the reader.

Such communication between unequals must be possible, or else one person could never learn from another, either through speech or writing.

What are the conditions under which this kind of reading —reading for understanding—takes place? There are two.

First, there is initial inequality in understanding. The writer must be “superior” to the reader in understanding, and his book must convey in readable form the insights he possesses and his potential readers lack. Second, the reader must be able to overcome this inequality in some degree, seldom perhaps fully, but always approaching equality with the writer. To the extent that equality is approached, clarity of communication is achieved.

We do not want to give the impression that facts, leading to increased information, and insights, leading to increased understanding, are always easy to distinguish. And we would admit that sometimes a mere recital of facts can itself lead to greater understanding.

Our subject, then, is the art of reading good books when understanding is the aim you have in view.

Enlightenment is achieved only when, in addition to knowing what an author says, you know what he means and why he says

Being informed is prerequisite to being enlightened. The point, however, is not to stop at being informed.

Montaigne speaks of “an abecedarian ignorance that precedes knowledge, and a doctoral ignorance that comes after it.” The first is the ignorance of those who, not knowing their ABC’s, cannot read at all. The second is the ignorance of those who have misread many books.

The Greeks had a name for such a mixture of learning and folly which might be applied to the bookish but poorly read of all ages. They are all sophomores.

We can, however, gain knowledge without being taught. If this were not the case, and every teacher had to be taught what he in turn teaches others, there would be no beginning in the acquisition of knowledge.

Discovery stands to instruction as learning without a teacher stands to learning through the help of one. In both cases, the activity of learning goes on in the one who learns. It would be a mistake to suppose that discovery is active learning and instruction passive. There is no inactive learning, just as there is no inactive reading.

Similarly, although the teacher may help his student in many ways, it is the student himself who must do the learning. Knowledge must grow in his mind if learning is to take place.

The reason is that listening is learning from a teacher who is present—a living teacher—while reading is learning from one who is absent.

If you are puzzled by what he says, you can save yourself the trouble of thinking by asking him what he means. If, however, you ask a book a question, you must answer it yourself.

But if you are seeking an explanation, you have to understand it or nothing has been explained to you.

There are four levels of reading. They are here called levels rather than kinds because kinds, strictly speaking, are distinct from one another, whereas it is characteristic of levels that higher ones include lower ones.

The first level of reading we will call Elementary Reading.

In mastering this level, one learns the rudiments of the art of reading, receives basic training in reading, and acquires initial reading skills.

this level of reading is ordinarily learned in elementary school

At this level of reading, the question asked of the reader is “What does the sentence say?” That could be conceived as a complex and difficult question, of course. We mean it here, however, in its simplest sense.

second level of reading we will call Inspectional Reading

characterized by its special emphasis on time. When reading at this level, the student is allowed a set time to complete an assigned amount of reading

Still another name for this level might be skimming or pre-reading.

When reading at this level, your aim is to examine the surface of the book, to learn everything that the surface alone can teach you.

the question typically asked at this level is “What is the book about?” That is a surface question; others of a similar nature are “What is the structure of the book?” or “What are its parts?”

We do want to stress, however, that most people, even many quite good readers, are unaware of the value of inspectional reading. They start a book on page one and plow steadily through it, without even reading the table of contents. They are thus faced with the task of achieving a superficial knowledge of the book at the same time that they are trying to understand it. That compounds the difficulty.

The third level of reading we will call Analytical Reading.

Analytical reading is thorough reading, complete reading, or good reading—the best reading you can do. If inspectional reading is the best and most complete reading that is possible given a limited time, then analytical reading is the best and most complete reading that is possible given unlimited time.

Reading a book analytically is chewing and digesting it.

Analytical reading is preeminently for the sake of understanding.

fourth and highest level of reading we will call Syntopical Reading. It is the most complex and systematic type of reading of all. It makes very heavy demands on the reader, even if the materials he is reading are themselves relatively easy and unsophisticated

Another name for this level might be comparative reading.

When reading syntopically, the reader reads many books, not just one, and places them in relation to one another and to a subject about which they all revolve.

With the help of the books read, the syntopical reader is able to construct an analysis of the subject that may not be in any of the books. It is obvious, therefore, that syntopical reading is the most active and effortful kind of reading.

Stages of Learning to Read

The first stage is known by the term “reading readiness.” This begins, it has been pointed out, at birth, and continues normally until the age of about six or seven.

Reading readiness includes several different kinds of preparation for learning to read. Physical readiness involves good vision and hearing. Intellectual readiness involves a minimum level of visual perception such that the child can take in and remember an entire word and the letters that combine to form it. Language readiness involves the ability to speak clearly and to use several sentences in correct order. Personal readiness involves the ability to work with other children, to sustain attention, to follow directions, and the like.

Delaying the beginning of reading instruction beyond the reading readiness stage is not nearly so serious, despite the feelings of parents who may fear that their child is “backward” or is not “keeping up” with his peers.

In the second stage, children learn to read very simple materials. They usually begin, at least in the United States, by learning a few sight words, and typically manage to master perhaps three hundred to four hundred words by the end of the first year. Basic skills are introduced at this time, such as the use of context or meaning clues and the beginning sounds of words. By the end of this period pupils are expected to be reading simple books independently and with enthusiasm

It is incidentally worth observing that something quite mysterious, almost magical, occurs during this stage. At one moment in the course of his development the child, when faced with a series of symbols on a page, finds them quite meaningless. Not much later—perhaps only two or three weeks later-he has discovered meaning in them;

this discovery of meaning in symbols may be the most astounding intellectual feat that any human being ever performs—and most humans perform it before they are seven years old!

The third stage is characterized by rapid progress in vocabulary building and by increasing skill in “unlocking” the meaning of unfamiliar words through context clues.

They learn that reading, besides being something one does at school, is also something one can do on one’s own, for fun, to satisfy curiosity, or even to “expand one’s horizons.”

Finally, the fourth stage is characterized by the refinement and enhancement of the skills previously acquired.

This, the mature stage of reading, should be reached by young persons in their early teens. Ideally, they should continue to build on it for the rest of their lives.

To this day, most institutions of higher learning either do not know how to instruct students in reading beyond the elementary level, or lack the facilities and personnel to do so.

We say this despite the fact that a number of four-year and community colleges have recently instituted courses in speed reading, or in “effective” reading, or “competence” in reading. On the whole (though there are exceptions), these courses are remedial. They are designed to overcome various kinds of failures of the lower schools. They are not designed to take the student beyond the first level or to introduce him to the kinds and levels of reading that are the main subject of this book.

This, of course, should not be the case. A good liberal arts high school, if it does nothing else, ought to produce graduates who are competent analytical readers

good college, if it does nothing else, ought to produce competent syntopical readers. A college degree ought to represent general competence in reading such that a graduate could read any kind of material for general readers and be able to undertake independent research on almost any subject (for that is what syntopical reading, among other things, enables you to do

But, as we noted in Chapter 2, the levels of reading are cumulative. Thus, elementary reading is contained in inspectional reading, as, indeed, inspectional reading is contained in analytical reading, and analytical reading in syntopical reading.

Practically, this means that you cannot read on the inspectional level unless you can read effectively on the elementary level. You must be able to read an author’s text more or less steadily, without having to stop to look up the meaning of many words, and without stumbling over the grammar and syntax.

there are two types of inspectional reading

They are aspects of a single skill, but the beginning reader is well-advised to consider them as two different steps or activities. The experienced reader learns to perform both steps simultaneously, but for the moment we will treat them as if they were quite distinct.

Inspectional Reading I: Systematic Skimming or Pre-reading

First, you do not know whether you want to read the book. You do not know whether it deserves an analytical reading.

Second, let us assume—and this is very often the case-that you have only a limited time in which to find all this out.

In this case, what you must do is skim the book, or, as some prefer to say, pre-read it. Skimming or pre-reading is the first sublevel of inspectional reading.

The habit of skimming should not take much time to acquire. Here are some suggestions about how to do it.

  1. LOOK AT THE TITLE PAGE AND, IF THE BOOK HAS ONE, AT ITS PREFACE

Before completing this step you should have a good idea of the subject, and, if you wish, you may pause for a moment to place the book in the appropriate category in your mind. What pigeonhole that already contains other books does this one belong in?

  1. STUDY THE TABLE OF CONTENTS

use it as you would a road map before taking a trip

In fact, many authors spend a considerable amount of time in creating the table of contents, and it is sad to think their efforts are often wasted.

  1. CHECK THE INDEX if the book has one—most expository works do

Make a quick estimate of the range of topics covered and of the kinds of books and authors referred to. When you see terms listed that seem crucial, look up at least some of the passages cited.

  1. From your general and still rather vague knowledge of the book’s contents, LOOK NOW AT THE CHAPTERS THAT SEEM TO BE PIVOTAL TO ITS ARGUMENT. If these chapters have summary statements in their opening or closing pages, as they often do, read these statements carefully
  1. Finally, TURN THE PAGES, DIPPING IN HERE AND THERE, READING A PARAGRAPH OR TWO, SOMETIMES SEVERAL PAGES IN SEQUENCE, NEVER MORE THAN THAT.
