item.title: Zero to One
item.description:
Entrepreneurship

  • Bureaucratic hierarchies move slowly, and entrenched interests shy away from risk. So, small group of people bound together by sense of mission have changed the world for better.
  • You should treat entrepreneurship as agnostic experimentation.
  • And yet the opposite principles are probably more correct: a. It is better to risk boldness than triviality. b. A bad plan is better than no plan. c. Competitive markets destroy profits. d. Sales matters just as much as product.
  • Rather than oppose the crowd, ask business version of the question. What valuable company is nobody building?

Competition

  • Creating value is not enough- you need to capture some of the value you crate.
  • If there is money to be made, new firms will enter the market, increase supply, drive prices down, and thereby eliminate the profits that attracted them in the first place.
  • Entrepreneurs are biased to understate scale of competition which is the biggest mistake a startup can make.
  • Creative monopolists give customers more choices by adding entirely new categories of abundance to the world. Creative monopolies’re powerful engines for making it better.
  • In business, equilibrium means stasis, and stasis means death. If your industry is in a competitive equilibrium, the death of your business won’t matter to the world; some other undifferentiated competitor will always be ready to take your place.
  • As Tolstoy says “All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.” In business, All happy companies are different: each one

earns a monopoly by solving a unique problem. All failed companies are the same: they failed to escape competition.
item.content:
Entrepreneurship

  • Bureaucratic hierarchies move slowly, and entrenched interests shy away from risk. So, small group of people bound together by sense of mission have changed the world for better.
  • You should treat entrepreneurship as agnostic experimentation.
  • And yet the opposite principles are probably more correct: a. It is better to risk boldness than triviality. b. A bad plan is better than no plan. c. Competitive markets destroy profits. d. Sales matters just as much as product.
  • Rather than oppose the crowd, ask business version of the question. What valuable company is nobody building?

Competition

  • Creating value is not enough- you need to capture some of the value you crate.
  • If there is money to be made, new firms will enter the market, increase supply, drive prices down, and thereby eliminate the profits that attracted them in the first place.
  • Entrepreneurs are biased to understate scale of competition which is the biggest mistake a startup can make.
  • Creative monopolists give customers more choices by adding entirely new categories of abundance to the world. Creative monopolies’re powerful engines for making it better.
  • In business, equilibrium means stasis, and stasis means death. If your industry is in a competitive equilibrium, the death of your business won’t matter to the world; some other undifferentiated competitor will always be ready to take your place.
  • As Tolstoy says “All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.” In business, All happy companies are different: each one

earns a monopoly by solving a unique problem. All failed companies are the same: they failed to escape competition.

  • Competition doesn’t have to be there. It’s an ideology that prevades our society and distorts our thinking.
  • Cutthroat culture of academia, business as war are some extremes where it exists.
  • Entities are different before they start fighting. They grow similar as they fight and finally lose sight of why they started fighting in the first place.
  • Startups leave other alone and prosper independently. But as they grow, they begin to focus on each other.
  • Credit card reading machines: Started with square, competed by triangles, cylinders and half moon shapes.
  • If you can’t beat a rival, it may be better to merge. Paypal with X.com
  • Sometimes you do have to fight. Where that’s true, you should fight and win. There is no middle ground: either don’t throw any punches, or strike hard and end it quickly.
  • Low growth businesses prosper in short term but are replaced by trendier alternatives in the long run. High growth startups follow the opposite trajectory.
  • Growth is easy to measure but durability isn’t. For a startup to be valuable, it must grow and endure.

Monopoly and Disruption

  • Proprietary technology: e.g. Google’s search algorithms. Makes your product more difficult or impossible to replicate. Rule of thumb is your tech must be 10x plus better than its closest substitute in some important dimension to lead to real monopolistic advantage.
  • Network effects: You can’t reap network effects unless its valuable to your very first users when network is necessarily small.
  • Economies of scale: For software companies, marginal cost of producing another copy of product is close to zero. So, they advantage a lot with economies of scale. e.g. Yoga studio vs Online Yoga Class
  • Branding: Apple has the brand value it needs with its minimalistic design, consumer experience, omnipresent advertising and so on.
  • Every monopoly dominates a large share of the market, so a startup must start

with a very small market. Generally those group who’re concentrated together but served by few or no competitors.

  • Originally, “disruption” was a term of art to describe how a firm can use new technology to introduce a low-end product at low prices, improve the product over time, and eventually overtake even the premium products offered by incumbent companies using older technology.
  • first mover advantage: if you’re the first entrant into a market, you can capture significant market share while competitors scramble to get started. But moving first is a tactic, not a goal.
  • You must study the endgame before everything else.

Definite and Indefinite world

  • A definite pessimist believes that future can be known and since it’s bleak, must prepare for it. An indefinite pessimist instead waits for things to happen and be merry in the meantime. Europe’s famous vacation mania.
  • China can grow so fast only because it’s starting base is so low. Easiest way for China to grow is copy what has already worked in the West.
  • Finance epitomizes indefinite thinking because it’s the only way to make money when you have no idea how to create wealth.
  • In an indefinite world, people actually prefer unlimited optionality; money is more valuable than anything you could possibly do with it. Only in a definite future is money a means to an end, not the end itself.
  • Eroom’s law —that’s Moore’s law backward—observes that the number of new drugs approved per billion dollars spent on R&D has halved every nine years since 1950.
  • U.S. households are saving almost nothing and U.S. companies are letting cash pile up into their balance sheets without investing in new projects.
  • Going lean is great but leanness is a methodology, not a goal. Making small changes to things that already exist might lead you to a local maximum, but it won’t help you find the global maximum.
  • Apple in 1976, Jobs saw that you can change the world through careful planning, not by listening to focus group feedback or copying others’ successes.
  • When the first iPod was released in October 2001, industry analysts couldn’t see much more than “a nice feature for Macintosh users” that “doesn’t make any difference” to the rest of the world. Jobs planned the iPod to be the first of a new generation of portable post-PC devices, but that secret was invisible to most people.
  • A business with a good definite plan will always be underrated in a world where people see the future as random.

Exponential Growth

  • Pareto Rule : 80-20 rule, 20% of the people owned 80% of the land in Italy—a phenomenon that he found just as natural as the fact that 20% of the peapods in his garden produced 80% of the peas. MONEY MAKES MONEY.
  • A venture fund makes money when the companies in its portfolio become more valuable and either go public or get bought by larger companies. They generally invest on many such companies and even if one of them gets to be the unicorn, the investment becomes worthy. The biggest secret in venture capital is that the best investment in a successful fund equals or outperforms the entire rest of the fund combined.
  • VC backed companies create 11% of private sector jobs and 21% of GDP where total of VC investment accounts to around 0.2% of GDP.
  • Power law is everywhere. One market will probably be better than the others, one distribution strategy dominates all others. You must remember the power law to operate a company.
  • Every correct answer to business question is necessarily a secret: something important and unknown, something hard to do but doable. If there are many secrets left in the world, there are probably many world-changing companies yet to be started.

Modern Problems

  • Kaczynski divided human goals into three groups:
    1. Goals that can be satisfied with minimal effort
    2. Goals that can be satisfied with serious effort
    3. Goals that cannot be satisfied no matter how much effort one makes.
  • Kaczynski argued that modern people are depressed because all the world’s problems have been already solved.
  • Modern Problems:
    1. Achieve limited : Taught that the way to proceed is one small step at a time. Overachieving even receives no credit.
    2. Risk Aversion: People are scared of being wrong.
    3. Complacency: Social elites have the most freedom and ability to explore new thinking but seem to believe in secrets the least.
    4. Flatness: People perceive the world as homogeneous, highly competitive marketplace: flat world.
  • Fermat’s Last Theorem was unproven for 358 years. It might make the problem seem impossible but someone proved it nonetheless. Many believed it to be impossible task.
  • There are two kinds of secrets: secrets of nature and secrets about people. Natural secrets exist all around us; to find them, one must study some undiscovered aspect of the physical world. Secrets about people are different: they are things that people don’t know about themselves or things they hide because they don’t want others to know.
  • A great company is a conspiracy to change the world; when you share your secret, the recipient becomes a fellow conspirator.

Decisions

  • “Thiel’s law”: a startup messed up at its foundation cannot be fixed.
  • Bad decisions made early on—if you choose the wrong partners or hire the wrong people, for example—are very hard to correct after they are made. It may take a crisis on the order of bankruptcy before anybody will even try to correct them. As a founder, your first job is to get the first things right, because you cannot build a great company on a flawed foundation.
  • Technical abilities and complementary skill sets matter, but how well the founders know each other and how well they work together matter just as much. Founders should share a prehistory before they start a company together— otherwise they’re just rolling dice.
  • A board of three is ideal. Your board should never exceed five people, unless your company is publicly held.
  • No CEO in VC backed startup receive more than 150k per year in salary since a cash poor executive will focus on increasing the value of company as a whole.
  • Giving everyone equal shares is usually a mistake: every individual has different talents and responsibilities as well as different opportunity costs, so equal amounts will seem arbitrary and unfair from the start.

Team Building and Culture

  • The founding moment of a company, however, really does happen just once: only at the very start do you have the opportunity to set the rules that will align people toward the creation of value in the future.
  • START WITH A THOUGHT EXPERIMENT: what would the ideal company culture look like? Employees should love their work. They should enjoy going to the office so much that formal business hours become obsolete and nobody watches the clock.
  • Have a team that’s similar to “PayPal Mafia”. They didn’t assemble a mafia by sorting through resumes and simply hiring the most talented people.
  • Find people who are excited to be working with one another and actually enjoy working together.
  • Recruiting should never be outsourced. People who are only good at paper are not the ones to look for.
  • Why would someone join your company as its 20th engineer when she could go work at Google for more money and more prestige? Good answers can be: answers about your mission and answers about your team.
    • You should be able to explain why your company is a unique match for them personally. If you can’t do that, that’s not the right match.
    • Everyone should be different in the same way. On the inside, every individual should be sharply distinguished by their work.
  • Most fights inside a company happen when colleagues compete for same responsibilities. Startups have a high risk of it since the job roles are fluid in the beginnings.
  • The biggest difference is that cults tend to be fanatically wrong about something important. People at a successful startup are fanatically right about something those outside it have missed.

Conflicts

  • Misalignment:
    • Ownership : Who legally owns a company’s equity?
    • Possession: Who actually runs the company on a day-to-day basis?
    • Control: Who formally governs the company’s affairs?
  • In theory, this division works smoothly. Financial upside from part ownership attracts and rewards investors and workers. Effective possession motivates and empowers founders and employees—it means they can get stuff done. Oversight from the board places managers’ plans in a broader perspective. In practice, distributing these functions among different people makes sense, but it also multiplies opportunities for misalignment.
  • Most conflicts arise between founders and investors on the board. As interests diverge, board member might want to take company public ASAP to score a win for his firm but founders may want to stay private and grow business.
  • However, anyone who doesn’t own stock options or draw a regular salary from your company is fundamentally misaligned.
  • At the starting phase, hiring consultants doesn’t work. Remote work should be avoided as well. Don’t let anyone be biased to claim value in the near term.
  • Sending out a company-wide email that lists everyone’s ownership stake would be like dropping a nuclear bomb on your office.

Distribution

  • People have the bias that distribution should flow magically from the creation of a good product.
  • It takes hard work to make sales look easy. Sales works best when hidden. That’s why people involved in distribution generally have a job title that has nothing to do with those things. People who sell advertising are called “account executives.” People who sell customers work in “business development.” People who sell companies are “investment bankers.” And people who sell themselves are called “politicians.”
  • Two metrics set the limits for effective distribution. The total net profit that you earn on average over the course of your relationship with a customer (Customer Lifetime Value, or CLV) must exceed the amount you spend on average to acquire a new customer (Customer Acquisition Cost, or CAC).
  • Higher the price of product, more you have to spend to make a sale.
  • Alex, who is Palantir’s CEO, spends 25 days a month on the road, meeting with clients and potential clients. The deal sizes range from $1 million to $100 million. At that price point, buyers want to talk to the CEO, not the VP of Sales.
  • The product needs a personal sales effort, but at that price point, you simply don’t have the resources to send an actual person to talk to every prospective customer. This is why so many small and medium-sized businesses don’t use tools that bigger firms take for granted. It’s not that small business proprietors are unusually backward or that good tools don’t exist: distribution is the hidden bottleneck.
  • PayPal users would get $20 per customer referral but it also lead to 7% daily growth means user doubled every 10 days. After 4/5 months, they had hundreds of thousands of users that ended up greatly exceeding their CAC.
  • Never assume that people will admire your company without a public relations strategy.

Future of Labor

  • The most valuable businesses in coming decades will be built by entrepreneurs who seek to empower people rather than try to make them obsolete.
  • Properly understood, technology is the one way for us to escape competition in a globalizing world. As computers become more and more powerful, they won’t be substitutes for humans: they’ll be complements.
  • At PayPal, they first flagged suspicious transactions : then used human with well designed interface to actually make the final judgement.
  • Computers might be able to do some of these tasks, but they can’t combine them effectively. Better technology in law, medicine, and education won’t replace professionals; it will allow them to do even more.

  • Doing something different is what’s truly good for society—and it’s also what allows a business to profit by monopolizing a new market. The best projects are likely to be overlooked, not trumpeted by a crowd; the best problems to work on are often the ones nobody else even tries to solve.

Jobs was an artist, preferred closed systems, and spent his time thinking about great products above all else; Gates was a businessman, kept his products open, and wanted to run the world.   • The single greatest danger for a founder is to become so certain of his own myth that he loses his mind. But an equally insidious danger for every business is to lose all sense of myth and mistake disenchantment for wisdom.
  • Our task today is to find ways to create the new things that will make the future not just different, but better to go from zero to one.

item.title: Quiet - The power of introverts in a world that can't stop talking
item.description:
• Introverts focus on the Meaning they make of the events swirling around them; extroverts plunge into the events themselves.
  • Introverts recharge their batteries by being alone; extroverts need to recharge when they don’t socialize enough.
  • Introverts are mostly slow and deliberate. So, there is a chance that they’re immune to the lures of wealth and fame.
  • Introverts, may have strong skills and enjoy business parties and meetings, but after a while wish they were home in their pajamas. Most have a horror of small talk, but enjoy deep discussions.
  • Shyness is inherently painful; introversion is not. People often overlap these two concepts.
  • The more a person talks, the more other group members direct their attention to that person, which means that he becomes increasingly powerful as the meeting goes on. It also helps to speak fast; we rate quick talkers as more capable and appealing than slow talkers. But, there’s no such link between more talking and greater insight.
  • “Bus to Abilene” anecdote reveals our tendency to follow those who initiate action - any action. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abilene_paradox People decide on a course of action that is counter to preferences of many or all individuals in the group.
  • Interesting findings:
    • More Creative people tend to be socially poised introverts. They described themselves as and individualistic.
    • Solitude can be a catalyst to innovation.
      • Only when you are alone, you can engage in deliberate practice.
      • Deliberate practice takes intense concentration. It requires deep motivation, often self-generated. It involves working on the task that’s most challenging to us personally.
    • Open Plan offices have been found to reduce productivity and impair memory.
    • Simple act of being interrupted is one of the biggest barriers of Productivity among knowledge workers.
    • Multitasking is a myth.
    • Group work is not as people point it out to be. Rather than creativity, social glue is the principal benefit from these sessions.

“Evidence from science suggests that business people must be insane to use brainstorming groups. If you have talented and motivated people, they should be encouraged to work alone when creativity or efficiency is the highest priority.” – Adrian Furnham

It also helps to speak fast; we rate quick talkers as more capable and appealing than slow talkers. But, there’s no such link between more talking and greater insight.
  • “Bus to Abilene” anecdote reveals our tendency to follow those who initiate action - any action. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abilene_paradox People decide on a course of action that is counter to preferences of many or all individuals in the group.
  • Interesting findings:
    • More Creative people tend to be socially poised introverts. They described themselves as and individualistic.
    • Solitude can be a catalyst to innovation.
      • Only when you are alone, you can engage in deliberate practice.
      • Deliberate practice takes intense concentration. It requires deep motivation, often self-generated. It involves working on the task that’s most challenging to us personally.
    • Open Plan offices have been found to reduce productivity and impair memory.
    • Simple act of being interrupted is one of the biggest barriers of Productivity among knowledge workers.
    • Multitasking is a myth.
    • Group work is not as people point it out to be. Rather than creativity, social glue is the principal benefit from these sessions.

“Evidence from science suggests that business people must be insane to use brainstorming groups. If you have talented and motivated people, they should be encouraged to work alone when creativity or efficiency is the highest priority.” – Adrian Furnham

  • Peer pressure can actually change your view of a problem.
  • Most effective teams are composed of a healthy mix of introverts and extroverts.
  • We need spaces where people are free to circulate in different sorts of interactions, and to disappear into their private workspaces when they want to focus or simply be alone.
  • Kagan’s experiment on children:
    • High and Low reactivity tend to correspond to introversion and extroversion.
    • Hypothesized that infants born with an especially excited amygdala would wiggle and howl when shown unfamiliar objects and were more likely to feel vigilant when meeting new people.
    • Conscientiousness and Agreeableness are about 40 to 50% heritable. Such studies show that extroversion also might be related to heredity although these studies are not perfect.
  • Public Speaking Anxiety: When our ancestors lived on savannah, being watched intently meant only one thing: a wild animal was stalking us. – Sociobiologist E.O. Wilson
  • Schwartz’s Research : We can stretch our personalities, but only up to a point. Our inborn temperaments continues to influence us.
  • Once we understand extroversion and introversion as preferences for certain levels of simulation, we can begin trying to situate ourselves in environments that favor our personality.
  • Desensitization : Doing what you are afraid of over and over again, in manageable doses.
  • Speakers sometimes need to talk about subjects that don’t interest them much, especially at work. This is projecting artificial enthusiasm.
  • Highly sensitive people tend to be keen observers who look before they leap.
    • They arrange lives in ways that limit surprises.
    • They have difficulty when being observed or judged for general worthiness.
    • They dream vividly, and can often recall their dreams the next day.
    • They love music, nature, art, physical beauty.
    • They feel exceptionally strong emotions.
    • They tend to notice subtleties that others miss - e.g. another person’s shift in mood.
    • They tend to be highly empathetic.
    • They tend to sweat more.
  • Extroverts:
    • Enjoy wider networks of social support, but commit more crimes.
    • Exercise more.
    • More sex partners but more divorce and adultery.
  • Introverts:
    • Fewer accidents and traumatic injuries.
    • Less sex partners but less divorce and adultery.
  • Sensitive people tend to enjoy small talk only after they’ve gone deep.
  • Reward seeking and reward-sensitivity is not only an interesting feature of extroversion; it is what makes an extrovert an extrovert.
  • Extroverts seem to get an extra buzz from the pursuit and attainment of their goals.
  • Introverts seem to be better than extroverts at delaying gratification, crucial life skill associated with everything from higher SAT scores and income to lower body mass index.
  • Extroverts are more likely to take quick-and-dirty approach to problem solving, trading accuracy for speed, making mistakes as they go. Introverts think before they act, digest information thoroughly, stay on task longer.
  • We need to find the balance between action and reflection.
  • If you enjoy depth, don’t force yourself to seek breadth. If you prefer single-tasking to multi tasking, stick to it.
  • Introverts should better share their stories using writing, highly produced lectures etc.
  • Jealousy is an ugly emotion, but it tells the truth. You mostly envy those who have what you desire.
  • It’s hard for introverts to understand how hurtful silence can be.
  • Different ways of problem tackling: “Confrontive Copers” vs “Conflict-Avoiders”.
  • Introverts like people they meet in friendly contexts; extroverts prefer those they compete with.
  • Cherish your nearest and dearest.
  • Relationships make everyone happier, introverts included, but think quality over quantity.
  • Use your natural powers – of persistence, concentration, insight, and sensitivity – to do what you love and work that matters.
  • Solve problems, make art, think deeply.
  • Carve out restorative niches.
  • Spend your free time the way you like, not the way you think you’re supposed to.
  • Don’t mistake assertiveness or eloquence for good ideas.

  • loc 4420 - Spend your free time the way you like, not the way you think you’re supposed to. Stay home on New Year’s Eve if that’s what makes you happy.

  • loc 4435 - Face-to-face contact is important because it builds trust, but group dynamics contain unavoidable impediments to creative thinking.

  • loc 4436 - Don’t mistake assertiveness or eloquence for good ideas.

item.title: The 22 Immutable Laws of Marketing
item.description:
Law of Leadership

  • Better to be first than it is to be better.
  • Use name that will define your category.

Law of Category

  • If you can’t be first in a category, set up a new category to be first in.
  • IBM was first in computers while DEC was first in minicomputers. Commodore wasn’t going anywhere until it positioned the Amiga as the first multimedia computer.
  • Instead of asking “How is the new product better than the competition?” ask “What category is this new product first in?”

Law of the Mind

  • It’s better to be first in the mind than it is to be first in the marketplace.
  • Law of mind modifies the Law of Leadership.
  • Being first in the mind is everything in marketing. Being first in the marketplace is important only to the extent that it allows you to get in the mind first.
  • It’s a marketing battle of perception, not product.
  • The single most wasteful thing you can do in marketing is try to change a mind.

Law of Perception

  • Marketing is a battle of perceptions.
  • There’s no objective reality, no facts, no best products; only perception in the minds of the customer or prospect.
  • To cope with the terrifying reality of being alone in the universe, people project themselves to the outside world. People cling firmly to the belief that reality is the world outside of the mind and that individual is one small speck on a global spaceship. Actually it’s the opposite.
  • Most marketing mistakes stem from the assumption that you’re fighting a product battle that’s rooted in reality.
  • What makes this projection battle even difficult is that customers make buying decisions based on someone else’s perception of reality. “EVERYBODY KNOWS” principle. If you ask people if they have experience with the product, most often they say they haven’t.

Law of Focus

  • Owning a word in prospect’s mind.
  • Law of Leadership enables first brand or company to own a word in the mind of the prospect.
  • You can test the validity of leadership claim by word association test. If given words are computer, copier, cola, the three most associated words are IBM, Xerox, and Coke.
  • If you’re not a leader, your word have to have a narrow focus and needs to be available.
  • The most effective words are simple and benefit oriented.
  • You become stronger when you reduce the scope of your operations.

Law of Exclusivity

  • Two companies can’t own the same word in prospect’s mind.
  • Volvo owns safety. Other companies like Mercedes-Benz and General Motors tried running marketing campaigns based on safety but couldn’t get in.
  • Even if you research and have the advantage but someone already owns the word, it’s no use.
  • In “Fastfood”, McDonalds was already associated with word “fast”. Burger King tried “Best food for fast times” program which became a disaster.

Law of the Ladder

  • Strategy to use depends on which rung you occupy on the ladder.
  • For each category, there is product ladder in the mind. On each rung is a brand name.
  • By admitting to be No.2, Avis: car rental company, which had been losing money for 13 years started to make money. It’s because it related itself to the position of the top company in the mind.
  • How many rungs are there in your ladder?
    • Depends on whether your product is low-interest or a high-interest product.
    • Furniture etc. have low rungs while cigarettes, cola, beer tend to have many rungs on their laddrs.
  • You tend to have twice the market share of the brand below you and half the market share of the brand above you.
  • What’s max no of rungs on a ladder? ==> Seems like it’s seven in prospect’s mind.

Law of Duality

  • Eventually, every market becomes a two-horse race.
  • In a maturing industry, third place is a difficult position to be in.
  • e.g. Video games : Nintendo 75%, Sega went on neck-to-neck with Nintendo and NEC lost it’s way.
  • Time for market to play out will vary.
  • Car Companies:
    • 1904 : 60 companies
    • In 10 more years, 531 started and 346 perished.
    • 1923: Only 108 remain.
    • 1927: Only 44 remain.

Law of the Opposite

  • If you are shooting for the second place, your strategy is determined by the leader.
  • In every market segment, there are two kinds of people:
    • Who want to buy from the leader.
    • Who don’t want to buy from the leader.
  • So, by positioning yourself against the leader, you take business away from all other alternatives to No.1.
  • Yet, too many potential No.2 brands try to copy the leader which is the error.

Law of Division

  • Over time, one category splits into multiples.
  • Computers: Mainframe, Mini computers, Supercomputers ==> Personal, Laptops, Notebooks etc.
  • Companies make mistake when they try to take a well-known brand namein one category and use the same brand name in another category.
  • Volkswagen brought multiple cars under the same brand name and only sold one category of cars. Honda instead introduced luxury car market with brand name Acura. Acura sold more cars than Volkswagen sold altogether.
  • You can’t get into prospect’s mind first unless you’ve prepared to spend some time waiting for things to develop.

Law of Perspective

  • Marketing effects take place over an extended period of time.
  • The long-term effects of alcohol are exactly the opposite of it’s short-term effects.
  • In short-term, a sale increases business. Sales decrease businesses in the long term b educating customers not to buy at ‘regular’ prices.
  • By having competing products from same company, you increase sales of one lineup but in the long run it may be harming the whole company.

Law of Line Extension

  • There’s an irresistible pressure to extend the equity of a brand.
  • Line extension involves taking the brand name of a successful product and putting it on a new product you plan to introduce.
  • Sounds logical but confused with different names will lead to dismal failures. Poultry Sauce vs Steak Sauce. People won’t know what one is referring to with one name.
  • Less is more. If you want to be successful today, you have to narrow the focus in order to build a position in the prospect’s mind.
  • IBM used to stand for “mainframe computers” but today, it stands for everything, which means it stands for nothing.

Law of Sacrifice

  • You have to give up something in order to get something.
  • Three things to sacrifice:
    • Product Line
      • Emery Air Freight services shipped everything. Fedex came and delivered small packages only overnight. That’s how product line sacrifice works.
      • Generalists are weak in the market.
    • Target Market
      • Where is it written that you have to appeal to everybody?
      • Pepsi sacrificed everything in the early sixties except the teenage market by hiring it’s icons: Michael Jackson, Don Johnson. By one generation, it closed the gap.
    • Constant Change
      • Where is it written that you have to change your strategy every year at budget review time?

Law of Attributes

  • For every attribute, there is an opposite, effective attribute.
  • Cavity prevention is the most important attribute in toothpaste. Once it’s taken by somebody, you have to come up with something else. You have to dramatize your value of attribute, and thus increase your share.
    • e.g. Sensitivity and Sensodyne.
  • You can’t predict the size of a new attribute’s share, so never laugh. Gillette came up with disposable razors once an upstart from France brought it.

Law of Candor

  • When you admit a negative, the prospect will give you positive.
  • Every negative statement you make about yourself is instantly accepted as truth.
  • When you can’t change the minds of people that’s already made up, your marketing efforts have to be devoted to using ideas and concepts already installed in the brain. e.g. Setting yourself as No.2 rather than No.1.
  • You have to state the negative and quickly shift it to positive to convince the prospect.

Law of Singularity

  • In each situation, only one move will produce substantial results.
  • Whether you try hard or try easy, the differences are marginal.
  • For bigger companies, law of averages wipes out any real advantage of trying harder approach.
  • Single Bold Stroke is the best way to go.

Law of Unpredictability

  • Unless you write your competitor’s plans, you can’t predict the future.
  • Problem with corporate America is short-term financial thinking.
  • Good short-term planning is coming up with angle or word that differentiates yourself. Then you set up a coherent long-term marketing direction that builds a program to maximize that idea or angle.
  • Domino’s pizza’s short term angle was “home delivery” and long-term was to build first nationwide home delivery chain.

Law of Success

  • Success often leads to arrogance, and arrogance to failure.
  • Ego is the enemy of successful marketing. Objectivity is what’s needed.
  • The more you identify with your brand or corporate name, more likely are you to fall into line extension trap.
  • Ego can be effective driving force in building a business.
  • Brilliant marketers have the ability to think like a prospect thinks.
  • The bigger the company, the more likely it is that the chief executives have lost touch with the front lines. Single most important factor limiting the growth of a corporation.
  • How do you get the bad news as well as the good? One possibility is to go “in disguise” or unannounced.
  • The next thing to cut back on are the meetings. Instead of talking thing over, walk out and see for yourself.

Law of Failure

  • Failure is to be expected and accepted.
  • Japanese seem to be able to admit a mistake early and then make the necessary changes.
  • It’s easier to live with “We were all wrong” than the devastating “I was wrong”.
  • When senior executive has a high salary and a short time to retirement, a bold move is highly unlikely. Nobody has been fired for a bold move they didn’t make.

Law of Hype

  • The situation is often the opposite of the way it appears in the press.
  • No soft drink has received more hype than New Coke but it didn’t happen. Less than 60 days after the launch, Coca-Cola was forced to come up with the original formula, now called Coca-Cola Classic.
  • The essence of the hype was not just that the new product was going to be successful. The essence of the hype was that existing products would now be obsolete.
  • The only revolutions you can predict are the ones that have already started.
  • If you’re looking for clues to the future, look in the back of the paper for those innocuous little stories.

Law of Acceleration

  • Successful programs are not built on fads, they’re built on trends.
  • A fad is a wave in the ocean, and a trend is the tide. A fad gets a lot of hype, and a trend gets very little.
  • Trend is almost invisible, but it’s very powerful over the long term.
  • If you’re faced with a rapidly rising business, with all the characteristics of a fad, the best thing you could do would be to dampen the fad. By dampening the fad, you stretch the fad out and it becomes more like a trend.

Law of Resources

  • Without adequate funding an idea won’t get off the ground.
  • Marketing is a game fought in the mind of the prospect. You need money to get into the mind. And you need money to stay in the mind once you get there. You’ll get further with a mediocre idea and a million dollars than with a great idea alone. Ideas without money are worthless.
  • Getting to rich company: Spend enough.

  • loc 211 - Du Mont invented the first commercial television set. Duryea introduced the first automobile. Hurley introduced the first washing machine. All are gone. Is something wrong with the law of leadership in chapter 1? No, but the law of the mind modifies it. It’s better to be first in the prospect’s mind than first in the marketplace. Which, if anything, understates the importance of being first in the mind. Being first in the mind is everything in marketing. Being first in the marketplace is important only to the extent that it allows you to get in the mind first. For example, IBM wasn’t first in the marketplace with the mainframe computer. Remington Rand was first, with UNIVAC. But thanks to a massive marketing effort, IBM got into the mind first and won the computer battle early. The law of the mind follows from the law of perception. If marketing is a battle of perception, not product, then the mind takes precedence over the marketplace.

  • loc 229 - Xerox was first in copiers and then tried to get into the computer business. Twenty-five years and $2 billion later, Xerox is nowhere in computers.

  • loc 232 - The single most wasteful thing you can do in marketing is try to change a mind.

  • loc 245 - Law 4: The Law of Perception. Marketing is not a battle of products, it’s a battle of perception.

  • loc 256 - Most people think they are better perceivers than others. They have a sense of personal infallibility. Their perceptions are always more accurate than those of their neighbors or friends. Truth and perception become fused in the mind, leaving no difference between the two. It’s not easy to see that this is so. To cope with the terrifying reality of being alone in the universe, people project themselves on the outside world. They “live” in the arena of books, movies, television, newspapers, magazines. They “belong” to clubs, organizations, institutions. These outside representations of the world seem more real than the reality inside their own minds. People cling firmly to the belief that reality is the world outside of the mind and that the individual is one small speck on a global spaceship. Actually it’s the opposite. The only reality you can be sure about is in your own perceptions. If the universe exists, it exists inside your own mind and the minds of others. That’s the reality that marketing programs must deal with.

When you ask shoppers whether they have had any personal experience with a product, most often they say they haven’t. Owning the word slow helps Heinz maintain a 50 percent market share. If you’re not a leader, then your word has to have a narrow focus. Even more important, however, your word has to be “available” in your category. No one else can have a lock on it.

Then Avis did the one thing you have to do to make progress inside the mind of the prospect. They acknowledged their position on the ladder. “Avis is only No. 2 in rent-a-cars. So why go with us? We try harder.” For 13 years in a row, Avis had lost money. Then, when it admitted to being No. 2, it started to make money, lots of money.

Products that are purchased infrequently (furniture, lawn mowers, luggage) usually have few rungs on their ladders. Miller, the average human mind cannot deal with more than seven units at a time.

  • loc 642 - A category starts off as a single entity. Computers, for example. But over time, the category breaks up into other segments. Mainframes, minicomputers, workstations, personal computers, laptops, notebooks, pen computers.

In the early seventies, Miller High Life was barreling along with sales increases averaging 27 percent a year. Miller’s success was fueled by “Miller Time,” a blue-collar campaign focused on rewarding yourself at the end of the day with a Miller beer. Then Miller got greedy and in 1974 introduced Miller Lite, a brilliant concept (chapter 2: The Law of the Category) buried under a line extended name. The high-water mark for Miller High Life was 1979, five years after the introduction of Miller Lite. In those five years Miller High Life’s annual sales almost tripled, from 8.6 million to 23.6 million barrels. This was the short-term effect of line extension. The long-term effect was grim. It sounds so logical. “We make A-1, a great sauce that gets the dominant share of the steak business. But people are switching from beef to chicken, so let’s introduce a poultry product. And what better name to use than A-1. That way people will know the poultry sauce comes from the makers of that great steak sauce, A-1.” But marketing is a battle of perception, not product. In the mind, A-1 is not the brand name, but the steak sauce itself. “Would you pass me the A-1?” asks the diner. Nobody replies: “A-1 what?” In spite of an $18 million advertising budget, the A-1 poultry launch was a dismal failure.

If you want to be successful, you have to reduce your product line, not expand it. Take Emery Air Freight. Emery was in the air freight services business. item.content:
Law of Leadership

  • Better to be first than it is to be better.
  • Use name that will define your category.

Law of Category

  • If you can’t be first in a category, set up a new category to be first in.
  • IBM was first in computers while DEC was first in minicomputers. Commodore wasn’t going anywhere until it positioned the Amiga as the first multimedia computer.
  • Instead of asking “How is the new product better than the competition?” ask “What category is this new product first in?”

Law of the Mind

  • It’s better to be first in the mind than it is to be first in the marketplace.
  • Law of mind modifies the Law of Leadership.
  • Being first in the mind is everything in marketing. Being first in the marketplace is important only to the extent that it allows you to get in the mind first.
  • It’s a marketing battle of perception, not product.
  • The single most wasteful thing you can do in marketing is try to change a mind.

Law of Perception

  • Marketing is a battle of perceptions.
  • There’s no objective reality, no facts, no best products; only perception in the minds of the customer or prospect.
  • To cope with the terrifying reality of being alone in the universe, people project themselves to the outside world. People cling firmly to the belief that reality is the world outside of the mind and that individual is one small speck on a global spaceship. Actually it’s the opposite.
  • Most marketing mistakes stem from the assumption that you’re fighting a product battle that’s rooted in reality.
  • What makes this projection battle even difficult is that customers make buying decisions based on someone else’s perception of reality. “EVERYBODY KNOWS” principle. If you ask people if they have experience with the product, most often they say they haven’t.

Law of Focus

  • Owning a word in prospect’s mind.
  • Law of Leadership enables first brand or company to own a word in the mind of the prospect.
  • You can test the validity of leadership claim by word association test. If given words are computer, copier, cola, the three most associated words are IBM, Xerox, and Coke.
  • If you’re not a leader, your word have to have a narrow focus and needs to be available.
  • The most effective words are simple and benefit oriented.
  • You become stronger when you reduce the scope of your operations.

Law of Exclusivity

  • Two companies can’t own the same word in prospect’s mind.
  • Volvo owns safety. Other companies like Mercedes-Benz and General Motors tried running marketing campaigns based on safety but couldn’t get in.
  • Even if you research and have the advantage but someone already owns the word, it’s no use.
  • In “Fastfood”, McDonalds was already associated with word “fast”. Burger King tried “Best food for fast times” program which became a disaster.

Law of the Ladder

  • Strategy to use depends on which rung you occupy on the ladder.
  • For each category, there is product ladder in the mind. On each rung is a brand name.
  • By admitting to be No.2, Avis: car rental company, which had been losing money for 13 years started to make money. It’s because it related itself to the position of the top company in the mind.
  • How many rungs are there in your ladder?
    • Depends on whether your product is low-interest or a high-interest product.
    • Furniture etc. have low rungs while cigarettes, cola, beer tend to have many rungs on their laddrs.
  • You tend to have twice the market share of the brand below you and half the market share of the brand above you.
  • What’s max no of rungs on a ladder? ==> Seems like it’s seven in prospect’s mind.

Law of Duality

  • Eventually, every market becomes a two-horse race.
  • In a maturing industry, third place is a difficult position to be in.
  • e.g. Video games : Nintendo 75%, Sega went on neck-to-neck with Nintendo and NEC lost it’s way.
  • Time for market to play out will vary.
  • Car Companies:
    • 1904 : 60 companies
    • In 10 more years, 531 started and 346 perished.
    • 1923: Only 108 remain.
    • 1927: Only 44 remain.

Law of the Opposite

  • If you are shooting for the second place, your strategy is determined by the leader.
  • In every market segment, there are two kinds of people:
    • Who want to buy from the leader.
    • Who don’t want to buy from the leader.
  • So, by positioning yourself against the leader, you take business away from all other alternatives to No.1.
  • Yet, too many potential No.2 brands try to copy the leader which is the error.

Law of Division

  • Over time, one category splits into multiples.
  • Computers: Mainframe, Mini computers, Supercomputers ==> Personal, Laptops, Notebooks etc.
  • Companies make mistake when they try to take a well-known brand namein one category and use the same brand name in another category.
  • Volkswagen brought multiple cars under the same brand name and only sold one category of cars. Honda instead introduced luxury car market with brand name Acura. Acura sold more cars than Volkswagen sold altogether.
  • You can’t get into prospect’s mind first unless you’ve prepared to spend some time waiting for things to develop.

Law of Perspective

  • Marketing effects take place over an extended period of time.
  • The long-term effects of alcohol are exactly the opposite of it’s short-term effects.
  • In short-term, a sale increases business. Sales decrease businesses in the long term b educating customers not to buy at ‘regular’ prices.
  • By having competing products from same company, you increase sales of one lineup but in the long run it may be harming the whole company.

Law of Line Extension

  • There’s an irresistible pressure to extend the equity of a brand.
  • Line extension involves taking the brand name of a successful product and putting it on a new product you plan to introduce.
  • Sounds logical but confused with different names will lead to dismal failures. Poultry Sauce vs Steak Sauce. People won’t know what one is referring to with one name.
  • Less is more. If you want to be successful today, you have to narrow the focus in order to build a position in the prospect’s mind.
  • IBM used to stand for “mainframe computers” but today, it stands for everything, which means it stands for nothing.

Law of Sacrifice

  • You have to give up something in order to get something.
  • Three things to sacrifice:
    • Product Line
      • Emery Air Freight services shipped everything. Fedex came and delivered small packages only overnight. That’s how product line sacrifice works.
      • Generalists are weak in the market.
    • Target Market
      • Where is it written that you have to appeal to everybody?
      • Pepsi sacrificed everything in the early sixties except the teenage market by hiring it’s icons: Michael Jackson, Don Johnson. By one generation, it closed the gap.
    • Constant Change
      • Where is it written that you have to change your strategy every year at budget review time?

Law of Attributes

  • For every attribute, there is an opposite, effective attribute.
  • Cavity prevention is the most important attribute in toothpaste. Once it’s taken by somebody, you have to come up with something else. You have to dramatize your value of attribute, and thus increase your share.
    • e.g. Sensitivity and Sensodyne.
  • You can’t predict the size of a new attribute’s share, so never laugh. Gillette came up with disposable razors once an upstart from France brought it.

Law of Candor

  • When you admit a negative, the prospect will give you positive.
  • Every negative statement you make about yourself is instantly accepted as truth.
  • When you can’t change the minds of people that’s already made up, your marketing efforts have to be devoted to using ideas and concepts already installed in the brain. e.g. Setting yourself as No.2 rather than No.1.
  • You have to state the negative and quickly shift it to positive to convince the prospect.

Law of Singularity

  • In each situation, only one move will produce substantial results.
  • Whether you try hard or try easy, the differences are marginal.
  • For bigger companies, law of averages wipes out any real advantage of trying harder approach.
  • Single Bold Stroke is the best way to go.

Law of Unpredictability

  • Unless you write your competitor’s plans, you can’t predict the future.
  • Problem with corporate America is short-term financial thinking.
  • Good short-term planning is coming up with angle or word that differentiates yourself. Then you set up a coherent long-term marketing direction that builds a program to maximize that idea or angle.
  • Domino’s pizza’s short term angle was “home delivery” and long-term was to build first nationwide home delivery chain.

Law of Success

  • Success often leads to arrogance, and arrogance to failure.
  • Ego is the enemy of successful marketing. Objectivity is what’s needed.
  • The more you identify with your brand or corporate name, more likely are you to fall into line extension trap.
  • Ego can be effective driving force in building a business.
  • Brilliant marketers have the ability to think like a prospect thinks.
  • The bigger the company, the more likely it is that the chief executives have lost touch with the front lines. Single most important factor limiting the growth of a corporation.
  • How do you get the bad news as well as the good? One possibility is to go “in disguise” or unannounced.
  • The next thing to cut back on are the meetings. Instead of talking thing over, walk out and see for yourself.

Law of Failure

  • Failure is to be expected and accepted.
  • Japanese seem to be able to admit a mistake early and then make the necessary changes.
  • It’s easier to live with “We were all wrong” than the devastating “I was wrong”.
  • When senior executive has a high salary and a short time to retirement, a bold move is highly unlikely. Nobody has been fired for a bold move they didn’t make.

Law of Hype

  • The situation is often the opposite of the way it appears in the press.
  • No soft drink has received more hype than New Coke but it didn’t happen. Less than 60 days after the launch, Coca-Cola was forced to come up with the original formula, now called Coca-Cola Classic.
  • The essence of the hype was not just that the new product was going to be successful. The essence of the hype was that existing products would now be obsolete.
  • The only revolutions you can predict are the ones that have already started.
  • If you’re looking for clues to the future, look in the back of the paper for those innocuous little stories.

Law of Acceleration

  • Successful programs are not built on fads, they’re built on trends.
  • A fad is a wave in the ocean, and a trend is the tide. A fad gets a lot of hype, and a trend gets very little.
  • Trend is almost invisible, but it’s very powerful over the long term.
  • If you’re faced with a rapidly rising business, with all the characteristics of a fad, the best thing you could do would be to dampen the fad. By dampening the fad, you stretch the fad out and it becomes more like a trend.

Law of Resources

  • Without adequate funding an idea won’t get off the ground.
  • Marketing is a game fought in the mind of the prospect. You need money to get into the mind. And you need money to stay in the mind once you get there. You’ll get further with a mediocre idea and a million dollars than with a great idea alone. Ideas without money are worthless.
  • Getting to rich company: Spend enough.

Which, if anything, understates the importance of being first in the mind. Being first in the mind is everything in marketing. Being first in the marketplace is important only to the extent that it allows you to get in the mind first. For example, IBM wasn’t first in the marketplace with the mainframe computer. Remington Rand was first, with UNIVAC. But thanks to a massive marketing effort, IBM got into the mind first and won the computer battle early. The law of the mind follows from the law of perception. If marketing is a battle of perception, not product, then the mind takes precedence over the marketplace.
