  • On experimenting with electrical probe to simulate neurons, it was discovered that simulation of a single neuron in the temporal lobes would reactivate entire memories in the patient.
  • TMS : Non-invasive procedure in which a brief magnetic pulse on the scalp simulates underlying cortical region.
  • Autoscopic experience: Experience of seeing one’s body from an external perspective.
  • Comatose state: Patients in such state show no signs of wakefulness or awareness. The brain activity during such states is similar to that observed during general anaesthesia.
  • Prefrontal Parietal Network: Frequently associated with consciousness, especially in so-called global workspace theories.
  • Qualia : Philosophical term broadly referring to the intrinsic properties of conscious experience.
  • Causality of EEG Signals : A slowly rising electrical brain signal seems to precede voluntary decisions to perform actions.
  • Supplementary Motor Area : Part of the frontal lobes and a possible neural source of the readiness potential. Direct simulation of this region produces the experiences of wanting to make a movement.
  • Daniel Dennett : Consciousness in terms of function that it supports and not by the raw essence of experience.
  • Binocular Rivalry : One image [ e.g. house ] shown to one eye and another image [ face ] shown to another eye. Brain cannot resolve this ambiguous input into single image, one’s conscious experience alternates betwen the house and the face.
  • Phantom Limb Syndrome : Brain builds a body model that doesn’t always match the physical body.
  • Global Workspace Theory : Specific mental contents such as perceptions, thoughts, intentions to act etc. remain unconscious unless or until they gain access to a global workspace, which broadcasts their contents across the brain, making them available for the flexible control of behavior.
  • Thalamic switch Theory : GAs turn consciousness off by reducing activity in specific parts of thalamus.
  • V4 : Samir Zeki in 1970s and has been closely associated with perception of color, although not limited to it.
  • Change Blindness : A phenomenon in which surprisingly large changes in visual scene go unnoticed if there is a gap between the images of if there are other more salient changes accompanying the transition.
    • A bed of roses will result in different mixture of wavelength during the dawn and the day but we will perceive the roses as a particular shade of red in both cases.
  • Super Colliculus : A pair of small structures beneath the cerebral cortex that play an important role in guiding fast visual reflexes, such as object tracking.
  • Some of the colors (such as magenta) don’t have corresponding wavelength - brain constructs it.
  • The key to understanding this comes from the fact that there is not just one route that connects the eyes to the brain but many ( around 10 in humans ), so damaging the brain might affect one route selectively.
    • Routes have evolved for different functions- one uses light to calibrate the biological clock and another is used to orient the eyes to sudden changes.
    • Fast seeing route ( via super colliculus ) that moves the eyes and a slow seeing route ( via the cortex ) that can detect the details of what is seen.
  • Synaesthesia : For small % of population, words may be colored, music may have a taste, or numbers may be visualized on a twisting, turning landscape.
  • Attention Mechanism: Since vision and rest of our senses are continually bombarded with information, brain has developed this mechanism to filter and prioritize ( such as amplifying its neural signal ) at the expense of other information.
  • Object Tracking:
    • Need to know the position of eyes in the socket.
    • Need to know position of the head relative to the body.
    • Signals from eye and neck muscles need to be linked to vision.
    • There appears to be separate pathways in the brain for locating and acting on an object versus knowing what the object is.
  • Sacks : The Man who mistook his wife for a hat, 24 essays reporting in from the extremes of the mind.
  • Alien movements : If our motor cortex becomes disconnected from the controlling regions, then movements are produced that are unexpected.
  • Medial Temporal Lobes : Related to long term memories.
  • Fragmentation of storage areas:
    • Semantic Memories [ Capital of France is] : Temporal Lobe
    • Memories from past events: Widely distributed across temporal cortex.
  • Broca’s area : Inferior Frontal Gyrus, is thought to play a central role in processing syntax, grammar and sentence structure.
  • Wernicke’s area: Superior Temporal Gyrus : Involved in comprehension of language.
  • Metacognition:
    • Think about thinking.
    • Not only important for monitoring how we learn new information, but also for communicating our subjective experiences with others.
    • Macaque monkeys, Dolphins and rats exhibit signs of metacognition when performing a perceptual or memory task. Others, such as pigeons don’t.
  • Negative emotional impact is twice as intense as the positive effect of gains, which affects our decision making in predictable ways.
  • Mirror Neurons : Activated during the execution of an action and by the sight of someone else performing that action.
  • Pheromones : Airborne chemical signals released by male mice that stimulate neurogenesis in the olfactory bulb and hippocampus in the brain of female mice.
  • Volume of Posterior Superior Temporal Sulcus pSTS predicted the level of loneliness in sample of people. It is linked to the processing of social cues.
  • Splitting the brain in half proved to alleviate the symptoms of epilepsy without apparent impairment.
  • Thought Insertions : Patients experiencing a lack of ownership of their own thoughts.
  • Schizophrenia : Perceptual hallucinations, false beliefs, thought insertions. Symptoms may arise from a failure to properly combine prior expectations with new sensory evidence.
    • Genes related to it : COMT, is involved in breaking down the neurotransmitter dopamine, involved in prediction-based learning.
  • Four meditation sessions were sufficient to increase working memory capacity. Five sessions showed increased performance on an attentional task that involved resolving conflict. Lessen sense of anxiety, anger and tiredness.

item.title: Siddhartha
item.description:
Knowledge is something you can never steal or take away. So, are experiences and inner beauty.

“No, Samana, I am not afraid of this. Did any Samana or Brahman ever fear, someone might come and grab him and steal his learning, and his religious devotion, and his depth of thought? No, for they are his very own, and he would only give away from those whatever he is willing to give and to whomever he is willing to give. Like this it is, precisely like this it is also with Kamala and with the pleasures of love. Beautiful and red is Kamala’s mouth, but just try to kiss it against Kamala’s will, and you will not obtain a single drop of sweetness from it, which knows how to give so many sweet things!”
item.content:
Knowledge is something you can never steal or take away. So, are experiences and inner beauty.

“No, Samana, I am not afraid of this. Did any Samana or Brahman ever fear, someone might come and grab him and steal his learning, and his religious devotion, and his depth of thought? No, for they are his very own, and he would only give away from those whatever he is willing to give and to whomever he is willing to give. Like this it is, precisely like this it is also with Kamala and with the pleasures of love. Beautiful and red is Kamala’s mouth, but just try to kiss it against Kamala’s will, and you will not obtain a single drop of sweetness from it, which knows how to give so many sweet things!”

Don’t judge anyone for what they have to offer to you. Everyone has something to offer that you may not ever know of.

“She beckoned him with her eyes, he tilted his head so that his face touched hers and placed his mouth on that mouth which was like a freshly cracked fig. For a long time, Kamala kissed him, and with a deep astonishment Siddhartha felt how she taught him, how wise she was, how she controlled him, rejected him, lured him, and how after this first one there was to be a long, a well ordered, well tested sequence of kisses, everyone different from the others, he was still to receive. Breathing deeply, he remained standing where he was, and was in this moment astonished like a child about the cornucopia of knowledge and things worth learning, which revealed itself before his eyes.”

All there is is pain.

He saw mankind going trough life in a childlike or animallike manner, which he loved and also despised at the same time. He saw them toiling, saw them suffering, and becoming gray for the sake of things which seemed to him to entirely unworthy of this price, for money, for little pleasures, for being slightly honoured, he saw them scolding and insulting each other, he saw them complaining about pain at which a Samana would only smile, and suffering because of deprivations which a Samana would not feel.

Death is the truth that you can never run from.

Was it not due to this death, that he was now like a child, so full of trust, so without fear, so full of joy?

You have to be able to give up what you love to get what you truly need. You cannot understand the true nature if you keep restricting yourself from the world. You have to face it all one at a time.

Now he saw it and saw that the secret voice had been right, that no teacher would ever have been able to bring about his salvation. Therefore, he had to go out into the world, lose himself to lust and power, to woman and money, had to become a merchant, a dice-gambler, a drinker, and a greedy person, until the priest and Samana in him was dead. Therefore, he had to continue bearing these ugly years, bearing the disgust, the teachings, the pointlessness of a dreary and wasted life up to the end, up to bitter despair, until Siddhartha the lustful, Siddhartha the greedy could also die. He had died, a new Siddhartha had woken up from the sleep.

Most of all, he learned from it to listen, to pay close attention with a quiet heart, with a waiting, opened soul, without passion, without a wish, without judgement, without an opinion.

No, there was no teaching a truly searching person, someone who truly wanted to find, could accept. But he who had found, he could approve of any teachings, every path, every goal, there was nothing standing between him and all the other thousand any more who lived in that what is eternal, who breathed what is divine.

Love and kindness not given without attachment is bondage. Don’t justify yourselves every time. There are sides of story you unravel and know. Just the right words and right actions don’t create right outcomes for everyone.

I knew it. You don’t force him, don’t beat him, don’t give him orders, because you know that ‘soft’ is stronger than ‘hard’, Water stronger than rocks, love stronger than force. Very good, I praise you. But aren’t you mistaken in thinking that you wouldn’t force him, wouldn’t punish him? Don’t you shackle him with your love? Don’t you make him feel inferior every day, and don’t you make it even harder on him with your kindness and patience? Don’t you force him, the arrogant and pampered boy, to live in a hut with two old banana-eaters, to whom even rice is a delicacy, whose thoughts can’t be his, whose hearts are old and quiet and beats in a different pace than his? Isn’t forced, isn’t he punished by all this?

You readily leave your parents to search for yourself but hesitate to leave your children to search for themselves.

Siddhartha stopped, he bent over the water, in order to hear even better, and he saw his face reflected in the quietly moving waters, and in this reflected face there was something, which reminded him, something he had forgotten, and as he thought about it, he found it: this face resembled another face, which he used to know and love and also fear. It resembled his father’s face, the Brahman. And he remembered how he, a long time ago, as a young man, had forced his father to let him go to the penitents, how he had bed his farewell to him, how he had gone and had never come back. Had his father not also suffered the same pain for him, which he now suffered for his son? Had his father not long since died, alone, without having seen his son again? Did he not have to expect the same fate for himself? Was it not a comedy, a strange and stupid matter, this repetition, this running around in a fateful circle?

Goals lead to suffering. Only way to truly live is to be here and now, right in this moment. You don’t bring old memories flooding to your brain or desire to create anything for the future.

Each one heading for his goal, each one obsessed by the goal, each one suffering. The river sang with a voice of suffering, longingly it sang, longingly, it flowed towards its goal, lamentingly its voice sang.

You reach a goal and create a new one. In this process, your suffering just changes forms but remains the same.

The image of his father, his own image, the image of his son merged, Kamala’s image also appeared and was dispersed, and the image of Govinda, and other images, and they merged with each other, turned all into the river, headed all, being the river, for the goal, longing, desiring, suffering, and the river’s voice sounded full of yearning, full of burning woe, full of unsatisfiable desire. For the goal, the river was heading, Siddhartha saw it hurrying, the river, which consisted of him and his loved ones and of all people, he had ever seen, all of these waves and waters were hurrying, suffering, towards goals, many goals, the waterfall, the lake, the rapids, the sea, and all goals were reached, and every goal was followed by a new one, and the water turned into vapour and rose to the sky, turned into rain and poured down from the sky, turned into a source, a stream, a river, headed forward once again, flowed on once again. But the longing voice had changed. It still resounded, full of suffering, searching, but other voices joined it, voices of joy and of suffering, good and bad voices, laughing and sad ones, a hundred voices, a thousand voices.

In searching, you discard everything that’s around except the one you are looking for. In finding, you are open and see everything there is.

“When someone is searching,” said Siddhartha, “then it might easily happen that the only thing his eyes still see is that what he searches for, that he is unable to find anything, to let anything enter his mind, because he always thinks of nothing but the object of his search, because he has a goal, because he is obsessed by the goal. Searching means: having a goal. But finding means: being free, being open, having no goal. You, oh venerable one, are perhaps indeed a searcher, because, striving for your goal, there are many things you don’t see, which are directly in front of your eyes.

Knowledge can be conveyed, but not wisdom. It can be found, it can be lived, it is possible to be carried by it, miracles can be performed with it, but it cannot be expressed in words and taught.

Love everything for what it is: not for what it was or what it will become.

But today I think: this stone is a stone, it is also animal, it is also god, it is also Buddha, I do not venerate and love it because it could turn into this or that, but rather because it is already and always everything— and it is this very fact, that it is a stone, that it appears to me now and today as a stone, this is why I love it and see worth and purpose in each of its veins and cavities, in the yellow, in the gray, in the hardness, in the sound it makes when I knock at it, in the dryness or wetness of its surface.

True teachings are expressed without words.

Therefore, teachings are no good for me, they have no hardness, no softness, no colours, no edges, no smell, no taste, they have nothing but words.

Knowledge is so strange that the giver also doesn’t know what he/she/it is giving away.

A thought, it might be so. I must confess to you, my dear: I don’t differentiate much between thoughts and words. To be honest, I also have no high opinion of thoughts. I have a better opinion of things. Here on this ferry-boat, for instance, a man has been my predecessor and teacher, a holy man, who has for many years simply believed in the river, nothing else. He had noticed that the river’s spoke to him, he learned from it, it educated and taught him, the river seemed to be a god to him, for many years he did not know that every wind, every cloud, every bird, every beetle was just as divine and knows just as much and can teach just as much as the worshipped river

I’m only interested in being able to love the world, not to despise it, not to hate it and me, to be able to look upon it and me and all beings with love and admiration and great respect.

Truth has no words or sentences. It creates a projection when it is conveyed with words. Sometimes, the projection represents most of the truth, sometimes less but it can never represent the whole of it.

But this very thing was discovered by the exalted one to be a deception. He commands benevolence, clemency, sympathy, tolerance, but not love; he forbade us to tie our heart in love to earthly things.” “I know it,” said Siddhartha; his smile shone golden. “I know it, Govinda. And behold, with this we are right in the middle of the thicket of opinions, in the dispute about words. For I cannot deny, my words of love are in a contradiction, a seeming contradiction with Gotama’s words. For this very reason, I distrust in words so much, for I know, this contradiction is a deception. I know that I am in agreement with Gotama. How should he not know love, he, who has discovered all elements of human existence in their transitoriness, in their meaninglessness, and yet loved people thus much, to use a long, laborious life only to help them, to teach them! Even with him, even with your great teacher, I prefer the thing over the words, place more importance on his acts and life than on his speeches, more on the gestures of his hand than his opinions. Not in his speech, not in his thoughts, I see his greatness, only in his actions, in his life.

Kindle highlights (2020)

  • loc 899 - She taught him, that lovers must not part from one another after celebrating love, without one admiring the other, without being just as defeated as they have been victorious, so that with none of them should start feeling fed up or bored and get that evil feeling of having abused or having been abused.

  • loc 953 - And there were many who came to him, many to do business with him, many to cheat him, many to draw some secret out of him, many to appeal to his sympathy, many to get his advice. He gave advice, he pitied, he made gifts, he let them cheat him a bit, and this entire game and the passion with which all people played this game occupied his thoughts just as much as the gods and Brahmans used to occupy them.

  • loc 966 - “You are like me, you are different from most people. You are Kamala, nothing else, and inside of you, there is a peace and refuge, to which you can go at every hour of the day and be at home at yourself, as I can also do. Few people have this, and yet all could have it.”

  • loc 1714 - Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was. It was nothing but a readiness of the soul, an ability, a secret art, to think every moment, while living his life, the thought of oneness, to be able to feel and inhale the oneness. Slowly this blossomed in him, was shining back at him from Vasudeva’s old, childlike face: harmony, knowledge of the eternal perfection of the world, smiling, oneness.

  • loc 1856 - Wisdom which a wise man tries to pass on to someone always sounds like foolishness

  • loc 1859 - Knowledge can be conveyed, but not wisdom. It can be found,

  • loc 1918 - Let the things be illusions or not, after all I would then also be an illusion, and thus they are always like me. This is what makes them so dear and worthy of veneration for me: they are like me. Therefore, I can love them. And this is now a teaching you will laugh about: love, oh Govinda, seems to me to be the most important thing of all. To thoroughly understand the world, to explain it, to despise it, may be the thing great thinkers do. But I’m only interested in being able to love the world, not to despise it, not to hate it and me, to be able to look upon it and me and all beings with love and admiration and great respect

item.title: No Excuses The Power of Self Discipline
item.description:
• Self Discipline

Circumstances do not make the man; they merely reveal him to himself. – Epictetus

Hold yourself responsible for a higher standard than anyone else expects of you. Never excuse yourself. Never pity yourself.

What you do speaks so loudly that I cannot hear a word that you say.

In reading the lives of great men, I found that the first victory they won was over themselves; self discipline with all of them came first. –Harry S. Truman
item.content:
• Self Discipline

Circumstances do not make the man; they merely reveal him to himself. – Epictetus

Hold yourself responsible for a higher standard than anyone else expects of you. Never excuse yourself. Never pity yourself.

What you do speaks so loudly that I cannot hear a word that you say.

In reading the lives of great men, I found that the first victory they won was over themselves; self discipline with all of them came first. –Harry S. Truman

  • Whenever you act in a way that is consistent with your values, you feel good about yourself. When you compromise your values, you feel bad about yourself.

  • Losers make excuses; Winners make progress. When you find yourself making an excuse, how do you find if it’s valid or not? You just look for people who made that same excuse and is successful anyway.

  • You have to be a different person well above the average to become successful.

Self discipline is the ability to do what you should do, when you should do it, whether you feel like it or not.

  • Path of Least Resistance

    • You come office at the last minute and leave at the first opportunity.
    • Get rich quick schemes and Easy Money.

  • Your ability to do what is necessary and right before you do what is fun and easy is the key to creating an wonderful future.

“Law of Perverse Consequences,” which says that “a short-term action aimed at immediate gratification can lead to perverse, or the opposite, consequences from those at which it was aimed.”

Successful people make a habit of doing the things that unsuccessful people don’t like to do.

  • Successful people : “Pleasing Results” Unsuccessful ones: “Pleasing methods”
  • The more you practice self-mastery and self-control, the more you like and value yourself. The more you practice self-discipline, the better is your image. Thus, self-discipline and self-esteem have a direct relationship.

The first and best victory is to conquer self. – Plato

General Definition of Success: Being able to live your life in your own way, doing only those things that you want to do, with the people you choose, in the situations you desire.

  • To achieve success, you must determine how success is achieved in that area and practice those skills and activities repeatedly until you achieve the same results.

There are only three requirements for success. First, decide exactly what it is you want in life. Second, determine the price that you are going to have to pay to get the things you want. And third, and this is most important, resolve to pay that price.

  • Continually upgrading your skills is like physical fitness. If you stop exercising, you don’t maintain the fitness at the same level.

To become someone that you have never been before, you must do something that you have never done before.

  • Self-ideal is composed of those values that you most admire in others and most aspire to possess in yourself.
  • Weak and irresolute people are fuzzy and unclear about their values.
  • When you see yourself as calm, positive, truthful, and possessed of high character, you behave with greater strength and personal power.
  • Your self-esteem is defined as “how much you like yourself” but it’s more than this. It’s that when you consider yourself important and worthwhile, you will treat others as important as well.
  • Role models have tremendous impact on shaping your character. More you admire someone and their qualities, more you try to become like them consciously and unconsciously.
  • Failure to accept responsibility undermines your character and weaken your resolve.
  • All negative emotions, depend for their very existence on your ability to blame someone or something else for something in your life that you are not happy about.
  • Your intelligence is like a double-edged sword. You can use your intelligence to rationalize, justify, and blame others, or you can use it to find reasons why you are responsible and take the action to resolve the situation.

Importance of written goals and plans

  • Only 3% of adults have written goals and plans, and this 3% earn more than all of the other 97% put together.
  • Act of writing forces you to think and concentrate.
  • Aristotle wrote that humans are teleological organisms, meaning they are purpose driven.
  • Many people are hesitant to even set goals. You don’t have to figure out the way before you set a goal.

Process

There are no unrealistic goals; there are only unrealistic deadlines.

The biggest goal can be accomplished if you just break it down into small enough steps.

Thoughts are causes, conditions are effects.

We are what we repeatedly do; excellence then is not an act but a habit.

  1. Decide exactly what you want.
  2. Write it down.
  3. Set a deadline for your goal.
  4. Everything you think you can do to achieve that goal.
  5. List of obstacles, additional knowledge and skills required.
  6. List of people whose support you will require.
  7. Do something every day that moves you in the direction of the major goal.[ Momentum ]
  8. Resolution that you will work as long and as hard as you can to achieve it.

Upping your skills

The fact that some have become wealthy is proof that others may do it as well. – Abraham Lincoln

The very best proof that something can be done is that someone else has already done it.

If you are not getting better, you are getting worse.

  • Not only asking for feedback is good. Taking action on the advice and reporting back to them is amazing.
  • For long term success, invest 3% of your income back to yourself.

Examples of how to be better

  1. Invest the first hour of the day reading something educational, motivational, or spiritual.
  2. Rewrite your goals everyday without looking back at what you wrote the previous day.
  3. Read sixty minutes in your field each day.
  4. Listen to educational audio programs in your car.
  5. Attend courses and seminars in your field regularly.
  6. Getting better at your key tasks.
  7. Plan every day in advance. Make list and priorities before you start off.

Courage to concentrate

Courage is not absence of fear; it is control of fear, mastery of fear.

Courage is rightly considered the foremost of the virtues, for upon it, all others depend. –Winston Churchill

To develop a quality that you lack, act as if you already had that ability in every situation where it is called for. –Aristotle

Law of Reversibility: If you feel a certain way, you will act in a manner consistent with that feeling.

No one can make you feel inferior without your consent. –Eleanor Roosevelt

I have worried about a lot of things in life, and most of them never happened. –Mark Twain

  • The brave person disciplines himself to confront, deal with, and act in spite of the fear.
  • Fear makes heart pound, mouth and throat go dry, make stomach churn, and feel like getting up and running to the bathroom.
  • Have affirmation, visualization, and acting help you to have the quality you desire.
  • You stand up straight, smile, move quickly and confidently, and in every respect act as if you already had the courage that you desire.
  • 100-Call Method: Salesperson way of training themselves. Calling prospects without caring at all whether or not he makes a sale.
  • According to The Book of Lists, 54 percent of adults rate the fear of public speaking ahead of the fear of death.
  • Systematic Desensitization: Slowly facing fears comfortably to get over a great fear.
  • When you back away from a fear-inducing situation or person, your fear grows larger and larger.
  • The most common quality of leaders is vision and then second most important one is courage. Leaders have the courage to do whatever is necessary to fulfill that vision.
    • Courage to launch " Going all in "
    • Courage to hang in there and continue fighting.

Dealing with fear and setbacks

Persistence is its own reward. Every time you persist, you feel happier and satisfied about yourself.

When god wants to send you a gift, he wraps it up in a problem. The bigger the gift that God wants to send you, the bigger the problem he wraps it up in. –Normal Vincent Peale

Within every problem or obstacle lays the seed of an equal or greater opportunity or benefit. Your job is to find it.

  • 99% of the things that you worry about never happen. And most of the things that do happen, happen so quickly that you don’t have time to worry about them in the first place.
  • Doing each task you face “the persistence test” where you face the failure, setback or problem. When this happens, you should remind yourself that it’s the “testing time”.
  • Optimism: Having a boundless confidence in yourself and your ability to ultimately succeed. For being optimistic, you must control and discipline your thinking when things go wrong.

Creating disaster report

  1. Define the worry situation.
  2. Identify the worst possible outcome.
  3. Resolve to accept the worst possible outcome.
  4. Begin immediately to improve on the worst.

Using your time to your best

The very worst use of time is to do very well what need not be done at all. – Brian Tracy

  • Calculate your hourly rate. Resolve to do only those things that pay you your hourly rate or better.
  • Key to doubling your productivity and output: When you work, you work. Don’t waste your time.
  • Being surrounded by time-wasting people and situations, it takes tremendous self-discipline to work all the time you are at work.
  • When you are done with your work, ask for more responsibility.
  • Asking for responsibilities and getting things done fast will build a reputation like no other.
  • Come in a little earlier, work a little harder, and stay a little later.
  • Ask each morning " Do I look like one of the top people in my field? " If the answer is NO, keep changing until you look like one of the top people in your business.

Being a leader

  • Vision and Clarity of Vision.
  • Self-discipline, willpower, self-control, and self-mastery.
    • Complete control over himself and of every situation.
  • Responsible for what is to be done rather than how it is to be done.
  • Accept responsibility for results.
  • Your behavior influences and affects everyone else.
  • Positive, Upbeat and Confident.
  • Sets standards for organization’s behavior, quality of work, personal organization, time management, and appearance.
  • Person everyone looks up to and wants to emulate.
  • Everyone should know what leader and the company stand for.
  • Continually encouraging people to find better, faster, cheaper and easier way to do what’s being done in the company.
  • Consistent, dependable, reliable, calm, and predictable in all situations.
    • Not blown away by every storm that comes.
  • Fears and misgivings private.
  • Plan, prepare, organize, and check every detail. Take nothing for granted.
  • Intensely action-oriented.

Self discipline in business

Errant failures lie at the root of every failure. –Peter Drucker

Success is the ability to go from failure to failure with no loss of enthusiasm. –Winston Churchill

  • First law of economics is scarcity and first law of business is competition.
  • False assumptions or incorrect conclusions can lead to business failure.
  • It is not unusual for an entrepreneur to be wrong 90% of the time in the beginning of his career.
  • Most entrepreneurs fail and underachieve because they lack discipline to study every aspect of the business before committing to it, testing their assumptions than jumping to conclusions and so on.
  • The key to long-term profitability is recommendations and referrals.
  • CAMEI : Continuous and Never Ending Improvement
  • To succeed in business, you need to be proactive rather than reactive. You need to focus on solutions rather than problems.
  • Every time you have to ask yourself if the thing you are doing right now is leading to a sale. If the answer is “NO”, stop everything and turn attention towards sales generation.
  • Focus on calling customers in one geographical region in one go.

Financial Independence

  • You need to rewire your attitude towards money first.
  • You need to program your subconscious mind to remove the connection between “spending” and “happiness”.
  • Financial advisors suggest that you need to save 15% to 20% of your income in order to achieve all your financial goals.
  • Everyone has increased income but using Parkinson’s law: Expenditures rise to meet income. And that money is never enough.
  • You need to have self-discipline combined with the ability to delay gratification in order to be financially independent.
  • Some things you do are 5 to 10 times more valuable than other things, even though they take the same number of minutes and hours.
  • Companies invest financial capital but individuals invest “human capital”.

Prioritizing Tasks

Law of Forced Efficiency: There is never enough time to do everything, but there is always enough time to do the most important things.

Experience is not what happens to a man; it is what a man does with what happens to him.

  • Before you commit to an activity, “Is this the very best use of my time?”
  • You should not just set priorities but posteriorities as well. These are things you do less of or later.
  • Task Classification:
    • A: Must do “Serious consequences for non-completion”
    • B: Should do “Mild consequences”
    • C: Nice to do “No consequences whether you do it or not”
    • D: Delegate “Everything you can to free up”
    • E: Eliminate “Discontinue all tasks that are no longer essential”
  • It takes tremendous amount of self-discipline to select your most important task and then to start on that task rather than doing anything else. Doing the most important task makes you feel positive and increases your self-esteem.

Solving Problems Effectively

You feel happy to the degree to which you feel you are in control of your own life.

  • Self actualization is the feeling that you are becoming everything you are capable of becoming.
  • The wonderful thing about self-actualization needs is that they can never be completely satisfied. As you strive with life and do more than before, you experience a steady flow of happiness and contentment.
  • Listen to people as if the other person is about to reveal a great secret and you will hear it only once.
  • Pause before replying is the single most important thing you can do to be a good listener.
  • Ask for clarification: Questions to the person who is speaking is great way to show your genuine appreciation for what the other person is telling you about.
  • Feed it back: Simply replying with their words in the end makes sure that you had listened.
  • If you want to have a friend, you must first be a friend. If you want people to like you, you should first like them.
  • The chief cause of negative emotions and the primary destroyer of inner peace is blame.
  • The second root cause of blaming is justification. You justify that you are entitled to be angry or upset.

Forgiveness

The Law of Forgiveness: You are mentally and emotionally healthy to the degree that you can freely forgive anyone who has hurt you in any way.

  • Forgiveness is a purely selfish act. Forgiveness has nothing whatever to do with the other person. You forgive others so that you yourself can be free of that emotional baggage.

item.title: Rig Veda
item.description:
1. Rig Veda is the oldest existing text in any Indo-European language.

Rig Veda was composed around 1700 BC with the oldest parts as early as 2000 BC. There is still no fixed time when it was first composed. The time expressed is based on the events that are described in this book.

  1. Rig Veda is the world’s oldest religious text in continuous use. 4000 years of unbroken tradition is something worth venerable.

  2. The Rig Veda was not written down until about 500 AD.
item.content:
1. Rig Veda is the oldest existing text in any Indo-European language.

Rig Veda was composed around 1700 BC with the oldest parts as early as 2000 BC. There is still no fixed time when it was first composed. The time expressed is based on the events that are described in this book.

  1. Rig Veda is the world’s oldest religious text in continuous use. 4000 years of unbroken tradition is something worth venerable.

  2. The Rig Veda was not written down until about 500 AD.

From 2000 BC till 1900, Rig Veda was transmitted orally from generation to generation by Brahmins.

  1. The Rig Veda is organized as Mandala (books), sukta (hymns) and riks (prayers). There are total of 10 mandalas, 1028 hymns and 10552 riks.

item.title: Essentialism
item.description:
Summary

  • Our generation is unprepared of the wide availability of choices and has become overwhelmed with it. “Decision Fatigue” is widespread now.
  • Connectedness <–> Social Pressure
  • Opinion Overload but not just Information Overload
  • Priority word means the very first thing but over the last 150 years, we pluralized the word.
  • Don’t force execution: instead create system to remove obstacles to make execution smooth and easy.
  • By trying to operate with incompatible strategies, you undermine your ability to be competitive as done by Airlines Companies mentioned in the story.
  • Saying YES now, you miss out on something meaningful later if you say YES just out of the fear of missing out.
  • Latin word for decision is “cis/cid” that forms the base of the word decision means “to cut or to kill”
  • In modern times, the work boundary has encroached the family territory and it’s yours to manage it.
  • Boundaries if you break them once are like sandcastle. You will be expected to break them again and again. So, stick to them.

Endowment Effect

Tendency to undervalue things that aren’t ours and overvalue things because we already own them. Sunk Cost Bias: More money you invest, more you want to invest even if it’s losing you money.

Summary

  • Our generation is unprepared of the wide availability of choices and has become overwhelmed with it. “Decision Fatigue” is widespread now.
  • Connectedness <–> Social Pressure
  • Opinion Overload but not just Information Overload
  • Priority word means the very first thing but over the last 150 years, we pluralized the word.
  • Don’t force execution: instead create system to remove obstacles to make execution smooth and easy.
  • By trying to operate with incompatible strategies, you undermine your ability to be competitive as done by Airlines Companies mentioned in the story.
  • Saying YES now, you miss out on something meaningful later if you say YES just out of the fear of missing out.
  • Latin word for decision is “cis/cid” that forms the base of the word decision means “to cut or to kill”
  • In modern times, the work boundary has encroached the family territory and it’s yours to manage it.
  • Boundaries if you break them once are like sandcastle. You will be expected to break them again and again. So, stick to them.

Endowment Effect

Tendency to undervalue things that aren’t ours and overvalue things because we already own them. Sunk Cost Bias: More money you invest, more you want to invest even if it’s losing you money.

  • How to not be trapped in it?

    See ref:Endowment-Effect for what you need to change.

  • What you should know

    1. Admit failure to begin success
    2. Stop trying to force a fit
    3. Get a neutral second opinion

Status Quo Bias

Tendency to continue doing something simply because you have always done this way. People tend to use the expense limits set from previous year due to which they don’t have a lot of improvement over their expenses. Instead, a new concept can be used. “ZERO-BASED BUDGETING”: You don’t start the expense by subtracting from previous year’s but start a new from zero and keep adding to it. It detects exaggerated budget requests, finds out obsolete operations and be clearer in purpose in terms of expense involved.

Why Essentialism?

  • To choose how we spend our time and energy
  • Finding valuable things from noise
  • Trade-offs are real and we need to value them.

Essentialists explore more options than non-essentialists.

Questions you need to answer first

These questions are at the heart of essentialism. Ask yourself these questions first.

Saying YES or NO

We typically say YES to things to please people. But our highest contribution might be saying NO.

Lack of Clarity

  • Sort of Clear vs Really Clear is a difference that people don’t note much but matters a LOT.
  • Lack of clarity means people experience confusion, stress and frustration.
  • Ask “How will we know when we’re done?'”

  • What happens when teams lack clarity?

    1. Playing Politics: Trying to win the manager. Creating and focusing on social game’s goal rather than the actual task’s goal.
    2. Leaderless Teams: People start acting on their own short-term activities which in no way contribute to the overall goal they are working to achieve.

  • Example of a clear Vision

    • “To build 150 affordable, green, storm-resistant homes for families living in the Lower 9th Ward.” is example of mission statement that clarifies what the end outcome should be so that each task can be discriminated based on if it closes the gap between the goal and the current situation rather than saying “To help people after the disaster.”

Say NO without ruining things

  • Separate the decision from the relationship

    You make sure the NO is about the task at hand rather than about your relationship with the person.

  • Saying NO doesn’t mean you have to use word NO

    • I am flattered that you thought of me but I am currently occupied.
    • I would very much like to but I’m over-committed.

  • Focus more on the trade-off

    More you think about what you’re giving up when you say YES to someone, easier it is to say NO.

  • Remind yourself that everyone is selling something

    People get disappointed with you in the short-term but start respecting you for your honesty. Generally, people meet all YES people around and thus you stand different and tall in terms of respect.

  • Tips when saying NO

    1. Awkward Pause: 4 5 seconds.
    2. Soft No: “No but”
    3. Let me check my calendar and get back to you.
    4. Email Bouncebacks
    5. Say “Yes. What should I deprioritize?” Useful in office situations.
    6. Say it with humor.
    7. You are welcome to X. I am willing to Y. : Indirect way of saying I can’t do this specific thing for you.

The Law of Vital Few

  • Japan used to be like China back then with low-cost:low-quality goods.
  • Joseph Mures Buran did a quality control experiment in Japan.
  • By resolving tiny fraction of problems and improving things that were truly important, “Made in Japan” has a different meaning now.
  • This is also known as the famous “Pareto Principle” or the “80 / 20 rule”.

Warren Buffett’s Investments

  • Rather than make hundreds of right investment decisions, invest in only few that he was absolutely sure of and bet heavily on them.
  • Buffet owes his 90% of wealth to just 10 investments.

Changing Perspective

Go from “What do I have to give up?” ——>“What do I want to go big on?”

Go from “What will I say yes to?” ——-> “What will I say no to?”

“To attain knowledge, add things every day” ——> “To attain wisdom, subtract things every day.” -Lao Tzu

Reducing friction with other person: “What obstacles or bottlenecks are holding you back from achieving X, and how can I help remove these?”

Go from “How much do I value this item?” ——-> “If I did not own this item, how much would I pay to obtain it?”

Go from “How will I feel if I miss out on this opportunity?” ——> “If I did not have this opportunity, how much would I be willing to sacrifice in order to obtain it?”

Go from “I should say YES to this project because of following things.” —–> “If I wasn’t already involved in this project, how hard would I work to get on it?”

Explore

What must you build on and for your journey?

  • Set aside time to look and listen
  • Space to think
  • Permission to play
  • Wisdom to Sleep
  • Discipline to apply highly selective criteria to choices you make.

  • Examples

    • Newton’s uninterrupted space during the plague allowed him to explore the universe.
    • Bill Gates goes to read books for a week twice a year. No cellphones, No connection.

Being Playful

Being busy and being hard on yourself means you don’t understand where creativity flows in. You get insights when you truly enjoy something out of the task you were pondering about. You let go of the worries and actually find yourself thinking out of the box.

  • Example

    • Einstein credited more for his ability to imagine and fantasize more than for absorbing knowledge.

Hell Yeah or No

  • Examples

    • Derek Sivers : If you feel a total and utter conviction to do something, say HELL YEAH. Else it’s a NO.
    • Company that employs candidate based on his one day work in an office.

Eliminate

How to Eliminate?

  • Write down the opportunity.
  • Write down 3 Minimum Criteria to pass in order to be considered
  • Write down 3 Extreme/ Ideal Criteria to pass in order to be considered

  • Evaluation

    • If it doesn’t pass all 3 of the minimum criteria, drop it.
    • If it doesn’t pass any 2 of the extreme criteria, drop it this time too.

Ways to not commit instantly

  1. Stop making casual commitments
  2. Pause before you speak
  3. Get over the fear of missing out: Use Reverse Pilot

  • Reverse Piloting

    To test an assumption that something is invaluable, rather than asking if people need it: you remove it completely. If people notice it, it’s valuable. Otherwise it’s not.

Kinds of Boundaries

  • Why do you need boundaries?

    In the working world, people try to use our sprinklers to water their own grass all the time. This may come in the form of a boss who puts you on a committee for her pet project, a colleague who asks for your input on a report or presentation or proposal she hasn’t taken the time to perfect yet herself, or a colleague who stops you in the hallway and talks your ear off when you have an important meeting to get to or a vital phone call to make or critical work on your desk

  • Dealing with boundary issues

    • Don’t rob people of their problems

      • When people make their problem our problem, we aren’t helping them; we’re enabling them. Once we take their problem for them, all we’re doing is taking away their ability to solve it.

    • Find your dealbreakers

      You need to find yours first for yourself and others: it may seem unrealistic if you don’t know yourself. How will you expect other people to respect them or even figure them out?

    • Craft Social Contracts

      Even if there are personal differences between you and people you work with, have an understanding up front about how not to waste each other’s time and do what’s essential in a way that the task at hand demands.

Execute

Expecting the Unexpected using Buffers

  • Essentialist looks ahead: creates plans, contingencies, buffer for the unforseen.
  • Use good time to create buffer for the bad.

  • Example

    • Norway enormously benefited from windfall taxes from oil but invested much of it’s good fortune in endowment having a government fund of over $400 billions.
    • Amundsen when going to the South Pole had all contingencies ready. For e.g. Instead of having one tonnes of food, he had taken three and so on in many different aspects of his travel thus being successful in it.

  • Methods

    • Conduct Scenario Planning

      • What risks do you face on this project?
      • What is the worst-case scenario?
      • What would the social effects of this be?
      • What would the financial impact of this be?
      • How can you invest to reduce risks or strengthen financial or social resilience?

Constraints

  • Check over the constraints more than anything else.

  • Example

    • If you have slow walking person in a group, you make them walk on the front so that the whole group can walk as a group. Or more you can carry backpack among others to speed up the slowest one. So, instead of trying to improve every aspect you try to improve only that’s the most problematic.

Motivation

  • The most effective forms of human motivation is “PROGRESS”.
  • Focus on minimum viable progress.
  • Do the minimum viable preparation.
  • Visually reward Progress

  • Example

    • Michael Phelps would be disciplined and visualize the whole competition end to end. He would do all the steps of the imagination as to feel that the final swimming is also a part of that one and did it as he dreamed of it.

Routines

  • Habit = Cue + Routine + Reward
  • Cue: Trigger that tells you to go to auto mode and choose habit to use.
  • Routine: Behavior itself
  • Reward: Figure out if this particular habit is worth remembering for the future.
  • Once the loop gets done multiple times, it strengthens itself.
  • So, rather than changing the habit : we need to find the cue that is triggering non essential activity and associate that same cue with something else.

  • Example

    • Every time you see McDonalds, you want to get a burger. Now, every time you see it, you just go and buy some fresh vegetables or eat some salad by the side. You change the cue to some new habit.

  • Mixing Up Routines

    • Jack Dorsey has his days labelled for different things such as Innovation, Business Meetings, Marketing and Growth and so on.

  • Tackle Your Routines One By One

    Often we feel the urge to change everything this very instant and slowly when we don’t do it as per expectations, we totally leave the process. So, go slow and go long.

Mindfulness

  • Kairos : Greek god for time that says opportune, right and different. It’s qualitative and experienced only in the moment itself.
  • Multitasking itself is not the enemy of Essentialism; pretending we can “multifocus” is.

  • How to be mindful?

    • Figure out what’s important right now
    • Get the future out of your head. Just note down what you want to achieve as a result of today so that you know it’s somewhere down and you don’t need to worry.

  • Pause that refreshes

    • Closing your eye after you come from work just before entering your home and taking a long breath can give you so much that you take a pause to not bring work pressures into home.

What being essentialist looks like?

“Once you become an Essentialist, you will find that you aren’t like everybody else. When other people are saying yes, you will find yourself saying no. When other people are doing, you will find yourself thinking. When other people are speaking, you will find yourself listening. When other people are in the spotlight, vying for attention, you will find yourself waiting on the sidelines until it is time to shine. While other people are padding their résumés and building out their LinkedIn profiles, you will be building a career of meaning. While other people are complaining (read: bragging) about how busy they are, you will just be smiling sympathetically, unable to relate. While other people are living a life of stress and chaos, you will be living a life of impact and fulfillment.”

Some essentialist tasks

  • Choosing to set aside a day in week to get free of social media
  • Choosing not to watch T.V. when traveling for business.

item.title: Flow
item.description:
• Flow State is such an interesting topic.
  • One of my best books.

Flow

- Intentionality - Phenomenology

  • Instinct
  • Psychic Entropy
  • 17 bits of information
  • 1/18 time to capture
  • Attention
  • Attention –> Self –> Attention
  • Same event –> Experiences differ for people
  • No threat and can fully attend towards moving to goal –> Optimal experience
  • Complexity: Differentiation + Integration
  • Differentiation: Individuality –> Egotism
  • Integration: Social –> No identity
  • Two facets of optimal experience:
    • Make environment work for you
    • Changing environment
  • May not be pleasurable at the time being –> Want to do it again –> Optimal
  • Our consciousness needs to grow complex
  • Pleasure from eating –> Pleasure is not complicated to achieve.
  • Child, Learning, Expression, Complexity
  • Optimal Flow tasks Features:
    • Can be completed.
    • Able to be concentrated into the task
    • Clear goals
    • Immediate feedback
  • Making optimal tasks:
    • Set overall goal + subgoals as much as feasible.
    • Way to measure progress
    • Keep concentrating on whatever is being done.
    • Make finer distinctions in challenges involved
    • Develop necessary skills to interact with opportunities available.
    • Keep raising stakes if it gets boring
  • How it looks like:
    • Deep effortless involvement
    • Exercise a sense of control over the actions
    • Concern for self disappears for now: gets stronger after the experience is over.
    • Sense of time is altered.
  • Competition: Good for skills perfection only
  • Enjoyment: Boredom vs Anxiety && Capacity to act vs Complexity
  • Relevant skills needed to cope with situation –> Complete absorption.
  • Exercise control in difficult situations –> Full attention
  • Surgeons <–> Heroine
  • Flow: Giving up control of psychic energy vs Unaware of body and mind
  • Sailor becomes the boat
  • Flow –> Self enriched by new skills and fresh achievements
  • Autotelic: Self goal –> Activity that is done such that doing itself is the reward.
  • Roger Caillois’s division of games:
    • Agon: Competition
    • Alea: Chance
    • Ilinx/Vertigo: Alter ordinary perception : Skydiving
    • Mimicry: Alternate realities (Arts)
  • Compete: Latin (Con petire –> To seek together)
  • Whatever the game, flow states:
    • Provide a sense of discovery
    • Creative feeling of transporting to new reality
    • Push to higher levels of performance
  • Anxious: Increase skills. Theoretically one can reduce challenges but once person knows that they exist, they can’t be ignored.
  • Family context promoting optimal experience:
    • Clarity of expectations and feedback from family interaction
    • Centering: Parents interested in concrete feelings and experiences rather than preoccupied with job or college.
    • Choice: Children should feel they have a lot of options to choose from including breaking parent’s rules as long as they are ready to face consequences.
    • Commitment: Trust that allows child to feel comfortable to set aside their defences and be un-self-consciously be involved in their interests.
    • Challenge: Increasingly complex opportunities for children
  • Enjoying leisures: Less expenditure, high investment of psychic energy. e.g Knitting, Gardening.
  • Avoiding chaos in consciousness: Habits that give control over mental processes to individuals rather than to some external source of simulation.
  • Remembering is enjoyable because it entails fulfilling a goal and so brings order to consciousness.
  • Rote learning and creativity are not opposites: original thinkers also have been known to have memorized music, poetry or historical info extensively.
  • Without the capacity to provide it’s own info, mind drifts into randomness.
  • Puns and double meanings can provide good training ground for children to understand the control of language and power of words.
  • If this is the case, history can do little to improve the quality of life. Knowledge that is seen to be controlled from the outside is acquired with reluctance, and it brings no joy.
  • Philebus:“The young man who has drunk for the first time from that spring is as happy as if he had found a treasure of wisdom; he is positively enraptured. He will pick up any discourse, draw all its ideas together to make them into one, then take them apart and pull them to pieces. He will puzzle first himself, then also others, badger whoever comes near him, young and old, sparing not even his parents, nor anyone who is willing to listen….”
  • “Blessed is he who has found his work; let him ask no other blessedness.”
  • People who can play with and transform opportunities in their surroundings are clearly more enjoyable than those who resign themselves to live with barren reality.
  • Important note: To enjoy agriculture one must play within a much longer time frame than in hunting: while the hunter may choose his quarry and method of attack several times each day, the farmer decides what crops to plant, where, and in what quantity only a few times each year.
  • Did you wish you had been doing something else?” The extent to which a person answers this with a no is generally a reliable indication of how motivated he or she is at the moment of the signal. The results showed that people wished to be doing something else to a much greater extent when working than when at leisure, and this regardless of whether they were in flow. In other words, motivation was low at work even when it provided flow, and it was high in leisure even when the quality of experience was low.
  • Conclusion: Thus we have the paradoxical situation: On the job people feel skillful and challenged, and therefore feel more happy, strong, creative, and satisfied. In their free time people feel that there is generally not much to do and their skills are not being used, and therefore they tend to feel more sad, weak, dull, and dissatisfied. Yet they would like to work less and spend more time in leisure.
  • Dissatisfaction with jobs [ American Study ]:
    • Lack of variety and challenge
    • Conflicts with other people on the job
    • Burnout: Too much stress, too little time to think for oneself and too little time to spend with family.
  • Ironically, jobs are actually easier to enjoy than free time, because like flow activities they have built-in goals, feedback, rules, and challenges, all of which encourage one to become involved in one’s work, to concentrate and lose oneself in it.
  • “The future,” wrote C. K. Brightbill, “will belong not only to the educated man, but to the man who is educated to use his leisure wisely.”
  • Adolescents: Need to learn to discipline themselves or difficulties in competitive environments. May not learn to enjoy leaving. Don’t acquire habit of finding challenges to find their potentials for growth.
  • Why meditate? “Whosoever is delighted in solitude,” goes the old saying that Francis Bacon repeated, “is either a wild beast or a god.”
  • Forcing children to all activities can be counterproductive after they start hating such activities.
  • Parents who enjoy leisure such as music, cooking, gardening are likely to have their children find similar activities challenging, attentive and making them grow.
  • Peer Learning
    • Lowest level: Get off of mental chaos for time being.
    • Highest level: Sense of enjoyment and growth.
  • Skills Classification:
    • Instrumental: Survival skills or intellectual tools or professional skills
    • Expressive skills: Attempt to externalize our subjective experiences such as music, painting, bowling etc.
  • Idea of modern marriage: Spouse as a friend: where you can let your guard down, share jokes, dance, sing and do more.
  • Friends: One who question dreams and desires, force to try new ways of being, expressively challenging.
  • Friends: Excitement, Discovery and Adventure.
  • Family and Relatives: Holidays and Vacations.
  • Hardships do not affect the possibility of having optimal experience Like Jesus Christ said, What does it benefit to man if he gains the entire world, but loses himself? I have tried first to conquer myself; I don’t care if I lose the world.
  • Person’s ability to cope with stress depends on:
    • External support / Social support : Family , Insurance, Friends.
    • Psychological resources: Intelligence, Personality, Education
    • Coping strategies
  • Strong sense of self:
    • Un-self-conscious self assurance: Implicit belief that destiny was in their own hands.
    • Focusing attention in the world: Transforming stress into enjoyable challenge.
    • Discovery of new solutions:
  • “AUTOTELIC SELF” is one that easily translates potential threats into enjoyable challenges, and therefore maintains its inner harmony. A person who is never bored, seldom anxious, involved with what goes on, and in flow most of the time may be said to have an autotelic self.
  • It does not matter where one starts—whether one chooses goals first, develops skills, cultivates the ability to concentrate, or gets rid of self-consciousness. One can start anywhere, because once the flow experience is in motion the other elements will be much easier to attain.
  • Not sufficient to learn how to control moment-by-moment states of consciousness. Necessary to have overall context of goals to make life senseful.
  • Few things are sadder than encountering a person who knows exactly what he should do, yet cannot muster enough energy to do it. “He who desires but acts not,” wrote Blake with his accustomed vigor, “breeds pestilence.”
  • Philosophies of giving meaning to life:
    • Sensate: Satisfy the senses. Playboy philosophy.
    • Ideational: Non material, Supernatural ends. Failure cannot be proved, so believer always believes he is right.
    • Idealistic: Advantages of both worlds.
  • Final step of flow: Turning away from self towards integration with other people and universal values. At this stage, enjoyment matters the most. Can encounter midlife crisis, career change, desperate straining against limitations of individual capability. Then lies the final step: Having discovered what one can and cannot do alone, merge with system larger than person: a cause, an idea or transcendental entity.
  • The inevitable consequence of equally attractive choices is uncertainty of purpose; uncertainty, in turn, saps resolution, and lack of resolve ends up devaluing choice.
  • Commitment to goals and rule it entails is easier when choices are few and clear.
  • Inner conflict: Result of competing claims on attention. Too many desires, too many incompatible goals trying to get the same psychic energy.
  • Putting end to conflict:
    • Vita Activa: life of action : Winston Churchill, Andrew Carnegie
    • Vita Contemplativa: Path of reflection
  • Making sense of life Action by itself is blind, reflection impotent.
  • Ask these questions :
    • Is this something I really want to do?
    • Is it something I enjoy doing?
    • Am I likely to enjoy it in the foreseeable future?
    • Is the price that I—and others—will have to pay worth it?
    • Will I be able to live with myself if I accomplish it?
  • It can happen only when the mind knows not only what is but also what could be. The more complex any system, the more room it leaves open for alternatives, and the more things can go wrong with it.
  • Disadvantage of rigorous search for purpose of life : Discovered life themes are fragile for a different reason: because they are products of a personal struggle to define the purpose of life, they have less social legitimacy; because they are often novel and idiosyncratic, they may be regarded by others as crazy or destructive.
  • So to extract meaning from a system of beliefs a person must first compare the information contained in it with his or her concrete experience, retain what makes sense, and then reject the rest.
  • A new religion per say If a new faith is to capture our imagination, it must be one that will account rationally for the things we know, the things we feel, the things we hope for, and the ones we dread. It must be a system of beliefs that will marshal our psychic energy toward meaningful goals, a system that provides rules for a way of life that can provide flow.

Kindle highlights (2020)

  • loc 392 - productive; better to face facts and take care to avoid becoming one of the statistics. There are figures that may be reassuring to some: for instance, in the past thirty years, we have doubled our per-capita use of

This challenge is both easier and more difficult than it sounds: easier because the ability to do so is entirely within each person’s hands; difficult because it requires a discipline and perseverance that are relatively rare in

  • loc 428 - She has to develop the ability to find enjoyment and purpose regardless of external circumstances. This challenge is both easier and more difficult than it sounds: easier because the ability to do so is entirely within each person’s hands; difficult because it requires a discipline and perseverance that are relatively rare in any era, and perhaps especially in the present.

  • loc 449 - Practically every desire that has become part of human nature, from sexuality to aggression, from a longing for security to a receptivity to change, has been exploited as a source of social control by politicians,

  • loc 452 - It is important to realize that seeking pleasure is a reflex response built into our genes for the preservation of the species, not for the purpose of our own personal advantage.

  • loc 462 - The only authority many people trust today is instinct. If something feels good, if it is natural and spontaneous, then it must be right. But when we follow the suggestions of genetic and social instructions without question we relinquish the control of consciousness and become helpless playthings of impersonal forces.

  • loc 470 - Submission to genetic programming can become quite dangerous, because it leaves us helpless. A person who cannot override genetic instructions when necessary is always vulnerable.

  • loc 475 - He may encounter thousands of potentially fulfilling experiences, but he fails to notice them because they are not the things he desires.

  • loc 488 - The most important step in emancipating oneself from social controls is the ability to find rewards in the events of each moment. If a person learns to enjoy and find meaning in the ongoing stream of experience, in the process of living itself, the burden of social controls automatically falls from one’s shoulders.

  • loc 499 - Marcus Aurelius wrote: “If you are pained by external things, it is not they that disturb you, but your own judgment of them. And it is in your power to wipe out that judgment now.”

  • loc 502 - The oracle’s advice in ancient Delphi, “Know thyself,” implied it.

  • loc 506 - The last great attempt to free consciousness from the domination of impulses and social controls was psychoanalysis; as Freud pointed out, the two tyrants that fought for control over the mind were the id and the superego, the first a servant of the genes, the second a lackey of society—both representing the “Other.” Opposed to them was the ego, which stood for the genuine needs of the self connected to its concrete environment.

  • loc 598 - Neuroscience, neuroanatomy, cognitive science, artificial intelligence, psychoanalysis, and phenomenology are some of the most directly relevant fields to choose from; however, trying to summarize their findings would result in an account similar to the descriptions the blind men gave of the elephant: each different, and each unrelated to the others.

  • loc 603 - I believe to be the clearest way to examine the main facets of what happens in the mind, in a way that can be useful in the actual practice of everyday life, is “a phenomenological model of consciousness based on information theory.” This representation of consciousness is phenomenological in that it deals directly with events—phenomena—as we experience and interpret them, rather than focusing on the anatomical structures, neurochemical processes, or unconscious purposes that make these events possible.

  • loc 609 - Yet in contrast to pure phenomenology, which intentionally excludes any other theory or science from its method, the model we will explore here adopts principles from information theory as being relevant for understanding what happens in consciousness. These principles include knowledge about how sensory data are processed, stored, and used—the dynamics of attention and memory.

  • loc 618 - The events that constitute consciousness—the “things” we see, feel, think, and desire—are information that we can manipulate and use. Thus we might think of consciousness as intentionally ordered information.

  • loc 629 - We may call intentions the force that keeps information in consciousness ordered. Intentions arise in consciousness whenever a person is aware of desiring something or wanting to accomplish something. Intentions are also bits of information, shaped either by biological needs or by internalized social goals. They act as magnetic fields, moving attention toward some objects and away from others, keeping our mind focused on some stimuli in preference to others. We often call the manifestation of intentionality by other names, such as instinct, need, drive, or desire. But these are all explanatory terms, telling us why people behave in certain ways. Intention is a more neutral and descriptive term; it doesn’t say why a person wants to do a certain thing, but simply states that he does.

  • loc 649 - But there are enough exceptions in every culture to show that goals are quite flexible. Individuals who depart from the norms—heroes, saints, sages, artists, and poets, as well as madmen and criminals—look for different things in life than most others do.

  • loc 662 - At this point in our scientific knowledge we are on the verge of being able to estimate how much information the central nervous system is capable of processing. It seems we can manage at most seven bits of information—such as differentiated sounds, or visual stimuli, or recognizable nuances of emotion or thought—at any one time, and that the shortest time it takes to discriminate between one set of bits and another is about 1/18 of a second. By using these figures one concludes that it is possible to process at most 126 bits of information per second, or 7,560 per minute, or almost half a million per hour. Over a lifetime of seventy years, and counting sixteen hours of waking time each day, this amounts to about 185 billion bits of information. It is out of this total that everything in our life must come—every thought, memory, feeling, or action. It seems like a huge amount, but in reality it does not go that far.

  • loc 693 - Therefore, the information we allow into consciousness becomes extremely important; it is, in fact, what determines the content and the quality of life.

  • loc 704 - All these complex mental operations must be completed in a few seconds, sometimes in a fraction of a second. While forming such a judgment seems to be a lightning-fast reaction, it does take place in real time. And it does not happen automatically: there is a distinct process that makes such reactions possible, a process called attention. It is attention that selects the relevant bits of information from the potential millions of bits available. It

• Flow State is such an interesting topic.
  • One of my best books.

Flow

- Intentionality - Phenomenology

  • Instinct
  • Psychic Entropy
  • 17 bits of information
  • 1/18 time to capture
  • Attention
  • Attention –> Self –> Attention
  • Same event –> Experiences differ for people
  • No threat and can fully attend towards moving to goal –> Optimal experience
  • Complexity: Differentiation + Integration
  • Differentiation: Individuality –> Egotism
  • Integration: Social –> No identity
  • Two facets of optimal experience:
    • Make environment work for you
    • Changing environment
  • May not be pleasurable at the time being –> Want to do it again –> Optimal
  • Our consciousness needs to grow complex
  • Pleasure from eating –> Pleasure is not complicated to achieve.
  • Child, Learning, Expression, Complexity
  • Optimal Flow tasks Features:
    • Can be completed.
    • Able to be concentrated into the task
    • Clear goals
    • Immediate feedback
  • Making optimal tasks:
    • Set overall goal + subgoals as much as feasible.
    • Way to measure progress
    • Keep concentrating on whatever is being done.
    • Make finer distinctions in challenges involved
    • Develop necessary skills to interact with opportunities available.
    • Keep raising stakes if it gets boring
  • How it looks like:
    • Deep effortless involvement
    • Exercise a sense of control over the actions
    • Concern for self disappears for now: gets stronger after the experience is over.
    • Sense of time is altered.
  • Competition: Good for skills perfection only
  • Enjoyment: Boredom vs Anxiety && Capacity to act vs Complexity
  • Relevant skills needed to cope with situation –> Complete absorption.
  • Exercise control in difficult situations –> Full attention
  • Surgeons <–> Heroine
  • Flow: Giving up control of psychic energy vs Unaware of body and mind
  • Sailor becomes the boat
  • Flow –> Self enriched by new skills and fresh achievements
  • Autotelic: Self goal –> Activity that is done such that doing itself is the reward.
  • Roger Caillois’s division of games:
    • Agon: Competition
    • Alea: Chance
    • Ilinx/Vertigo: Alter ordinary perception : Skydiving
    • Mimicry: Alternate realities (Arts)
  • Compete: Latin (Con petire –> To seek together)
  • Whatever the game, flow states:
    • Provide a sense of discovery
    • Creative feeling of transporting to new reality
    • Push to higher levels of performance
  • Anxious: Increase skills. Theoretically one can reduce challenges but once person knows that they exist, they can’t be ignored.
  • Family context promoting optimal experience:
    • Clarity of expectations and feedback from family interaction
    • Centering: Parents interested in concrete feelings and experiences rather than preoccupied with job or college.
    • Choice: Children should feel they have a lot of options to choose from including breaking parent’s rules as long as they are ready to face consequences.
    • Commitment: Trust that allows child to feel comfortable to set aside their defences and be un-self-consciously be involved in their interests.
    • Challenge: Increasingly complex opportunities for children
  • Enjoying leisures: Less expenditure, high investment of psychic energy. e.g Knitting, Gardening.
  • Avoiding chaos in consciousness: Habits that give control over mental processes to individuals rather than to some external source of simulation.

  • Without the capacity to provide it’s own info, mind drifts into randomness.
  • Puns and double meanings can provide good training ground for children to understand the control of language and power of words.

  • Did you wish you had been doing something else?” The extent to which a person answers this with a no is generally a reliable indication of how motivated he or she is at the moment of the signal. The results showed that people wished to be doing something else to a much greater extent when working than when at leisure, and this regardless of whether they were in flow. In other words, motivation was low at work even when it provided flow, and it was high in leisure even when the quality of experience was low.
  • Conclusion: Thus we have the paradoxical situation: On the job people feel skillful and challenged, and therefore feel more happy, strong, creative, and satisfied.     • Lack of variety and challenge
    • Conflicts with other people on the job
    • Burnout: Too much stress, too little time to think for oneself and too little time to spend with family.

    • External support / Social support : Family , Insurance, Friends.
    • Psychological resources: Intelligence, Personality, Education
    • Coping strategies
  • Strong sense of self:
    • Un-self-conscious self assurance: Implicit belief that destiny was in their own hands.

  • It does not matter where one starts—whether one chooses goals first, develops skills, cultivates the ability to concentrate, or gets rid of self-consciousness. One can start anywhere, because once the flow experience is in motion the other elements will be much easier to attain.
  • Not sufficient to learn how to control moment-by-moment states of consciousness. Necessary to have overall context of goals to make life senseful.
  • Few things are sadder than encountering a person who knows exactly what he should do, yet cannot muster enough energy to do it. “He who desires but acts not,” wrote Blake with his accustomed vigor, “breeds pestilence.”

    • Sensate: Satisfy the senses. Playboy philosophy.

  • Making sense of life Action by itself is blind, reflection impotent.

    • Is this something I really want to do?
    • Is it something I enjoy doing?
    • Am I likely to enjoy it in the foreseeable future?
    • Is the price that I—and others—will have to pay worth it?
    • Will I be able to live with myself if I accomplish it?
